The first cycle was the method for those of superior faculties, wherein the provisional [teachings] were opened by directly establishing the three vehicles and the one vehicle.
The middle cycle explained them through the parables of the three carts and the one cart. Now, the Dharma is fundamentally not established for the sake of parables;

yet, because parables are employed to correspond to the gates of the Dharma, once the parable has successfully corresponded to the Dharma, it is said that the Dharma itself also functions as a parable. This is the original intent of the Dharma.

The analogy is indeed appropriate for what is identical; however, because the literary forms cannot always remain so, they may be extensive or concise, preceding or following, hidden or manifest, identical or different.
These appearances and disappearances, these combinations and transformations—this analogy and the Dharma are at times not perfectly aligned, for it is only their underlying meaning that matters.
If some would wish to regulate them into uniformity, how could this possibly be achieved?
If one understands this principle, how could the composition of such a text be difficult? For those who have not yet attained this understanding, I shall further elaborate upon it.

Now, literary compositions possess a method wherein metaphors and their meanings must necessarily correspond; by following what precedes and grounding what follows, the meaning of the metaphor becomes clear.

Thus, the seeker of the vehicle must first discuss what is appropriate for that pursuit—this is the core meaning of the "Seeking the Vehicle" chapter. This is the application of the "Light and Abiding" (Guangzhai) school.
Tiantai also employed this [method] and subsequently evaluated it, asking: "Wherein lie its strengths and weaknesses? He replied:
"The reason why the strengths and weaknesses differ despite the text being identical lies nowhere else than in whether one seeks through illumination or through verbal inquiry alone.

If one claims to seek directly within the 'small' [text] while remaining unaware of other underlying intentions, this is how Guangzhai failed. If one claims that although the mouth seeks the small..."
Since the capacity and inclination (*kāya-citta*) lie in the "Great," this is why Tiantai is considered to have attained [the truth].

If capacity and inclination lie in the Great, then the arousal of the capacity for the Mahāyāna is surely not other than the aspiration to seek the Buddha-way; this serves as the basis for the analogy. Therefore, the *Record* (*Ji*) also says the same. Furthermore, it states:
"If one says that the inclination seeks the Great, there is no error. It also says: "The first name is given because of the capacity for the Mahāyāna."
The movement [of the mind] serves as a later illustration for "seeking a vehicle," whereas the original text simply does not mention "seeking a small [vehicle]"; this is the evidence.

However, while the text merely describes the "small" and does not say "seek," this is intended to forcefully refute the interpretation of the ancients; it is not that such a meaning is entirely impossible.
One must understand that the single character "seek" (索) inherently contains this significance. If we discuss "verbal seeking," it precisely accords with the original intent.

The reason the text of the "Three Requests" was not adopted as the analogy is that it is intended to manifest how the full text inherently contains all three searches (*paryeṣaṇā*). Thus, the text concerning the "sentiments of the capacity" (*jīngqíng*) is taken as the analogy for the search;

fundamentally, if one were to follow the literal search from the mouth, there would be differences in what is spoken, and the Great and Small [Vehicles] would not coincide, which is why it was not adopted.
This is precisely why it was stated previously that the Dharma and the analogy may be the same or different—it is truly for this reason. Up to this point...

Regarding the three "seekings" (*suo*) explained in the Commentary, there are also differences between what is produced through the Dharma and through analogies; I shall now clarify them directly with two statements.

To speak of the reality of the matter, it is by relying on the Dharma that [the meaning] is clarified. For instance, in the passage explaining the aspiration for the Buddha-way, it says: "This is precisely seeking the Great, not seeking the small fruit.
It further states, "The seeking has three meanings," and so forth. This is because the analogy follows the Dharma; thus, when speaking of "seeking," one must first turn back to the Dharma.
This refers to the three requests. He relies exclusively on this passage to claim that the "mouthless begging" (*mukharahita-yācanā*) specifically points to the three requests;

this is because he fails to understand that the referents of the Dharma and the analogy are different. If one follows the literal text, it employs the metaphor to illustrate the actual reality, as is the case in the explanation of the passage concerning the begging for the carts.
Since it is spoken by way of a metaphor, how could one not apply the term "may you grant me" (*anuprayaccha*)?
As for the "search by mouth" (*kǒu-sò*) mentioned in the text, since its underlying mechanism and sentiment (*jī-qíng*) do not differ from what preceded, it is not treated separately.

If one speaks of the Dharma and the analogy together, it is as the text says: "Now, adding the search by mouth. (This is called "adding" because it involves both the previous mechanism and the two searches of sentiment; thus, it is said "addition.

Because [the Bodhisattvas] heard the initial verse of the "Expedient Means" chapter, their past doubts were stilled and moved, leading them to speak and make three requests. Furthermore, the search by mouth was originally...
In the analogy, the three requests made within the section on skillful means (*upāya*) are a transferred metaphor that follows from the Dharma.
Immediately following this, it says, "seeking the reality of what was previously taught. This "reality of what was previously taught" refers precisely to the three vehicles;

for one uses the Dharma to harmonize with the analogy, as there is nothing that is not sought through verbal inquiry. Without this demonstration, the meaning of the text would truly be difficult to clarify.
How could it be that after three earnest entreaties, he would instead seek only the former reality? This is the general outline of its characteristics.
Regarding the three meanings of "seeking the vehicle" (the latter part): Alas!
The doctrines handed down through tradition have misled people for a long time; this is certainly not limited to a single point. Let us now attempt [to explain] by means of...

To speak of this from a single perspective, regarding the discourse on seeking the small or large vehicle, since the time this difficulty first arose, it is unknown how much time has passed or how many people have spoken upon it.
Yet, none of them took the phrase "grant us [a vehicle]" as the text for seeking the small;
they seemed to believe that the karmic conditions were actually directed toward the Tathāgata himself when making this request. Thus, there are those who say one seeks the Great Vehicle.
The principle of non-returning pertains to the conditions of the faculties and dispositions; although there may be differences in opinion, the general conclusion is largely as stated above.

As for those who, finding themselves at a loss, claim that this text describes the Small Vehicle rather than seeking [the Great], these are all merely speculations based on empty echoes and are difficult to fully enumerate.
Yet they have never heard of one who uproots the foundation and blocks the source, cutting off the very root of what makes it difficult.
This is precisely because it has been shifted through the influence of traditional exegesis. To speak of it in the present context, this analogy was originally taught by the Tathāgata;
it was intended for those of middling capacity at the beginning of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, and thus it is appropriate that such a request should have been made.
Although its specific wording is not found in the sutra itself, since it was narrated by the Tathāgata, there is no harm in attributing it to Śāriputra.
The three requests all share this underlying intent: those of superior capacity abandon the small to seek the great, while those of middling capacity cling to the small while seeking the great.
Thus, it was necessary for the Tathāgata to employ these analogies; only then could Śāriputra’s merit from his universal exhortation be seen, as its grace would then moisten both himself and others.
Therefore, it is said that by making three requests, he sought the reality of what had been taught in the past; this is precisely the point.
Furthermore, it is said that the three "sought" (so) all strike upon the Ultimate Sage, and the "responding" (fu) is likewise distinguished as manifest or esoteric;

these are all instances where the capacity of the recipient and the response of the Buddha are darkly harmonized, such that the timing of their meeting is never mistaken. How could this be known by the masses of non-timely [beings], let alone by others, and let alone by those of future generations?
Discussing it from this perspective, how could the karmic conditions ever act as the "seeker" (so) themselves? Nevertheless, the *shu* (commentary) was composed.
This commentary merely arranges the sequence according to the textual order of the sūtra to conform with its established analogies; it does not claim that things are actually so.

The reason for discussing this is twofold: first, to rectify the errors of previous interpretations, and second, to show that this meaning already exists within the "three requests," thereby establishing that its source has a specific origin.
Nevertheless, when one examines the text, there are distinctions of greater and lesser significance. Now...
He resolved this by means of two points: first, that while their spoken words may differ, their underlying intent must be the same;

second, that when one speaks of the "Dharma," it follows from the "Great" (Mahāyāna), whereas the "Small" (Hīnayāna) serves as a metaphor. This is because those of superior faculties, having previously practiced the skillful means of hearing and cultivation, recognize that what they heard was not the ultimate truth.
Knowing that there is a "Great" [Vehicle] beyond this to be sought, they no longer hesitate, but immediately speak out to request the Great.
The principle regarding those of dull faculties in the intermediate stage is not thus: although they have heard and practiced the skillful means, they know them to be not ultimate;
yet, because what was previously taken as real is not easily forgotten, how could they still remain so hesitant regarding the true fruit now?

Because one seeks that which has been attained by examining that which was lost, one speaks of it as being "small. This dharma is used as an analogy for the distinction between the small and the great; therefore, it is called a "dharma."

It is said that those of superior faculties among the middling class awaken easily, and thus there is no parable of seeking a vehicle; whereas those of middling faculties remain deluded, and thus there is the parable of seeking a vehicle.

As for the question of why the seeking of a vehicle is sometimes present and sometimes absent, this is spoken specifically in reference to the Small and Great Vehicles. Therefore, the *Record* further states:
[and so forth]. This is the proof. Indeed, it is only when the capacities and dispositions are identical that one must rely on the oral teaching to fully manifest those capacities.

When the emotional disposition reaches the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, there is nothing that is not "Great. However, for those of superior faculties, the disposition and the expression are one, and thus their manifestation is easy to perceive.
For those of middling faculties, the expression and the disposition differ, and thus their intent is difficult to clarify.

Therefore, by employing a selection of examples to explain this, it is said: "[...]". The *Commentary* states that the present [passage] also illustrates this by citing the "Expedient Means" chapter (*Upāyakauśalya-parivarta*).

It is like a rope that possesses both [the physical cord and its function]; because its underlying principle (*jīng*) and its emotional expression (*qíng*) penetrate both the Great and the Small, it is said:

"In the past, Xu [Zhi] permitted three [vehicles]; was this not the Small? Yet he also attained the One; was this not the Great? To speak of the Great, the underlying principle and emotional expression must be identical;

to speak of the Small, there is a difference in what is expressed. Now, the meaning is elegantly consistent. Furthermore, when the *Jì* (Record) distinguishes between the provisional and the real, it says: "... and so forth.
If one attains what was intended by this text, it is not difficult; it merely consists of these two meanings.
However, because this discussion is presented according to the sequence of the "three searches" (sō), its sentiment encompasses both Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna as its distinction.

Thus, regarding what is called "borrowing from the mouth," did I not say previously that there are instances where words are spoken while the underlying intent is not necessarily so—is this not precisely "borrowing from the mouth"? This is still a matter of oral praise.

To disparage this in one’s heart is a grave error! Alas, regarding the meaning of "seeking the vehicle," although it is the essential principle of the structural framework of the *Lotus Sūtra* alone, many commentators have failed to apply their full hearts to it;
they speak in a fragmented and superficial manner, causing the sūtras and commentaries to all become inconsistent.
Thus, the great, pervasive intent of the Buddhas and Patriarchs is not seen—this is truly laughable and also lamentable.
Exploring the Profound Meaning of the Sūtras (Part 2, Upper) "Limiting" (*qi*) refers to delimiting what has been received;

it also means delimiting the stages already traversed. This refers to those of the Two Vehicles who receive the Small Teaching and pass through five periods. Alternatively, if "limiting" refers to the activities of the *nirmāṇakāya* (transformation body), it is both restricted and universal;

it is not limited solely to the transformation [body], for it extends beyond that limit. "Exploring" (*tan*) means passing beyond what was limited; this includes everything illuminated by the *dharmakāya* prior to the arising of the transformation. Although the time period is extended when exploring the Dharma, the Dharma itself does not differ from what was previously limited.
"Small [teachings] are small *cīvara*, and large [teachings] are large; all are encompassed by these two categories, hence they are called the 'two *cīvara*.
Regarding the so-called 'the two *cīvara* of *cīvara* and *tāpana* (investigation) in the *Fahua shuji* (Commentary on the Lotus Sutra), commentators consider this one of the most difficult points.
Upon examining the reasons for its difficulty, it is said to lie in the confusion of terminology and meanings, as well as the pervasive and restricted nature of the textual structures."

Regarding the relative scale of its sections, the opening and closing of its beginning and end, the unlocking of its internal and external relations, and the similarities and differences between its commentaries and sub-commentaries, it is difficult to reach a definitive judgment;
thus, debates on these matters have continued to swirl without resolution until the present day.

I once went to examine its text and found that it was indeed inconsistent and internally contradictory, such that I left it as something to be preserved without further discussion for a long time. Later, however, because...
On a day of leisure, I read the text three times; thereupon, my mind was suddenly relieved and my understanding became harmonious and smooth.
How could the previous sense of obstruction have remained? What was it that made this possible? He replied: "There is nothing else; it is simply a matter of beginning and end, priority and sequence.
All that was previously difficult arose because one prioritized the secondary and deferred to the primary, becoming confused by the superficial appearances of the text."
That which constitutes the present *Yi* (Exegesis) takes the fundamental first and the derivative second, providing a commentary based on the intent of the Sūtra.

As for this commentary based on the Sūtra’s intent, its text is fundamentally rooted in the "Chapter on Faith and Understanding" (*Śraddhābhūmi*), where the four great disciples, headed by Kāśyapa, having heard the parables, attained entry into the Great [Vehicle].
Once that was established, the parable of the "Poor Son" was set forth in full detail.

By examining the characteristics of the Tathāgata’s teaching from its inception to its conclusion, one can infer that his prior discernment was such that he perceived the reception of the Dharma would not be in vain;
thus, the Tathāgata further corroborated this through the Parable of the Medicinal Herbs.

This is, in brief, the manner in which teacher and disciple attained and shared their mutual understanding. According to the text, there are five sections, though they may be combined into four, as follows:
When father and son lose each other and meet again, they pursue, entice, and lead one another back; whatever they communicate is entirely a matter of leading.

However, when analyzed according to the categories of the Teaching Gate (Jiaomen), there are those that are "aligned" (*qi*) rather than "probed" (*tan*). These are precisely the two categories of "meeting" and "losing.

Although these belong to the time of being probed, the meaning of "probing and leading" has not yet been manifested; nevertheless, even speaking from the perspective of aligning with one's own portion, this is already so.

The inclusion of "investigation" (*tan*) within "receiving" (*ling*) is also a case of revealing what precedes by means of what follows; this is because, when discussing investigation, it reaches as far as the section on "inducing" (*youyin*).

Although there are instances where investigation is not [explicitly] "equal" (*qi*), the text adds the phrase "receiving and entrusting" (*lingfu*) following the passage on "other days," and both the topical headings and the concluding summaries of the commentary refer to "investigating and receiving" (*tanting*); thus, one knows that this is investigation rather than equality.

Although it is not a case of aligning the texts [of different schools], speaking from the perspective of what has been experienced within one's own domain, one may still align them in terms of comprehension, as that comprehension is already contained therein;
it is simply not a case of aligning one's own specific teaching. There are instances where one probes for both [aspects] simultaneously, such as the passage concerning "inducing" (*yòuyǐn*).

This refers to the very act of wishing to induce one's children and others toward comprehensive understanding. Furthermore, one may also probe for and comprehend [the meaning] at another time. This is also permissible.

Regarding the division into these preceding and succeeding sections [of "alignment" (*zhèi*) and "exploration" (*tàn*)], the reason they are so designated is that there can be no exploration without alignment;

thus, alignment comes first and exploration follows. This is precisely what the *Miaole* (The Wonderful Joy) means when it says that the sequence of alignment followed by exploration is explained according to the ritual of transformation (*huà-yí*).

Nevertheless, one must necessarily distinguish them in this way because alignment refers to the reception of the Dharma and the parable, while the Dharma and the parable are received only up to the point of this alignment.

The commentary states that this concludes the section on the "parable of the Dharma" (*dharmopama*), because for those of the Two Vehicles, the explicit text and complete meaning regarding their own realm and teaching were already established within the Deer Park.

Therefore, from this point onward, the opening of the investigation and the simultaneous comprehension of the subsequent flavor do not pertain to the "Dharma" or the "Parable. The commentary further states that this refers to "thoroughly knowing the family estate."

This is like the passage "this is not the collar and so forth," which serves as an illustration; furthermore, it may be said that while the text originates from this section, its meaning pervades both the beginning and the end.
Thus, the "equal collar" (齊領) applies not only to what precedes but also extends to what follows, and the "probing collar" (探領) applies not only to what follows but also extends to what precedes.

This is because, as in the subsequent *Tonglun* (Comprehensive Discussion), when one analyzes the text according to its topical divisions (*kejie*), the "equal collar" is restricted [to its specific section].

Regarding the Deer Park, there are those who claim it is "wondrous bliss" (*sukha*); thus, while the teaching is aligned with the *Zheng* (the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*) as a provisional reception, and specifically the initial stage of the gradual teaching, it nevertheless includes the *Avataṃsaka*, because the text is also traced alongside it and is provisionally aligned with the *Zheng*.
The "investigative reception" (*tantou ling*) is restricted to the four flavors (*catasraḥ paripācya-rasāḥ*), and the text does not involve the *Avataṃsaka*, as can be seen in the sūtra itself.
This is why I previously stated that, based on these preceding and succeeding sections, they are distinguished between the "Aligned" (*Qi*) and the "Investigative" (*Tan*).

There is indeed a profound reason why those who provide inducement encompass both [the *Śrīmālā-sūtra* and the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*]. Although the structural analysis (*ko-p'an*) is thus, there is no divergence in the essential intent of the sūtras;

whether categorized as "equal" (*ts'ai*) or analyzed as "probing" (*t'an*), both are equally applicable to the five periods. As for why the probing approach encompasses all five periods, the Commentary states:

"Probing and receiving the five flavors"—this passage is the source. One must still synthesize the discussion to fully perceive this meaning; since its probing already extends to the equal, how could it not...?

When a specific office presides over the five flavors, it may fear the teaching and resort to minor rebukes; yet when the teaching is transformed, is there anything that does not fall within one’s own domain?

What has been experienced—could this not be both uniform and pervasive? If this is so, then as for what are called the entanglements of names and meanings, or the variations in textual form and scope, there is nothing left to doubt.
Furthermore, if one understands this principle, then the Great and Small [vehicles] that one presides over can be followed accordingly.

How could "comprehensive understanding" (tong) necessarily involve raising difficulties based on the literal text? It should simply consist in identifying and determining the meaning according to the text.

Thus, when it is said that "comprehensive understanding is limited to the minor," this refers to the teaching of the *Samantapāsādikā* (the *Qi jing*). When it is said that it "penetrates the remaining flavors," this is explained from its own specific perspective.
Although both meanings are encompassed by "comprehensive understanding," they are what explain the name *Samantapāsādikā* through its concise dharma, concise principle, and concise person.

Regarding the three explanations, it is because of this. However, although what is received according to one’s own portion generally follows the Dharma from the person, one’s own realm remains restricted.
This is truly because "receiving in common" refers primarily to what is discussed in relation to oneself;

based on these four periods, one only receives the Small [Vehicle], and only upon reaching the point where one possesses the power capable of receiving the Great [Vehicle] does one receive it. This refers to the small and great [vehicles] received in common. As for "exploring and receiving," it is restricted.

Regarding the "lesser" [teachings], they should be explained according to their specific categories; regarding those that "pervade both the lesser and the greater," they are explained by combining the latter with the former.
Thus, while the preceding text corresponds to the general headings and correctly outlines the categories, this current passage speaks specifically of the "lesser. Therefore, it says:

"Taking the meaning, one understands that the stage of the Dharma-body has long been illuminated, and that skillful means were not first realized at the Bodhi tree. This explains the application of the "lesser" and so forth, as well as the text for future sections.

The intention is that because these two characters permeate all subsequent flavors, they are explained by means of three meanings. Since "it" (the other) refers generally to both the Great and Small Vehicles, it says:

"About to lead [beings] to the ground of the Dharma-body, long illuminating the capacities of both the Great and Small Vehicles, and bestowing transformations through 'one' and 'three'"—this is precisely that meaning.
Furthermore, if one discusses this from the perspective of equality and investigation, then what is led is no different in its universality or limitation from [the previous].

The preceding clarification is correct; however, because we are currently investigating the essential principles that ought to be discussed, the scope of what is grasped must be determined according to the Dharma, even though there are further distinctions within the "small" category.
Thus, one knows that the Master’s intention consists of both a general principle and a specific application, each having its own appropriate place, and is certainly not in vain.
Not knowing the underlying meaning, those who speak recklessly say: [the rest of the passage].
Investigating the Profound Meaning of the Sūtras (Part II):
Now, it is generally understood that words each have their proper application; this principle is relatively easy to clarify.

However, when speech fails to find its proper application—such as when a single phrase is delivered as a definitive instruction yet possesses the same literary form as an introductory exhortation—the distinction between them is vast.
The Master’s opening and closing discussions of this matter are, as in other writings, like a direct probe into the collar;
they merely provide a long-term perspective while explaining the three meanings of "self," "other," and so forth through both detailed and concise treatments.

That these points are reiterated throughout the *Shuji* (Commentary) represents the profound intent of the Patriarch, which is most difficult to comprehend. I shall now discuss them in sequence, beginning with the "transmission of the collar" (*ryōfu*).
The reason for synthesizing the discussion of the five flavors is to unify the intent of the sūtra’s teachings through systematic categorization.
Why is this so? If one were to rely solely on these categories, each would correspond only to its respective passage;

thus, while there might be a beginning and end to the guidance, it would not be the ultimate end, and while there might be an end to the entrustment, it would lack a true beginning in terms of near or far. If this were the case, the intent of the sūtra would be severed at its source.

If the flow [of the text] does not penetrate through, how can it be considered a correct interpretation? Therefore, the Great Master (Dashi) still adopts the meaning of "penetrating downward" from another occasion, and furthermore, he specifically values this passage as a text that "receives and conveys" what precedes it.
He synthesizes the five periods of teaching into a single transformation (*eka-vyūha*) and explains their essential intent based on this.
Thus he says: (as stated above). Furthermore, did not Jingxi say: "What is it that the subsequent explanation explains?"

Emerging together, they form a single beginning and end that mutually identify the five flavors. However, when it says "now both leading," this refers to the two aspects of beginning and end, not the two types of "exploring" (探) mentioned in the *Zhìqǐ* [Treatise].
That is to say, by combining the two preceding instances of beginning and end with the subsequent equal bestowals, they are collectively named "beginning";
only the entrustment of the treasure is designated as the "end. Therefore, it is said: "Exploring at the beginning and leading at the end; taken together, these discuss the five flavors."
The summary of the concluding text probes and encompasses the five flavors. Some may mistakenly perceive this as an exertion of force;

however, since it does not explicitly mention "simultaneous" (*qi*), how could it be intended as something distinct? It is simply because one knows from the text regarding other days that this refers to the distant vision of the Dharma-body.
If one takes the five periods of the present as the boundaries traversed by oneself, these too are indeed encompassed simultaneously. Therefore, it was said previously:
Furthermore, it may also be that they were equally ordained within [the community], yet this was not through their own instruction.

Speaking from this perspective, whether the five periods of teaching were uniform or selective, comprehensive or restricted, small or great, open or closed, acceptable or rejected—those which cannot be fully recorded are simply a matter of where the underlying principle lies. Therefore...
The text of the "Other" (Ita) chapter explains by means of three meanings: it states that "exploring and receiving" refers to the Buddha-wisdom’s illumination of capacities.
Regarding the term "Buddha-wisdom," there must be both the provisional and the real; the meaning of "illuminating capacities" likewise encompasses both self and other.

Furthermore, if one summarizes this according to the gates of teaching, there are the three pairs of self and other, and so forth, wherein the provisional and the real encompass the entirety of the Buddha's transformation. Herein, we clarify the "Other."

The *Riju* (Direct) [Expedient Means] not only applies to the literal text but also extends to the meaning of the entire transformation (*ekavyūha*). Since its scope encompasses both [the literal and the intended], its principle truly accords with this; therefore, it is used to explain this [text].
However, among these three [types of reception], the first pertains to the capacity of the recipient (*yogya*) and thus refers to the sense of "receiving simultaneously";

the latter two pertain to the response of the Buddha and thus refer to the sense of "receiving by seeking out. Furthermore, the first [of the latter two] refers to the reception by the Two Vehicles when viewed from the perspective of the Buddha, while the latter two refer to the application of the Tathāgata’s power.
Furthermore, the first [of these] uses the Dharmakāya to illuminate the capacities of others; this is that which is employed by the Two Vehicles.
The latter two, however, use the provisional means within the Tathāgata’s own practice to benefit others; this is not that which is employed by the Two Vehicles.

Although all such meanings are clearly explained in the texts, I have first made this distinction for the sake of easy understanding. Nevertheless, since the Japanese and Chinese [traditions] are fundamentally one Buddha-wisdom, how could...?
The reason why the explanations differ despite their commonality is that they are distinguished by the specific objects they respond to; thus, three interpretations are formed.
If this wisdom is contrasted with the skillful means (*upāya*) used to transform others, it then belongs to the "Teaching for the Capable" (*tongjiao*) as it accords with their capacities.

If this wisdom is contrasted with the reality of one's own practice (*svayam-pratipatti*), it then belongs to the "Exploration and Realization" (*tanting*) as it accords with the response. Although the objects of contrast differ, the wisdom that performs the contrasting remains the same.
Therefore it is said that both "two kinds of benefiting others" (liang ta) refer to the Dharmakāya; however, they differ in meaning according to the capacity of the recipient.

The reason why these two kinds of benefiting others are different is that what they correspond to is distinct: one is of the same substance (tongti), while the other is of a different substance (yiti).

Because it is of a different substance, it is that which is employed by the Two Vehicles; because it is of the same substance, it is not that which is employed by the Two Vehicles. Thus, the record further states:

It is said: "To 'probe the center' refers to the Dharma-body; at that time, the provisional Two Vehicles find it difficult to receive the teaching, and the provisional Two Vehicles of the same essence do not understand [the principle of] equality—this is its meaning.
(If one were to explain this from the perspective of the provisional and real meanings of the Dharma-characteristics of self and other, it would be as clarified elsewhere.

However, this is merely the literal text, yet there is further intent therein. As for why the commentary specifically restricts itself to three meanings, it is precisely because of the "other" [factor].

The Sun-Piercer (Nirai Kan) received the imperial decree to restore the unified teaching; thus, the Dharma-body he presided over discerns capacities, not only illuminating the provisional but also discerning the real.
Having long known that the Great and Small, One and Three, are one in their manifestation of the teaching, these words are indeed verified.

Therefore, the provisional and real aspects of his transformation of others correspond to the textual investigation and realization of this very passage; as for the realization of oneself and others, they correspond to what follows.
Regarding the various flavors, when transforming others, it is also said that "unifying and leading" (*qí lǐng*) does not merely mean unifying and leading;
rather, it arises from the perspective of the other in relation to oneself, for one's own [practice] pertains to the matters of the three vehicles. Thus, for the time being, we speak of "unifying.

If, however, one proceeds from the perspective of the other, it then belongs to "exploring and leading" (*tàn lǐng*), which is what Jingxi refers to as "unifying the teachings while exploring and leading. Therefore, there is only this single "exploring and leading," wherein the small and the great are not distinct.

Regarding the term "other" (*tā*), although it generally encompasses three meanings—referring to the provisional, the other, and that which is distinct from oneself—it must necessarily refer to the provisional and also to the other.
Nevertheless, there is not a lack of the teaching that "the realization of reality is oneself. This is because, first, it accords with the meaning of the character "other" as explained;

second, it is spoken from the perspective of the respective stage of the two vehicles; and third, it may also be explained by taking the provisional and the other as the basis for these three meanings.
Since one must distinguish [the teachings] according to their actual reality, it is necessary to discuss both self and other in relation to the capacities of sentient beings;

thus, although it may suffice to explain them directly as a single meaning, from the perspective of what is appropriate, the three meanings are eternally fused and there is originally no distinction between self and other.

From the perspective of the capacities of beings, however, since they were distinct in the past, the gates of the teaching cannot be left undifferentiated. As for the characteristics of these three interpretations, the meaning is inexhaustible; fearing prolixity, I shall cease here.
Now, the explanation of Qi’s inquiry is roughly like this: if scholars simply take this as a framework to unify those various texts, then there will be no text that remains unexplained;
if one refutes heterodox arguments, then there will be no argument that remains obscure.
As for other matters, even if there were one or two points that hit the mark, their general principles would remain obscure and are thus not worth mentioning.
The division of the *Zhengyi* (Correct Meaning) into three parts and the commentary on the sutras (*Shijing*) into three parts has long been established;

it originated with Dharma Master Mitian and has been inherited from that time onward without dispute, precisely because it accords with the sutras and treatises. Now, we of Tiantai likewise inherit and employ this system.
Yet, regarding the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* alone, there are two distinct methods of textual division, as [the text] states (and so forth). Subsequently, it says:
"Now, this record follows the previous three revisions for the elimination of the text; furthermore, when about to explain the 'True Teaching' (*samyak-artha*), it further says:

'For now, let us follow the immediate [approach] and divide the 'Trace Gate' (*jia-men*) main exposition into two parts,' and so forth. Regarding this, among those who have studied and lectured on the teachings throughout ancient and modern times...

This [position] maintains both ends of the doubt: does it follow the three-part explanation from the previous section, or the threefold explanation from the subsequent section, or do they require one another such that neither can be used in isolation?
Although commentators may say various things, their explanations ultimately do not exceed these three views.
Now, I shall evaluate them with a single word: none of them escape the faults of contradiction and deficiency.
Therefore, this is not yet the ultimate treatise. Now, it is certainly impossible to apply this unilaterally, nor is it necessary to grasp both simultaneously;

one must first understand its fundamental intent (*yuan-yi*) and the principles of its general application (*da-ti-yong*), and only then can one demonstrate the characteristics of its progression, regression, sublation, and resolution.
As for the fundamental intent, one must investigate how these two successive divisions of the scripture are uniquely distinct from the rest.
The reason for this organization is none other than that the pedagogical functions revealed through the two gates of the "True" (Zheng) and the "Trace" (Ben) differ;
thus, the division of the text cannot be treated as uniform. It is essential to first establish the two gates of the True before the purport of the Trace can be fully revealed.
Therefore, without a separate division, one would have no means to distinguish the differences between the two gates; yet, without a comprehensive division, one would have no means to achieve unity.
Because the sections are mutually pervasive, we know that the intent of the individual divisions emerges from the primary teaching, while the general divisions return to the introductory overview;
this is merely their fundamental meaning. Furthermore, one must understand that when the text is divided, it is not yet the time for exegesis.
While the divisions may be presented side by side, in the act of exegesis, meanings cannot coexist. Since these meanings cannot coexist, [the former must yield].

Because there are both collateral and primary applications, the introduction (*nidāna*) is explained as being primarily applied to the general division while secondarily encompassing the specific division.
Indeed, the primary application to the general division is what the Commentary refers to when it says: "Now, this record explains the text according to the preceding three sections.

When explaining the main body (*śarīra*), however, the primary application is to the specific division while secondarily encompassing the general division. Indeed, the primary application to the specific division is what the Commentary [refers to].

This refers to following the immediate [text] to reach the underlying traces. It is precisely because these all encompass the meaning of "comprehensive penetration" (*pángjiān*) that they avoid the fault of being incomplete or deficient.
Nevertheless, how can one prove that the interpretation of the characteristics is thus? The *Miaole* states:

"If one interprets the General Preface according to the 'Comprehensive Penetration' method, then every sentence must pervade the four [sections], including the Main Body and the Propagation; therefore, this is the primary application of the 'General Division' (*zǒngfēn*)."
Regarding the explanation of the individual preface (*pṛthag-nidāna*), the text may consist of three or four sections, with some parts treated as separate divisions.

Since it is thus for the explanation of the preface, the same applies by analogy to the dissemination (*saṃprakāśana*). Therefore, it is said: "If one explains the dissemination, one must again possess all four [sections] to encompass it completely.

Regarding the orthodox doctrine (*saddharma*), however, since the dissemination always follows and its meaning is universally applicable, it is not further restricted to the distinction of three or four sections. Furthermore, it is said: "If one explains the orthodox doctrine..."

The "threefold" divisions of both the *hon* (original) and *soku* (traces) represent the primary classification based on their distinct application; the "fourfold" meaning refers to the secondary, inclusive classification.

Regarding the explanation of the "Preface Chapter" (*shōbon*), there are further considerations of inclusion or exclusion: if one follows the inclusive classification, the entire chapter should be designated as the "Preface," and it should accordingly be explained through four modes of interpretation.

However, when explaining the "Separate Preface" (*betsusho*), three modes may be used, because each corresponds to the "Original Preface" (*honsho*) and possesses its own specific basis and conditions.

Although there may be three [categories] used, there is a distinction between the Exoteric and the Esoteric: the four [sections] that manifest the traces (*traces*) constitute the sequential division of the Exoteric;

the four that manifest the fundamental [reality] (*root*) constitute the sequential division of the Esoteric. Thus, while both the general and specific divisions alike designate the "Preface Chapter" (*Nidāna-parivarta*) as the sequence, they differ in their Exoteric and Esoteric approaches regarding whether [the sequence] proceeds or not.
By this analogy, the universal preface (*sādhāraṇa-nidāna*) should also be understood in this way; however, the universal [premise] can be [applied].
Furthermore, while the specific [analysis] does not necessarily encompass the comprehensive [understanding], it is as follows (and so forth).

Moreover, if one were to explain the main body (*saddharma*) according to its specific divisions, then according to the principles of the recorders, one ought to first cite the passage that divides the single period into two parts, each opening with three sections.

Having first explained the introductory section (*nidāna*) as indicated above, one would then proceed directly from the main body to the concluding section (*parīndanā*) below. However, this is not the case.
Setting aside the separate divisions, one should employ a general explanation of the meaning so that the structure is orderly;

yet the commentary does not do so, but rather, from within the main body of the text itself, it introduces the general exposition and simply says, "If one were to provide two formal expositions," etc. This is because the Great Master has already explained the Preface Chapter and no longer refers back to it;
thus, for the sake of convenience, he proceeds from the main body itself until reaching the passage on the "Leaping Forth," where he finally opens the major section.
Since this is the third part of the *Honmon* (Original Gate), one knows that the textual structure of the *Jikimon* (Trace Gate) is abbreviated;

yet many people do not perceive this, and thus either treat the two-thirds division of the *Shōjūbun* (Main Body) as an extension of the *Jōbun* (Introduction) and *Ryūtsūbun* (Circulation), or, while knowing this to be so, they wish to follow the aforementioned indications but find the text remains unintelligible—neither of these approaches is correct. Now that the sections have been organized and clarified...
The characteristics of this explanation shall be further elaborated and examined in the subsequent text.

Regarding the remaining meanings of the three divisions, it is inherently difficult to establish the discourse, and the discourse itself is not easily understood. Because understanding the discourse is not easy, this discourse was established.

Therefore, that which is most difficult is as previously indicated by the theory of the three divisions; because the textual characteristics of the preceding and following sections appear to be in conflict, the text is divided to explain the sūtra.

By resolving this difficulty through two meanings, and because the explained meanings of the sūtra cannot stand as two separate entities, the "oblique" and "direct" aspects are used to complete the exposition.
Although it is said that the meanings cannot coexist, this is precisely how they are made to coexist.

To preserve it is also like what the world calls "when two forces cannot coexist, one must weigh the circumstances to find a suitable way to accommodate them," so as to strive for its complete preservation.
Only by doing so can one be said to have skillfully fulfilled what is appropriate.

Nevertheless, even so, the selection and discernment of the textual meanings within the *Shu* (Commentary) remain difficult to clarify; as for the *Ji* (Record) and the *Shi* (Explanations), they are truly not easy to master.
Hao has always been hindered by the obscurities of commentators; now, I am able to clarify them. However, the question asks: "Why are there two [introductions] for one sūtra?

(This refers to the two sequences of the *ben* [origin] and *ji* [trace]; if it referred to the two sequences of the *tong* [general] and *bie* [specific], it would not be what is being asked). This is indeed a question regarding the subsequent explanation.

Yet, since the text follows the preceding section, and the current record proceeds from the three prior segments to interpret the text, the result is that they do not seem to connect. Now, since we proceed from the three [prior segments]...
To treat them as separate sections would mean setting aside the specific to follow the general; why, then, does the text pose a question regarding the two subsequent explanations?
This is because the intent of the inquiry already exists within the record. Since both explanations are present, what harm is there in questioning the latter?
Is it not precisely because of the preceding context that we know the intent of the question lies therein? For indeed, every question possesses an underlying intent.

Regarding the question of the text: the meaning of the question can be understood because, while the preceding section generally follows the previous [passage] and thus maintains a collective division, the subsequent question instead seeks the meaning of the later explanation and thus maintains a distinct division.

Considering both together, the intent of the question lies in these two explanations; since the intent of the question resides in these two explanations, one may provisionally inquire about the later explanation alone.

Therefore it is said: "What harm is there in questioning the latter [explanation]? This is why two explanations are provided. Regarding the phrase "the middle" [in the commentary], this further explains the intention behind not specializing solely in the latter explanation.
If, then, the answer already states that "neither contradicts the single scripture," and thus there is no harm in having two sequences, why not specialize solely in the latter explanation?

It is because the former establishes the *liutong* (circulation) prior to the main text; therefore, [specializing only in the latter] would be a significant loss of the principle of universal circulation (*tong*).
The purport of this passage is that the subsequent explanation is merely a provisional one.

Some may claim that the "Original" (Ben) and "Correct" (Zheng) [sections] cannot establish the "Circulation" (Liutong) [section], but this is also incorrect. Since these are all original scriptural texts, how could it be said they cannot establish it?

One might only say that if they were divided into separate parts, they would greatly deviate from the intent of circulation; therefore, it is stated thus. Precisely because they are all provisional, it is necessary [to treat them as such].
Although both [interpretations] are preserved, their meanings cannot be explained simultaneously; therefore, one must be primary and the other secondary. Thus it is said:

"Although both are preserved"—this means that, as far as the division of the text is concerned, they may be listed side by side. Yet it further says: "Furthermore, employ the initial meaning"—this means that among the applications, there is a primary and a secondary.
Consequently, when the text states that the intent lies in two explanations, what is employed now is the secondary one.

This is the reason for [the term] "correct. If one were to engage in the practice of acceptance and rejection such that the meanings of the present [texts] could not coexist, then one would have missed the point;
such a person is surely not one who understands words.
This concludes the general explanation of the three doubts.
The preface is placed at the beginning of all sutras to benefit the path of realization of the Buddhas of the three periods;
yet, because it carries the meaning of establishing faith and dispelling doubt, its utility as a prologue is profound. As the *Huayan He Lun* (Compendium on the Avatamsaka) cites the *Sūkṣma-vinaya*:
"When Ānanda ascended the Dharma throne to compile the treasury of the Dharma, his body was fully endowed like that of a Buddha."
When the multitude beheld these auspicious signs, they gave rise to three doubts (as briefly cited in the *Miaoshu*): ... [omitted] ...
even to the point where it says, "It is solely by the power of the Dharma that I have been made to resemble the Buddha," and after descending from his seat, he returned to his original form;

such are the meanings of the "doubts. Furthermore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "By citing the time and place, one causes people to give rise to faith"; this refers to the "testimony of faith. And as for the heavens...
The Platform [Sutra] cites these to establish the conditions for causality; thus, a single interpretation is sufficient as a basis for reliance.

However, regarding the meaning of "dispelling doubts," there have been questions concerning the "general and the three specific" [aspects] (the question regarding the subtle essence of the inquiring spirit, etc.). Consequently, within the teachings, there arose the discourse on the "three doubts.
Speaking from the present perspective, the question was indeed raised lightly, and the respondent likewise failed to investigate its fundamental source. Therefore—
It must also be understood that all [previous] explanations have failed to clarify the fundamental universality of doubt, while the present compilation concerns its fundamental particularity;
yet, by using the name "absence of doubt" from the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna) to obstruct the Great Path (Mahāyāna), how could the true meaning of doubt be grasped?

Now, by providing a comprehensive explanation to demonstrate this, the points of contention will no longer be seen. Why is this so? Because, generally speaking, there are two types of doubt: great doubt and... [the text continues].
There are minor doubts that vary in depth—whether concerning persons, dharmas, phenomena, or principles—but whenever there is something not fully understood regarding any dharma, doubt arises.
When one hesitates and cannot reach a decision, it is doubt; when one deviates from what is fundamentally known, it is doubt;
when one is bewildered and cannot fathom why things are as they are, it is doubt. These are not of a single kind and cannot be exhausted, as seen in the cases of Mañjuśrī, Maitreya, and others.
If even those at the high rank of Equal Enlightenment (Samyaksaṃbodhi) still possess doubt, how much more so those on the lower stages, those of the partial vehicles, and ordinary beings?
Even if one were to say that their doubts are provisional, such provisionality must lead toward the ultimate; it cannot be said that they are entirely without doubt.
Since none who have not yet reached the stage of Wondrous Enlightenment and Universal Knowledge can escape doubt, how can one rely on the testimony of these one thousand minor sages?
Because of these doubts, it was concluded that among the three types of doubt arising during the council, there were some that ought not to be doubted; how narrow-minded this is!
One fails to realize that the matter of the council pertains entirely to the Hinayana transformation and should not be discussed in terms of the Mahayana teachings. Why is this?
For instance, when Ānanda was about to participate in the council, he had not yet realized the fruit of the fourth stage (Arhatship); consequently, he was sent away by Kāśyapa.

Only those who have realized the fruits [of the path] and attained supernormal powers can be counted among them; ultimately, they became the leaders of the compilation (the text is found in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, etc.).

Furthermore, as for the three matters of doubt, these all involve the Lesser Vehicle (*Hīnayāna*) because they are doubts; thus one knows that these entirely conform to the intent of the Lesser Vehicle’s transformation.

How could they be matters subsequent to the opening of realization and the attainment of prediction (*vyākaraṇa*) according to the Great Teaching (*Mahāyāna*)? Therefore it is said: "The matter of the compilation is fundamentally restricted [to the Lesser Vehicle]. Such is the case.

Even if among these one thousand there were those who possessed both the provisional and the real, and who had attained profound stages while manifesting traces, they still ought not to have raised such doubts here;

how much less so for this group of one thousand, who were incapable of being free from doubt, at a time when Ānanda had only just begun to receive the Buddha’s transformative empowerment—how could they not have doubted?
From this it may be seen that doubt originally should not have been restricted, yet it was restricted.
Since ancient times, why have they been restricted by the difficulty of compilation? Originally, it was intended to be universal; why do people today suffer so much in failing to understand it?
If one grasps this meaning, then the three doubts will be resolved without question. Nevertheless, what of the doubt regarding the title "One Thousand"?

As for what is called "without doubt," it does not refer to all phenomena. To investigate the origin of how that name was obtained: [The text continues with the explanation of the term *Amitābha* and its etymological derivation.]
Regarding the two types of speech associated with wisdom within the respective categories:

because one has studied the four Vedas and other such texts, one knows all internal and external scriptures, and thus receives that specific designation. However, as for the Mahāyāna, there are still many things one does not understand.
This is what the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* means when it says: "One has no doubt regarding the Four Noble Truths, yet one has doubts regarding all phenomena."
"It is true that you speak of faith; however, since the meaning of these three doubts is something that should not exist in the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna), why do they arise?
I reply: It is precisely because they ought not to exist that they are doubted. If they were indeed appropriate [to exist], one would simply state them as such—what room would there be for doubt?
This refers to what was previously called 'contrary to what is fundamentally known. Furthermore, it is because one cannot decide among these three."

Furthermore, the term "yi" (義) carries the sense of being hesitant and indecisive. If this is so, then regarding the discourse on doubt and non-doubt, the underlying principle is fundamentally straightforward;
why, then, must one employ so many expedients to dispel it?

Regarding the various difficult points concerning the teachings of the *Bujiao* (School Teachings) tradition, there are generally several such instances, and this text contains three of them: first, the opening of the three teachings at the stage of the fruit;

second, the former claim that the Perfect [teaching] was not opened; and third, the assertion that the initial mind of the Perfect is separated from the partial [teachings] (and so forth). Based on these...
If commentators continue endlessly with such discursive treatises on the interconnections of the teachings, who could possibly stop them?

Now, I shall directly explain the text so that objections cannot even arise; what need is there to speak of providing further exegesis? To investigate this text, it clearly elucidates the Buddha-wisdom (*buddhajñāna*).
As for why the term "opening" (*kai*) is necessarily used, it is because the word "Buddha-wisdom" is a name whose scope is broad while its underlying meaning is profound.

Although one may speak of "partial" [teachings] even regarding the provisional teachings mentioned previously, it is only by correlating them with the specific divisions of the scriptural teachings (*śāsana*) that their definitive meaning is revealed.
Since the terms "opening" (*kai*) and so forth were applied to the flavors of the past, this makes it difficult to distinguish between the teachings and the divisions.

Consequently, in the response, the divisions are used to explain the teachings; thus, there is a passage intended to provide a critical discrimination (*vibhāga*). That being so, the three vehicles' fruits are opened.
The statement regarding the provisional and the real at the level of the fruit is because the fruit itself is the Buddha, and the provisional and the real are the two types of wisdom.

According to the *Sūtra Commentary* on the "Expedient Means" chapter, it is explained that each of the three teachings has ten pairs [of concepts] (and so forth). These are precisely the provisional and the real realized within the realm of the fruit;
now, these various forms of the provisional and the real are opened up as nothing other than the Middle Truth—the principle and wisdom—which is the Buddha-wisdom of the present sutra.
In the past, some said that because the *Fuxing* (Subcommentary) and this text differ in their methods for persons and dharmas, there is a distinction between "opening" and "not opening.

Now, I accept this point; however, it is not yet fully satisfactory because it does not clearly explain how, from the perspective of the fruits themselves, there can be both "opening" and "not opening.

I now maintain that this is neither exclusively one way nor exclusively the other—it is both "opening" and "not opening. Why? Because regarding the provisional fruits of the preceding three teachings, they are defined in terms of "opening."
This reveals that every word of the school’s intent is none other than the Perfect Buddha. Now, if it is already called the "Perfect Buddha," how could there be anything further to open?
And yet, once it is termed the "Perfect Buddha," how could it not be opened? Whether it is opened or not, the mystery lies therein;

There are points regarding the meaning that may be subject to doubt and those that need not be doubted. If one does not doubt what is doubtful, there is naturally no fault;
but if one forcibly doubts what need not be doubted, what benefit is there? The *Fahua shu*’s explanation of the title of the "Expedient Means" chapter may be said to be exhaustive.
