yet, those who are deluded do not examine the reasons why this is so, but instead take the "expedient means" (upāya) to be a mere provisional authority of the past, obstructing the true reality of the present. That the titles and texts appear inconsistent is likely the fault of the questioner.
Those who deliberate ought to rely solely on the commentaries (*śāstra*) to rectify the terminology; why then do our predecessors fail to investigate the origins?
The root of their confusion lies in the fact that various Śramaṇas and Śākyas incessantly engage in mutual refutation and establishment;

it is for this reason that such debates become ever more numerous yet ever more remote from the truth. Therefore, those who provide an exposition today should fundamentally base it upon the intent of the texts to demonstrate it clearly.
If one were to directly question and refute them, the skillful means of the teaching would not fall into the proliferation of superfluous words.

Why is this so? For instance, the commentary on the *Fangbian* (Expedient Means) generally relies upon three meanings: the application of the Dharma (*dharmaprayoga*), the capacity for penetration (*abhigama*), and the secret and wondrous (*guhyamandala*).
It further states that while the former two may explain other sutras, they are not the intent of the present chapter; the intent of the present chapter is the secret and wondrous expedient means.
How could a secret and wondrous expedient mean be the same as the provisional (*upāya*) of the past and different from the reality (*tattva*) of the present? This cannot be so.
What is meant by "the title and the text are not consistent"? Since this [title] expresses a single meaning, yet it is further condensed into three phrases for brevity, it is said:
"The subsequent explanation is the skillful means (*upāya*) of the same essence," which refers to the provisional [teaching] of self-cultivation according to one's own intent.

Furthermore, when analyzed through the four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*) regarding the contrast between skillful means and the provisional, this corresponds to the fourth proposition, that of mutual identity (*paraspara-saṃbheda*). Moreover, there is an extensive explanation.

Citing the various masters of antiquity, each elucidated the provisional and the real; yet, as they all failed to harmonize them, it was said: "The name does not encompass the meaning, and the meaning is not fused with the wondrous;

thus it cannot be employed to explain this present chapter. Furthermore, citing the treatise, seventeen different names are listed, the thirteenth of which is "Great Skillful Means" (*mahopāyakauśalya*).
It states: "This is the Tathāgata’s skillful means that encompasses all dharmas, just as space contains all things."
How could the various masters, with their single branches and individual schools, possibly explain the greater part of the Dharma-realm?

As for the judgment that all dharmas are provisional according to the four propositions—beginning with "all are provisional" and so on—this corresponds to the third category, the "provisional half-phrase. It states:
"If all dharmas are provisional, up to being neither provisional nor real, what is there that cannot be sublated? This is as previously cited.

How could the various masters dare claim their own nests as secure, merely listing names and viewing from afar with a superficial grasp of this vast, lofty, and profound [teaching], let alone discussing its underlying purport?
Furthermore, regarding the provisional and the real, ten pairs of phrases are further opened up to demonstrate it;
beneath each passage, it is said: "The provisional possesses the function of revealing the real; therefore, the Tathāgata..."

From the "Praise of Expedient Means" (*upāya*) down to the eight sections that collectively explain the ten pairs—whether through general conclusions, specific conclusions, or mutual combinations spanning several pages—all of this is nothing other than the manifestation of the principle of expedient means.
It encompasses the beginning and end, exhausting the profound and reaching the ultimate subtlety;
what could possibly exist that is not this very expedient means? If this is so, then to open up the expedient means of the past is itself [the realization of the ultimate].
The skillful means of reality; the skillful means of the same essence; the skillful means of the Tathāgata; the skillful means that encompasses all dharmas;
the skillful means of synonymous names; the skillful means that unifies three phrases into one phrase;

the skillful means that subsumes the ten pairs and governs the ten provisional teachings; the skillful means that penetrates a single sūtra; and the skillful means that synthesizes the entire transformation.

Such are the skillful means (*upāya*). To equate these skillful means established in the past with the provisional teachings of that time, while asserting they differ from the current reality in their ultimate intent, is indeed difficult.
Thus, we know that the fault lies with the questioner; for this reason, what was said previously could have remained unasked and unexplained.

Nevertheless, although the discourse concerns the ultimate truth (*tattva*), it specifically employs skillful means to designate its categories. When one traces back its profound purport, is it not the case that...?
This means that how could anything be added to this commentary? To add anything to this commentary would be false. Therefore, I shall now restate it according to my previous intention, saying:

"The substance underlying a name encompasses both the provisional and the real; the names and phrases applied to that substance have a partial meaning for the former and a universal meaning for the latter.

Only because the substance encompasses both the provisional and the real do the designations of "expedient means" possess both the provisional and the real, while the designations of "true reality" [possess only the real].
Principle likewise possesses both the provisional and the real, for they are but one wondrous essence.

Thus, when words are partial while the meaning is complete, some speak of "expedient means" (upāya), which is partial to the provisional, while others speak of "ultimate reality" (bhūtatathatā), which is partial to the real.

Although their words may be partial, their intent is always complete. Because this intent is complete, that which is revealed as ultimate reality is designated by the name of secret and wondrous expedient means.

What is so wrong with simply following the words as they go? It is not that there is no reason; it is because "expedient means" (*upāya*) is broad in its designation, whereas "ultimate truth" (*paramārtha*) is narrow in its application.

Indeed, if the words of expedient means are truly as you have indicated, then what dharma would not be subsumed, what meaning would not be contained, what virtue would not be manifested, and what principle would not be revealed?
How could this possibly be encompassed by the single name "ultimate truth" alone?
It is for this reason that the chapter is appropriately titled "Expedient Means" (Upāya); there is indeed a profound significance to this. Yet, one might ask:

"How can it be said that the 'Wenyan' (Words and Phrases) are the ultimate reality? It is because the "Wenyan" being called reality does not necessarily encompass the whole; it merely reveals a single aspect.

One fails to realize that what is expounded in the opening passage—which rejoices in the provisional and extols the real—fully describes the entirety of the Buddha's transformation (the One Transformation). How could it be limited to the single aspect of "reality" alone?
Having already provided the reasons, I shall now address the title itself by saying: A title is certainly not a provisional device, yet its meaning is not exclusively literal.

Because its meaning is not exclusively literal, the text encompasses the entirety of a single transformation; everything therein is nothing but a skillful means (*upāya*). Is it therefore not appropriate that this work be categorized under such a title?

If one understands this principle, then the title and the text will be in harmony. Who would say they are divergent paths? To fail to comprehend this intent is merely to display a superficial categorization.

The textual intent regarding the provisional and the real concerning the Dragon Girl’s attainment of Buddhahood demonstrates the power and function of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*. The commentary on this sūtra is cryptic and difficult for readers to understand;
it is precisely because of the doubts raised by Jñatikauṇḍinya, who could not believe that Śākyamuni could attain Buddhahood given the vastness and distance of his past practices.
In the case of the Dragon Girl of Swift Timing, she merely manifested before the Buddha and praised him with verses; what text explains this point of doubt?
Furthermore, when Śāriputra raised doubts that the path of the Buddha was remote and vast and that a female body was not a fit vessel, the Dragon Girl simply offered a perfect pearl to the Buddha.
How could one know where the removal of doubt lay? It would not be possible [to understand] were it not for our Patriarch who, by means of his concise indications, revealed it.
The text is indeed difficult to comprehend; however, what Zhijí doubted was based on a dualistic attachment.

When he praised the Buddha with verses, he directly clarified the Perfect [Teaching] to resolve his doubts—namely, that which the verses refer to as "profoundly penetrating the equality of sin and merit.

Since he has profoundly penetrated that both sin and merit are nothing other than the true mark (dharmatā), and further states that the Dharma-body possesses the marks and uses the primary and secondary characteristics to adorn the body, then...

Since the text and its underlying meaning manifest both cultivation and nature, and the characteristics of these are clearly revealed, how could this not be a profound realization that cultivation and nature are non-dual?

Having already described self-realization and praised the Buddha, it follows that the reason the Tathāgata is called "Buddha," the reason the Dragon Girl attained Buddhahood, and the reason the various sentient beings encountered the Buddha—all do not transcend this principle; this is precisely the resolution of doubts. As for Śāriputra’s...
Those who harbor doubts conceal them within; yet, by offering a pearl to the Buddha, one removes doubt through its roundness and reality.

As the commentary states: "Offering it signifies the manifestation of perfect understanding (*pariniṣpanna-jñāna*); the pearl represents the perfect cause. To hold it up and present it to the Buddha is to employ the cause to achieve the fruit—how swift this is!
If this is so, why labor over trivial matters to dispel [doubts] or insistently strive to resolve them?
The purport of the *Śākyamuni Sūtra* is indeed as stated above. As for the commentary on the passage concerning the attainment of Buddhahood, its meaning is especially difficult to discern;

consequently, some have raised doubts regarding the provisional and the ultimate (*upāya* and *tattva*). (And so forth. Were it not for the Master of the Record (*Shōki-shu*) clearly adjudicating these doctrines, how could they be reconciled?
Furthermore, the initial question-and-answer section at the beginning of the Record was not intended merely for his own analytical clarification; rather, it is entirely... [text ends]

I shall append the meaning of the commentary (*śū*) to resolve these difficulties. As for what is called a "difficulty" (*parihāra*), the commentary cites the intent of the *Garbha-sūtra* to establish this objection:

"If that [sūtra] lacks the neutral sensation (*upekṣā-vedanā*), how can there be such a transformation here? From the words "In the South," etc., is the explanation of the text itself; thus the *Jì* (Record) asks:

"Does one attain Buddhahood without abandoning the stage of limited existence (*paricchinna-bhava*)? This question is posed by taking the intent of the *Garbha-sūtra* as its basis. Furthermore, it says: "If..."
The statement that "one does not attain Buddhahood in this very body" is posed as a question based on the example of the Dragon Girl;
thus, the concluding inquiry and so forth, as well as the subsequent answer, merely serve to illustrate a specific passage from the commentary.

The intended meaning is that, while it is a matter of fact (*tattva*) that the former [the Dragon Girl] lacks the sensation of equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*), the latter [the practitioner] possesses transformation, which is a skillful means (*upāya*). Setting aside the matter of actual attainment for a moment, let us discuss the provisional.
The skillful [expedient] means that because the conditions in this land of the south involve the maturation of sentient beings, it is appropriate to manifest such transformations.

However, since the provisional and the real differ slightly, what prevents these two from being distinct? How could one speak of sacred traces in a single, uniform manner? Therefore, the Record states:
"Now, the passage concerning the Dragon Girl is spoken according to the provisional; those verses from the *Garbha-sūtra* are spoken according to the real. These two approaches serve as..."
The discussion on skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*) is not that they lack actual practice; for how could there be actual practice without skillful means? Thus it is said:
"If one practices according to reality, skillful means are not urgent"; and again: "If one has attained reality, all are equal.

Therefore, although there may be no [actual] relinquishment or reception in the attainment of reality, if it accords with what sentient beings prefer, it is permissible to manifest supernatural transformations (*ṛddhi-prātihārya*); thus there is no hindrance to the occurrence of transformative events, such as the skillful means of the Dragon Girl.

Although skillful means (*upāya*) involve transformation, if one realizes non-arising (*anutpāda*), it does not hinder the fundamental principle that from the beginning there is nothing to be abandoned or received.
As the *Garbha-sūtra* states, since the provisional and the real are fundamentally identical, when the meaning of the sūtra is realized, both are attained. It further says:

"Thus, the meanings of the provisional and the real are equal, and this principle is not in vain. It also states: "In all such cases, one must necessarily realize the non-duality of the provisional and the real."

To resolve further doubts and obstacles, it is said: "Therefore, both the provisional and the real meanings are established through the power of the sūtra. Yet the Master of the Commentary (*Ji-zhu*) further states:
"Regarding what is called 'provisional skillfulness,' one need not invariably provide a provisional interpretation.

This is precisely because he feared that students might mistake the general textual passages concerning the provisional and the real for definitive meanings regarding the fundamental and the manifested, thereby conflating them with other interpretations and suppressing the functional utility of the sūtra.
This is indeed correct. Thus, what is now called "expedient skill" (upāya-kauśalya) refers simply to the expedient skill of essence and function.

If one understands the purport of the sutras, commentaries, and records in this way, then the discourse on the provisional and the real regarding the Dragon Girl will be harmonious and logically consistent;
how could there be any contradiction?
Resolving Doubts by Anticipating Objections (píng-hū):
The preface to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* contains questions and answers concerning the causes for the manifestation of auspicious omens that give rise to doubts.

In the past, Guangzhai recounted this to Master Zhao based on the text of Maitreya’s fourfold "hidden doubts" (*sì fúyí*), while Tiantai, through his ingenious insights beyond the literal text, [elaborated upon them] extensively.
They were unaware that Mañjuśrī had also refuted the four hidden objections, which the ancient masters failed to perceive;
this is why Tiantai’s work is so perfect and complete. The words in the *Shuji* (Commentary) are exhaustive on this point. Nevertheless, the *Shiqian* (Sub-commentary) states:

"Maitreya initially raised hidden doubts as latent objections, and Mañjuśrī consequently provided a latent explanation for those hidden doubts. Regarding the objection, it says: "The fourfold assembly rejoiced..."
The commentary by Yang (仰) states: "I see the lamp-light," and so forth. This passage is extremely subtle and dense; for this reason, it has long been a source of confusion that remains unresolved.

There are three reasons for this confusion: first, while the original text is clearly difficult to manifest, both the [original] manifestation and the commentary are expressed in hidden language—this is the first cause of confusion.
Second, in the initial passage, Mañjuśrī’s question is difficult to understand, yet Maitreya’s response conversely speaks of it—this is the second cause of confusion.
Furthermore, as for the subsequent texts where the words do not correspond and yet are labeled "Difficulties" (Nan) and "Explanations" (Shi), these are due to three types of delusions.
Consequently, although there are many such theories, none of them reflect the intention of Jingxi; they are unworthy of discussion. I shall now directly demonstrate his intention.
What is that intention? It is the desire to unify the two texts into a single consistency to clarify the doubts and difficulties.
Yet, within these difficult explanations, there are mutual reflections of underlying meanings; such is their intended purport.
How may this be clarified? If each of the two texts were merely explaining its own respective doubts, then they would simply correspond to their own specific passages.
How could one know that they originally follow a single sequence of question and answer? Therefore, [the meaning] is found within Maitreya’s words that resolve the difficulties.

In the phrase "difficult and not speaking," the intention of the commentator is to reveal that this is not merely an explanation of the immediate text to settle latent doubts, but also serves as the basis for the subsequent passage where Mañjuśrī raises a challenge and requests an answer.

Once the latent doubts are explicitly manifested, the explanation is inherently contained therein. Furthermore, if one considers it from the perspective of implicit expression, it is evident that the explicit explanation emerges from within;
thus, while the explanation of Mañjuśrī’s resolution of doubts is described as "implicit," its presence is clearly discernible.

Yet he does not explicitly state "manifest" (*xian*); for while "latent" (*qian*) signifies the hidden, "pattern" (*wen*) is manifest. Although the meaning is thus clarified, the doubts underlying the text remain;
therefore, by employing the sense of "latent" to manifest the explanation, it can be understood that this response corresponds to the preceding question.
Subsequently, when he says "the objection states," etc., he takes up the words of the preceding objection and explanation, unifying the two passages into a single consistency.
Although the text does not explicitly address [these points], they are all difficult to explain in general terms. This being so, what need is there for the three delusions mentioned previously?
Nevertheless, while it would have sufficed to proceed with a direct exchange of questions and answers, why was it necessary to do so in this manner?

It was because he wished to manifest that each doubt and difficulty has its own specific cause, and furthermore, to set forth these latent doubts in turn so as to reveal the underlying intent of the other.
The meaning beyond these words is even more profound and obscure. Alas! This is a doctrine of exquisite ingenuity from a former age, a discourse held uniquely by this single school.
While the commentaries on the sutras consist of hundreds or thousands of words, Jingxi has exhausted their full significance in just a few sentences.
That he could capture such depth of meaning in this way clearly demonstrates the profundity of his intent; it is only fitting that later generations should revere him.
I was particularly confused and could not resolve it; formerly, when I had not yet grasped its meaning, looking at the text was like viewing a tangled skein.

Now that I have finally attained it, I see its underlying principle and no longer see its disorder. Truly, the Patriarch never intended to use such difficult-to-understand language merely to trouble people;
it is simply that students have not yet reached the point where the Ancients applied their intent, and thus they are deluded. How foolish!
It is because [the truth] can thereby be brought forth.

Among the six layers of primary and derivative manifestations (*honji-suijaku*), nothing is more difficult than resolving textual discrepancies; those that are profound and obscure rank next. Indeed, even that which is profound and difficult to comprehend...

One should contemplate this deeply and seek it with diligence to attain it; it is only because the literary patterns are easy to understand that those passages which appear contradictory or inconsistent are difficult to comprehend.

For a long time now, the citations used as evidence to demonstrate the six levels of "original" (*hon*) and "traced" (*saku*) in the *Shiki* (Commentary on the *Fahua wenju*) have been a difficulty for students of later generations.
Indeed, upon examining the texts, five of them pertain to the gate of the traced (*saku-mon*), while only one pertains to the gate of the original (*hon-mon*).

It is not that this is difficult to perceive; yet the *Zhǎn* (Commentary) states that "the first three [sections] cite the traces (*jì*), while the latter three cite the source (*běn*)," which is almost unintelligible.
Is it an error? If one examines its explanations, they do not seem crude or superficial; yet if one calls them non-erroneous, then the discrepancies between the texts are nearly beyond remedy.
Although there have been many commentators since antiquity, they all offer circuitous justifications; I have yet to see a direct one.
Regarding the intent of the [original] text and the purpose of the citations, I have not yet ventured to offer my views.

I shall first examine and record the commentaries (*jishi*), then present the explanations of the general and specific (*tongbie*), and finally verify that they are not erroneous; thus, this ultimate discourse may not be misinterpreted by later generations.
To speak of it now, generally, what is esteemed in the commentaries and sub-commentaries (*zhangshu*) is that which is explained therein.
If there are arguments that transcend conventional expectations, yet one fails to offer any correction or refinement beyond the literal text, such a person cannot be esteemed.
Furthermore, regarding the citations in the *Xuanwen*: if they were indeed as definitively established as claimed, it would have been sufficient simply to present them directly;
why then did one repeatedly correct the text, saying "it says so and so"? One must investigate the underlying reason for this.
It is precisely because the Great Master cited scriptural evidence with a profound underlying intention, such that the wording was somewhat inconsistent;
therefore, rather than being constrained by the literal text, he directly determined the meaning and specifically corrected the phrasing. This is just as it is said:

"To determine the text according to the meaning ensures that there is not even one error. Thus, one must first understand the doctrine of the six levels of commonality and distinction before [proceeding].
Why is it that the specific points of the cited evidence are first presented? It is because there are generally several directions [of interpretation].
First, the first five are general while the last one is particular, as stated in the *Shiguan* (Commentary on the Sutra) and so forth. Second, they are both general and particular:

because they are both general, although they pertain to the present and the future, they also extend to the past; thus the other five can be understood. Because they are both particular, although they pertain to the first five...
All belong to the "original" (hon), and the latter [the "trace"] can be understood accordingly, as indicated by the *shiki* (commentary) [and so forth].
If one were to contrast one's own present state with the preceding five layers to discuss the general and the specific, such would indeed be the natural intent of the text;

yet, to further divide these six layers into "original" and "trace" based on the principle of cause and effect is incorrect. While it may be permissible to distinguish between cause and effect, how could this ever...?

If one were to discuss the fundamental and the manifested based on this, it would be like discussing cause and effect; yet the fundamental and the manifested of cause and effect are not what is being discussed here.

Now, I maintain that because the Great Master cited the passage from the *Juryō-hon* (Life Span Chapter) to prove the meaning of essence and function, one knows through this internal division that the latter three [chapters] all clarify the fundamental.
However, although the two passages concerning the fifth and sixth [chapters] appear in the section on the manifested gate, they are taken as proof for no other reason than...

Since the meaning of the teaching on the reality of skillful means is already pervasive, when it pertains to the traces (*jì*), it resides in the traces; when it pertains to the source (*běn*), it resides in the source.

Furthermore, to reiterate the principle that the upper penetrates the lower, one must ultimately return to the source. If one were to restrict this solely to what is produced in the text, then the provisional and the real would already belong to the present [trace].

While it may be acceptable for the present to belong to the trace, if both the past and the present were also made to belong to the trace, then [the Great... (Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly. The translation reflects the available portion.)
The essential point is that the Master of this Record (Dharmapāla) did not inquire into the sequence of the text, but rather directly indicated it based on its general purport.

Furthermore, when he stated that "the first three are both common to the latter three and distinct," this was because he was looking at them from the perspective of their being both common and distinct simultaneously.
Thus, this "common" is the common within the distinct, and this "distinct" is the distinct within the common; it is a case of differentiating without differentiation.

There has never been a settled theory; it is simply that because the general principle is such, and the supporting evidence is as follows, and furthermore because the meaning of "dividing in the middle" is obtained, I have composed this annotated explanation.
Nevertheless, since the textual characteristics are so clear, how can one prove that they are not erroneous?
[I reply: Where the essential meaning resides, why must one seek it solely in the literal text? However, there is one passage that can serve as proof that this is not a mistake, as follows:

Following this text, [the author] commented on the passage concerning "dust motes" within the *jita* (trace) aspect, arguing that it is inappropriate to cite the passage regarding Maitreya’s ignorance as part of the *jimon* (trace gate), and proceeded to deliberate upon it through two meanings, and so forth.

Furthermore, he sought a definitive resolution from his teacher, who said, "I fear there may be another intention. Thus, when interpreting matters of ambiguity and resemblance, one must not act with casual ease.
In this way, how could there be room for error in the texts he himself presented?
Yet even Zuo Xi did not dare to speculate, saying only, "I fear there may be another meaning," which reflects an attitude of acknowledging one's ignorance.
Modern people view the Patriarch from afar and yet rashly offer their own arbitrary critiques; do they not feel shame before the words of Master Zuo Xi?

Composed by the Shramana Baiting Shan Yue of Siming.

In the "Chapter on Teaching," regarding the "Treatise on the Examples of the Secret *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*," it is stated that all followers of Esoteric Buddhism regard the presence or absence of secrecy during the period of the *Lotus Sūtra* as a single point of doubt; this is according to the *Xuan*.
The text states that the *Lotus Sūtra* is manifest (*vivṛta*) and not secret (*guhya*). From this, one knows that at this time there could certainly have been no such teaching.
Yet, the *Shiqian* (Sub-commentary on the *Zhiguan*) contains the statement that "there is no time when it is not pervasive" and that "it exists in every flavor.

If this is taken as a general principle, what is the meaning? One might say: there is truly no need for doubt; it is only because of a lack of clarity regarding the textual structure (*vyañjana-lakṣaṇa*) that doubt arises. Let us now attempt to resolve this.
This clarification first demonstrates the intent behind the existence and non-existence [of these teachings].

Furthermore, because in the past the capacities of sentient beings (*jī*) and the teachings (*jiào*) were not yet unified, it was necessary to employ such concealment and provisionality to reach them. However, as for the present sutra, since the capacities are now pure and unified and the teaching has likewise been revealed and clarified, what further use would there be for such provisional teachings?
It is like military strategy: it is employed during the time of actual combat, but is truly not used once the enemy has been defeated.
This is because the *Lotus Sūtra* subsequently shattered the great array [of opposing doctrines]; thus, the *Xuanyiwen* (Profound Meaning) is indeed trustworthy.

Yet, as for the text itself, some passages are difficult while others are easy; therefore, I have further searched through other texts and summarized them according to four general principles to demonstrate this:

namely, that there are cases where the words are identical but the intent differs, where the capacity [of the audience] is secret while the teaching is not, and where the discourse is expansive yet the meaning ultimately lacks textual corroboration.
However, for those whose minds are naturally limited, the text says: "The Lotus Sūtra is a secret [teaching] entrusted to the bodhisattvas.
This means that the present sūtra is purely perfect and purely wondrous; it is the secret among secrets, the most subtle and esoteric, and the treasury of the secret sūtras.
This is what is meant by "the words are the same, but the intent is different. Furthermore, the text states: "In the Dharma-exposition, there is secrecy."
Regarding the passage, "Hearing the gate of the Great Vehicle’s tracks, there is a secret hearing of the lifespan," this refers to the capacity of the recipient (*yogya*);

thus, although it is secret in terms of the recipient, it remains manifest in terms of the Dharma, because both are the Perfect Vehicle (*paripūrṇa-yāna*). The *Myōryaku* (Wondrous Joy) also states: "Though secret, it is manifest"—meaning that while the recipient is secret, the teaching (*śāsana*) is not.
Furthermore, the *Shiki* (Sub-commentary) says: "What prevents the *Lotus Sūtra* from also being mutually [related] with the other teachings throughout the ten directions?"

Regarding the Exoteric and Esoteric teachings, [the opponent] replies: "In the ten directions there may be one seat, but certainly not this cause. The *Genmon* (Profound Meaning) presents three pairs of characteristics;

while in the ten directions this seat may accommodate such a teaching, in terms of its meaning it is peripheral. In reality, the Esoteric teaching properly discusses the relationship between the one and the many.
Furthermore, since they do not know this, it is explained here for beginners and those among humans and devas who have been granted this opening.
That which follows the occasion [of the teaching] is certainly what is known; moreover, one has heard that in the Root Gate (Mūla-mukha), there is nothing that is not known.

What is meant by "even if one discusses it exhaustively, the meaning ultimately remains inexhaustible"? If one speaks according to the text, it seems to encompass all five flavors rather than being restricted to any single flavor;
thus, even three or four flavors may be spoken of. Furthermore, regarding the intent of the initial passage, the inquiry therein refers only to the *Avataṃsaka* and the other three [scriptures].

At that time, when faced with difficult questions, one answers by responding cryptically; thus, it is known that this passage applies universally across the three periods and its intent extends through the *Prajñāpāramitā*—this meaning is also clear.

Furthermore, although the flavor of the phrasing in the subsequent text is not fixed, these five points merely connect to the preceding text concerning the vertical progression of the single path, which is why they are so difficult to interpret.
Now, examining the intent of the text, the upper and lower sections are fundamentally not connected; this is how it should be understood.

If one explains this by way of its sections, there is no harm; that is, immediately following the "Correctly Clarifying" section, the main text directly points to the "Profound Text" (*Xuánwén*) to refute the ancients.
Furthermore, beneath the "Taste of Taste" (*Wèiwèi*), the Master of the Record (*Jìzhǔ*) added a refutation of the ancients.

The reason he added this refutation of the ancients was his intention that our school not only establishes [the truth] by refuting their partial errors, but also that every single "taste" possesses the secret and the indeterminate.
To judge and explain this, it is certainly not something he could have known. Since Wönwu (Xuanwu) did not hold this view, we know that these [passages] are interpolations and refutations.
Thus, the statement "all possess [it]" reverts to its original context. This is what is meant by the words being universal while the meaning is inherently restricted.
Now, if one grasps these four points, it is clear that the *Lotus Sūtra* ultimately cannot contain such esoteric teachings. Furthermore...
Furthermore, what cause for doubt is there?

Regarding the threefold cycles of transformation in the teachings of the sūtras, there are aspects that are difficult yet easy, and easy yet difficult; as illustrated in the *Lotus Sūtra* regarding the merits of the six sense faculties.
Regarding the number one thousand two hundred and eighty, the text says nothing at all about how this number arises naturally;

it is only through the interpretation of the Dharma-characteristics by the Four Reliances that the principle is established, such that no master of men dares to dispute it—is this not both difficult and yet easy?
As for the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, which delineates the directions and worlds as they undergo circular transformation, it establishes the merits of the six sense-faculties through three successive cycles.
If the teacher of men, on the contrary, is actually muddled, is this not a case of making the easy difficult? I have once sought the explanations in the commentaries;

although there are several schools of the Master’s teachings (as fully presented in the *Jijie*), they are all vague and lack definitive criteria. As for the separate interpretation of Xiachuan, it says:
"The Buddha’s intent is difficult to fathom, and I do not yet dare to correlate it with his *dharmalakṣaṇa*. I, being foolish, have privately harbored doubts regarding this.
How could there be a text that possesses the words but lacks the substance, serving merely to display numerical figures?
Or how could it conceal its true meaning and fail to explain it, leaving one to merely guess and speculate? Consequently, I examined the text and read through it carefully several times;
when I encountered the passage stating that there are ten directions and three flow-numbers, I finally understood the meaning clearly and realized what these changing numbers signify.
The Sūtra has indeed stated this: is it not that the cardinal directions are precisely defined to express the number of ten generations, which are then considered as three?
Furthermore, there is no doubt regarding the remaining numbers; thus, one not only grasps their actual reality but also understands the principle of flux and transformation.
Therefore, I shall further explain them: "the shifting of the three periods" is called *liú* (flux), and "the changing of the ten directions" is called *biàn* (transformation).
This is precisely what constitutes the completion of the one thousand two hundred merits; it lies in this alone. Why?

Because when the first layer is applied to the ten directions, the six [intermediate] directions are excluded, leaving only the four cardinal directions to intersect with the world and establish the fundamental number of twelve.
This is what is meant by "three times four and four times three, revolving to make twelve," as viewed from the perspective of the subsequent two generations.
Thus, including those belonging to the past up to the second layer, one encounters those existing in the present;
taking one from the previous twelve as a point of reference and speaking of the transformation within this single direction, one further multiplies it by ten, thereby forming the ten directions.
Since it is thus for one direction, the same applies to the other directions, resulting in one hundred and twenty. This continues until the third layer, when [the future] is yet to come.

In the next life, one proceeds by taking ten from among the one hundred and twenty; based on these ten directions, they are further transformed into another hundred examples, totaling one thousand two hundred.
This is what is meant by the "threefold transformation of the flow" (liubian sandie): ten, hundred, and thousand.
Thus, in the first stage, six are eliminated and four are retained because this establishes the fundamental positions; subsequently, the remaining six are taken back.
That which is sufficient to constitute the ten directions does so by defining them primarily through the second world-period (*dvitīya-loka*) in terms of their phenomenal transformation;
thus, it is able to include the remaining six indeterminate directions. However, previous commentators were confused by the initial passage and remained ignorant of this point.

If one were to strictly exclude them and not employ them, why would the subsequent text repeatedly mention the ten directions while also including the four intermediate points (*vidiś*)? Therefore, the directions must necessarily be expanded to ten.
This is because direction shifts according to thought or changes as it pursues objects; thus, direction is not fixed. A single direction may change into ten, and ten may change into a hundred.
This is because the world inevitably reaches these three stages, and the transformations reach their ultimate limit here.

Although this was originally intended to demonstrate the merits of the six faculties, it is expressed in terms of "direction" and "world" because the faculties and consciousnesses universally encompass the extent of the objects they perceive.

Since they do not depart from this, it is for this reason that one first speaks of each of the six faculties as having twelve hundred [units], yet further distinguishes their relative superiority and inferiority, as well as their varying increases and decreases;
this is because they are described differently according to the faculties, the directions, and the worlds.
Indeed, what are now called "merits" are spoken of in terms of delusion and its functions; therefore, there are the figures of twelve hundred and eight hundred. If...

Regarding the similarities and differences with the *Fahua lun* (Treatise on the Lotus Sutra), although the numbers of increases and decreases are the same, the meaning of their merits is entirely different.
That [treatise] speaks from the perspective of the Dharma based on the virtues that serve as adornments; thus it says, "By means of these merits, one adorns the six sense organs.

Consequently, there are differences such as excess or deficiency and equality. As for why there is excess or deficiency, it is because they manifest mutual functioning through increase and decrease. It is not [the case that]... [the text continues].

Because the faculties (*indriya*) and powers (*bala*) possess varying degrees of strength and weakness, they are further characterized as "equal" to manifest their non-duality; when the virtue of non-duality reveals the purity of the six faculties, there is no difference.

These points all reflect the intent of the sutra commentaries and the *Xuanyiwen*; if one wishes to know them in detail, they can be understood by examining the texts.

The *Dedede Daoyulun* (Treatise on Attaining What is Attained) states that there are things which appear small but are actually great, and matters which seem slow but are actually essential. To say "attaining what is attained" refers to the completion of karma. Those who do not understand take this to be the fruit (*phala*).
What is it that is set aside because those who understand its principles consider it too minor to discuss?

Or even if it were discussed, few would grasp the reality of its names and characteristics, and it would be nothing more than empty talk. Yet one does not realize there is something both great and essential that must be distinguished.
A person cannot remain without action; if there is action, it is either evil or good. If it is good—
Although evils differ, the characteristics of their fruition are uniform. Generally, when karma arises, it is extremely swift and easy to accomplish;

beginning subtly, it becomes manifest in the end. When it continues without interruption, it is called "binding" (*śreṇī*); when it is not abandoned, it is called "seeding" (*bīja*). These are all the meanings of how karma attains its fruition.

If one truly knows that evil karma is thus, can one not fear it and abandon it? As for goodness— *(Note: The provided text ends abruptly with "As for goodness," leaving the subsequent commentary on merit incomplete.)*

Since karma is thus, should one not diligently strive to practice it? This "acquisition of acquisition" (*prāpti-prāpti*) is the most supreme and essential teaching for a strategy to migrate toward goodness and distance oneself from transgression.
Examining that minor school (*kṣudraka-nikāya*), it also possesses four gates;

the meaning of "acquisition of acquisition" likely originates from the Sarvāstivāda school, which is why the *Fuxing* (Supplementary Practice) says: "Based on the Sarvāstivāda, 'acquisition of acquisition' is established, gradually following after [the primary acquisition]."

Because each attainment is attained by a preceding attainment, it enables past karma to reach the future; thus, when karma is completed in a single moment, there is the dharma of karma, which possesses both great attainments (*mahāprāpti*) and small attainments (*prāpti*).

These are also called the "root dharma" (*mūladharma*), the "attainment of the dharma" (*dharmaprāpti*), the "attainment of the attainment of the dharma" (*dharmaprāptiprāpti*), and so forth—all of which are synonymous terms.

This applies generally to both manifest (*vijñapti*) and unmanifest (*avijñapti*) karma, whether virtuous or non-virtuous minds, as they are analyzed through every moment across the three periods of time.
The details thereof are as set forth in that text; here they are omitted for brevity. For now, I shall merely indicate two points by which it is difficult [to establish]:
first, the source from which the name is derived; second, the magnitude of the attainment. What is meant by "the source from which the name is derived"?

It refers to the sense of "acquisition" (*prāpti*) and also the sense of "accomplishment" (*siddhi*). Furthermore, acquisition is equivalent to accomplishment, and accomplishment is equivalent to acquisition; these terms are mutually synonymous.
(As seen in the *Vibhāṣā*, the *Prajñapti-śāstra*, and other treatises) why is this stated repeatedly? Some say it may be spoken of by generally encompassing both the Great and Small Vehicles;

although this explanation is comprehensive, it does not precisely capture the intended meaning. Now, it is said that because there are four reasons, the name is established based on the third [reason]:

first, because a single moment is sufficient; second, because the number three is completed; third, because the subsequent depends upon the preceding; and fourth, because the names and meanings are identical.
Therefore, it is said that "the subsequent attainment (pṛṣṭhalabdha) subsequently attains the prior attainment"—this is precisely its meaning.

Furthermore, since the *Abhidharmakośa* explicitly designates the third [moment] as "attainment-of-attainment" (*prāpti-prāpti*), if one were to follow the second [moment], what would be the point of the various superior intentions? Why would there be a distinction between "great" and "small" attainments?

It may be designated as such based on whether one or two [moments] are attained; or it may be called "great" or "small" based on whether they occur successively or simultaneously; or it may be determined by their relative strength.
"Through weakness there is joy" (and so forth)—these are all the arguments of former masters, whose relative merits are not easily determined.

Nevertheless, whether one has attained [the fruit] to a greater or lesser degree, let us for now accept the name; yet if its actual substance has not been attained, it may all be considered "not yet realized.
It is essential first to demonstrate the reality underlying the name before one can speak of its magnitude. What is called "reality" refers to the attainment of the dharmas of karma.

This is the meaning [of karma]. Generally, whether an action is wholesome or unwholesome, it must have both causes and conditions. Sometimes the mind serves as the cause and the environment serves as the condition;

sometimes the environment serves as the cause and the mind serves as the condition. This extends to the various *pāramitās* and so forth—all are phenomena of karma (*karmadharma*), and are merely what are called the "expedients" (*upāya*) of karma.
If one's mental thoughts have not yet conjoined with external objects, it is still merely a phenomenon of karma. Essentially, apart from the mind...

Only when the provisional body and speech interact with that [mind] can they perform and create; this is what is meant by the principle of the "attainment of great attainment" (*mahāprāpti*) regarding karma.
When body and speech arise, if they are not simultaneously impelled by mental karma (*manas-karman*), they will likewise be useless—how then could there be "great attainment"?
If even for a single moment there is an interval, the body and speech cannot move of their own accord, let alone karma.
That by which this can be accomplished is what is meant by the principle of attaining the great through attaining the small. Thus, the *Abhidharmakośa* says:

"When one attains attainment (*prāpti*), one achieves the dharma. This is precisely what that refers to. If one were to have only this thought, yet body and speech did not operate in conjunction with it, could the karma intended to be accomplished be attained?
Therefore, if body and speech do not at that time accomplish the dharma of the prior karma, [the attainment would likewise fail].
It is able to bring about the subsequent moment; this is what is meant by the principle of "attaining the great through attaining the small. Therefore, the *Abhidharmakośa* states:

"When a dharma arises, one acquires that dharma as well as the acquisition of the acquisition (*prāpti-prāpti*). This is precisely for this reason. Although [the acquisition and the acquisition of the acquisition] are spoken of as preceding and following, they are fundamentally not at different times;
rather, within a single *kṣaṇa*, there is this mutual attainment of one another. Since this applies to both body and speech...
If one considers "great attainment" (*mahā-lābha*), it manifests outwardly and is coarse and apparent; thus, it is appropriately called "great.
If one considers "small attainment" (*parīttaka-lābha*) as the mental action (*manas-karman*), it is stored within and is subtle and hidden; thus, it is appropriately called "small.

Therefore, it is known that these two attainments do not transcend the principle of the three actions being either great or small; this meaning is now made clear. Nevertheless, here we shall demonstrate their greatness and smallness.

Regarding its characteristics, although it is explained in terms of karma, it is accomplished through the three types of karma; yet these three are not [the karma itself], as they are designated as "karma" only in relation to the body and so forth.
The *Fuxingyu* (Subcommentary) states: "The attainment of 'action' and 'non-action' merely accompanies the physical form; therefore, it is called 'attainment.

Because it is neither matter nor mind, the *Abhidharmakośa-śāstra* classifies it under the category of non-associated formations (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*). This is precisely its meaning. Speaking from this perspective, it is "attainment."

This should be divided into two parts: there are acquisitions (*prāpti*) that perish along with the form (*rūpa*), and there are acquisitions that do not perish. Since the acquisition of karma that has been completed does not vanish, it is said:
"When karma enters the past, its acquisition extends into the future. This refers to the acquisition that does not perish. Furthermore, it is said:

"When the body dies, the acquisition perishes, and the retribution of the future arises. This refers to the acquisition that perishes. These [two] modes of presentation have not been composed here as a single exposition.
Although this is indeed difficult to clarify, neither the *Śāstra* nor the *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary) explicitly states this; why then do you present it here as proof? It is said:
Although this originates from the Sarvāstivāda school, it is known through the Sautrāntika school. Why is this so? As the *Fuxing* states:
"If, according to the Sautrāntika tenet, that which is attained is merely provisional, then one simply says that it is formed by the union of the mind with body and speech."
Karma is conventionally designated as the "seed" that reaches into future births; based on this, it is discussed as being entirely comprised of the three types of karma.

Although their designations differ, the verification of the attainment of the Great and Small Vehicles shows no difference in their essential substance. Though their doctrinal tenets may diverge, the reality of the Dharma does not differ. Since one attains this through that, is this not a clear textual authority?
Once the fundamental principle is clarified, the remaining passages can be understood; there is no need for trivial doubts and difficulties. This is insufficient [to cause confusion].
Those of eminent learning and clear insight will surely understand this for themselves.
The aforementioned practice of circumambulating to the right is a ritual of reverence; for the Dharma originated in Western India and began with the deities and humans paying homage to the Buddha.

This is the practice of those who act according to principle; although these ritual protocols have not been heard of before in this region, they are now transmitted here to be handed down to future generations.
All who perform acts of reverence and circumambulate while reciting should follow this example, for there has never been a single day when it was not practiced.
This is something that must be rectified: if one examines the standard rituals, proceeding from the east to the south and from the west to the north is what is called "right" (dextral).
One circles around it and inevitably acts upon it, whether thinking it is right or acting upon it while knowing it is wrong.
If it is indeed right, one cannot avoid the objections of others; if one acts upon it while knowing it is wrong, it is merely self-deception.
How can there be a lifelong practice of constant conduct that both tolerates deception and error? One must surely seek what is correct. Furthermore, as for those who call it wrong—what of them?

To be unable to compose this oneself is all the more a form of deception. As for what is called "anomalous ritual" (*yìyí*), although I have not yet seen other texts on the matter, I have previously encountered such an account in the *Cǎ'ān Lù* (Record of the Thatched Hut).
Its general purport does not go beyond taking that which is to one's right as being "self" and that which is to the Buddha's right as being "non-self";

thus, it uses the right side—such as lying on the right, baring the right shoulder, and circumambulating to the right—to signify goodness. Even a sage’s [distinctions] are no more than a hair’s breadth.

Regarding the claim that the clockwise circumambulation (*pradakṣiṇa*) and other such signs serve as proof [of the Buddha's superiority], the account that after his parinirvāṇa the golden coffin rose by itself and circumambulated the city to the right is an error of the translators.
That which I call "right" refers to the Way of Earth; it symbolizes the virtue of flexibility and compliance, and nothing more.
As for whether this is indeed the case, I say: these are the words of the great elders of former generations.
How could one now discuss this, and how would I dare to grant it privately? I request that you permit me to speak of it publicly as follows:

practices such as exposing the right side or baring the right shoulder are consistent with universal principle. What is currently practiced is the standard ritual for the right side and is also in accordance with the sacred teachings.
Each conforms to its proper significance; how could one dare to contravene it? It must be that we do not abandon universal principle nor revert to the ordinary.
If one’s ritual conduct does not contravene the sacred teachings, it may be called "good. Judging by present standards, the three statements mentioned above do not exceed two meanings:
namely, following what is appropriate for oneself on both the left and right, and applying that to the left and right of another.

Since what is appropriate for oneself is as previously described (as in the meaning of "thoroughly following principle"), so too is what is applied to others (as in the meaning of "constantly conforming to the two cosmic principles and the sacred teachings").

The two [traditions] agree in their words but differ in their underlying principles. Thus, the current clarification that circumambulating from the right is precisely the act of circumambulating the Buddha is a principle applied to that [context].
How can one take what is appropriate for oneself and apply it to the contrary case?
Nevertheless, while this may be called straightforward, it cannot yet be said to be exhaustive. Let us attempt to explain further by building upon the previous meaning.
It is said that what accords with one's own self is universally applicable throughout the world without change, while what is applied to others follows the preferences of each particular region.

Precisely because it is universally applicable throughout the world without change, there is no principle that is not identical; thus, practices such as baring the right shoulder or the right side all accord with the "right" of one's own self.
Even the great sages who have transcended the world and the customs of India (Gāndhāra) do not differ in this regard.
Since external customs cannot possibly contradict this principle, the doctrine of the grass hut is entirely correct; thus it is said that it does not abandon the universal principle.
Indeed, one must follow what each region values: the customs of India differ greatly from those here.
Just as this land honors the left while that land honors the right, the meaning of circumambulating to the right is simply a matter of local custom.
The reason why the nirvana and the circumambulation of the golden coffin necessarily proceed clockwise from the city is likely because the Tathāgata bestowed his final gift there;
it is also due to the significance of following the cardinal directions. Knowing this, one should realize that the established ritual conforms to this principle.

Could it then be considered an error? Therefore it is said: "Not deviating from established ritual is also to follow the holy teachings. Moreover, since he has already performed the circumambulation clockwise, [the subsequent rites must likewise follow].

This [circumambulation] should properly be performed on one's left, which is the Buddha’s left from one’s own perspective; furthermore, as this accords with general principles, why should it not be so?
However, because the ritual originated there [in India], it cannot be practiced here [in China].
Although circumambulating from the right does not contradict the local rules of propriety for worship, this is because that which is appropriate for oneself cannot be applied to others.

When one person bestows something upon another, it cannot necessarily accord with one's own convenience; since both cannot be achieved simultaneously, one must first deliberate upon what is appropriate regarding their relative weight.

Thus, there are cases where one abandons oneself to follow another, and cases where one follows oneself through the agency of another. In the present case, circumambulating the Buddha by keeping him to one's right is of primary importance;

it is therefore fitting to abandon one’s own custom of keeping the right side toward oneself and instead follow the Buddha’s tradition of keeping the right side toward him. This is the intended meaning.
This method of greeting an elder should likewise be understood in this way. From this it follows that the ritual of circumambulation is performed for others and not for oneself;
thus, in principle, it must proceed from the person [being honored], as it originates there and not here.
Alas! These words exhaust the matter.
The Ten-Chapter Treatise on the Integration and Separation of the Nature of Cultivation and Perfection (Yuanwan Xiuxing Lihelun).
Part One: An Exposition of the General Principles.
The Dharma-Gate of the Universal Characteristics of the Great Perfect Enlightenment Essence: The Natural Unity of the Three Dharmas, Harmonizing the Various Sects.
Blended yet ever more distinct, beyond discourse and beyond thought, neither joined nor dispersed; in its essence it is complete, and through cultivation, that essence becomes cultivation.

When cultivation arises from the essence, the essence entirely becomes cultivation. The essence does not shift, and cultivation remains eternally as it is. Whether in delusion or awakening, cause or effect, all are thus.
This is truly because the wondrous body has no fixed form, while the comprehensive explanation encompasses all; beginning with the equality of the one nature, it culminates in ultimate realization.

The Three Virtues reach their ultimate within this [Middle Way]. One’s own delusion is resolved through understanding; based on that understanding, one establishes practice; through cultivation, there is realization.

Realization is divided into the true and the semblance, proceeding from cause to fruit. When cultivation reaches its limit, it returns to the source. From beginning to end, the ultimate consummation lies herein. To summarize: it does not exceed the Three Truths.
Since the nature of the Three Truths is extinguished and their phenomenal characteristics are void and profound, the essence reaches its ultimate and the aspects merge harmoniously.
Thus, there are three [truths] and nine phrases; as they vary according to their meaning, they are sometimes combined and sometimes separated.

It is for this reason that this particular school’s Perfect Teaching (Yuanzong) demonstrates the union and separation of cultivation and nature (*xiuxing*). Now, what are the Three Truths? They are the innate, natural virtue of one's nature (*xingde*).
Furthermore, it is said that the Three Truths are the designation for "One. Because of their harmonious inclusion, to raise up "One" is immediately "Three," and the entirety of "Three" is "One."
One separated becomes three, making nine; these nine combined become three. This is not because they produce one another, nor because they contain one another;
rather, it is the spontaneous nature of the essence of *dharmatā*. Thus, to raise one and immediately have three is the natural law (*dharmatā*);

that the entirety of the three is one is because their essence is without difference. That separation of the three results in nine manifests their perfect completeness; that the combination of the nine returns to three [demonstrates]...
This is indeed the meaning of "predominance. Thus, one is not fixed as one; one is precisely three. Three is not fixed as three; three is precisely one.
Neither three nor one, yet nine and three—when discussing its essence, it is invariably without even a single [unit].
How could there be nine or three? It is neither separate nor combined. Yet, in accordance with names and meanings, it is both separate and combined; this is simply...
When discussing their separation and union from the perspective of their single essence: where they are separated, they are always united; where they are united, they are always separated.

Thus, the principle of separation and union is established, and the perfect purport resides therein. To illustrate this: it is like a great round mirror, like diamond dust, like the letter *i*, and like the two eyes of heaven;

through subtle union, [the truth] may be known. This is the general outline. However, rather than taking the three virtues (*triguṇa*) and so forth as the basis, one here defines them according to the three truths (*trisatya*).
As for "showing," it refers to the fact that the three truths are the truth of the rational nature; they are neither delusion nor enlightenment, being pervasive and without distinction.

Therefore, they are collectively summarized as "separation and union. If one understands this, the fundamental meaning becomes easy to comprehend and the source is recognized; having realized this, one has already mastered more than half of the task.
Second, showing cultivation and nature:

Before discussing separation and integration, one must first demonstrate cultivation and nature. For "cultivation and nature" is the name for the determined reality, while "separation and integration" is the meaning of pervasive transformation.
Since the meaning of pervasive transformation does not manifest of itself, it is clarified by means of the reality.
That is to say, the Middle Way within the aforementioned Three Truths is the nature (*xing*), while the True and the Conventional are the cultivation (*xiu*);

thus, both are cultivated together, or alternatively, the Three Truths are the nature and the three contemplations (*san guan*) are the cultivation. In this case, "cultivation" refers to the application of effort and contrivance, whereas "nature" refers to that which is originally present and unchanging.

"Nature" speaks to the principle (*li*), while "cultivation" speaks to the phenomenon (*shi*). As for the phenomenon, it is the transformation and creation of the three thousand [realms] through cultivation.
All phenomena within the middle [realm] are not merely the three thousand [worlds]; it is insufficient to exhaustively cultivate their principle without reaching the ultimate.

Their essence is fundamentally quiescent; the three thousand natures are all-encompassing within all phenomena. It is not that the three thousand are insufficient to fully realize the subtlety of nature.
This indeed captures the reality. To further clarify this by means of dharmic characteristics: the objective realm is itself the rational nature of the three virtues.
"Equality" and so forth are all nature; "wisdom" is the understanding of the three virtues, while "practice" is the contemplation of the three virtues—these and others are all cultivation.
Extending this principle broadly, it encompasses the beginning and the end. Thus, the three paths, the three consciousnesses, and the other ten sets of triads are none other than these.
As for the general framework of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanzong*), any phenomena related to principle and fact, or cultivation and nature, are included therein.

All of these can be harmonized and integrated (and so forth). To examine their underlying intent, it is precisely to manifest that the nature is inherently complete and that they mutually constitute and reveal one another.
Only because the inherent completeness of the nature is clearly manifested does the principle of the Perfect Teaching hold that there is no dharma that is not the nature;

since all dharmas are extinguished within the nature and are without fabrication, it is said: "If one does not understand that the mind-only manifests the body of inherent completion, [this is not] the Sudden-Perfect [teaching]."

This is precisely the meaning of "the principle being established as merely a vain application. Indeed, it is through mutual establishment and manifestation that cultivation cannot manifest nature, and nature cannot establish cultivation;
neither can be missing. What is called "nature being thus from the beginning, yet relying on wisdom to initiate cultivation;
through cultivation one illuminates nature, and through nature one gives rise to cultivation," and so forth, refers to these two meanings alone. Although there is... [text ends]

The meaning of this is already somewhat remote; thereafter, one should know that the nature-virtues (*prakṛti-guṇa*) involve both arising and inclusion, while the cultivation-virtues (*bhāvanā-guṇa*) involve both conformity and opposition.
Regarding the nature-virtues, there are two further meanings within this "inclusion":

first, the nature of the natural nature-virtues, which refers to the principle of nature as it naturally includes all phenomena; second, the nature that points to cultivation as being identical to nature, as it is said:

The inherent virtues (*prakṛti-guṇa*) are simply the *dharmadhātu*; within a single thought-moment of this *dharmadhātu*, the three dharmas are fully present, which are also the three paths and the three virtues, and so forth.
Because these are inherently complete, when the inherent nature gives rise entirely to cultivation, this constitutes all phenomena within that cultivation.

Although these phenomena are numerous, they do not transcend the "contrary" and "conforming" aspects; according to the Perfect Teaching (*yuan-quan*), they all arise entirely from the inherent nature, being nothing but the full manifestation of the natural state (*tianran*).

That which arises from the nature-merit (*prakṛti-guṇa*) permeates both the adverse and the favorable; for although the adverse may turn away from the nature, the nature has never turned away from itself.

If one were to discuss arising solely in terms of cultivation as identical to the nature, then such arising would be exclusively in accordance with cultivated practice. Consequently, there are cases where all three truths give rise to the three contemplations;

cases where the entire wondrous object gives rise to wisdom and practice, each discussed in terms of its own three factors; and cases where the single *zhengyin* (correct cause) alone [gives rise to them].

Regarding the two types of cultivation—cultivation through conditions and through understanding that arise from the nature—and the two types of cultivation—cultivation of the principle of realization and cultivation of the manifestation of function that arise from the single nature:

this is because the characteristics of phenomena involve both separation and integration, the stages of practice involve both horizontal and vertical progression, and the pointing toward cultivation involves both advancement and retreat (the meaning of which will be seen later).

In reality, there is no divergence in the path of the Dharma; furthermore, because these follow the order of cultivation, there is separation and integration, whereas in the case of reverse cultivation, such distinctions are not considered.

If one were to discuss them in terms of "contrary" and "conforming," they would simply be matters of cultivation; thus we know that it is not by means of the three paths and three virtues as contrary or conforming that this is established.

Rather, it is by means of the partial and the perfect teachings, and by delimiting the scope of emotional intellect (*qing*) and wisdom (*zhi*), that this is discussed. Yet even this is still a discourse concerning the relative opposition of cultivation and nature (*xing*);

it has not yet revealed the principle of "single integration" (*yihé*). If it is not yet single integration, how much less could it be "fusion and dissolution"? As for that which is truly single integration: [The original text continues with the definition of single integration.]
As for this merging and dissolution, its stage begins with the Perfect Abiding (*yuanzhu*) and reaches its ultimate consummation in Wondrous Enlightenment (*miaojue*). Therefore it is said:

"Cultivation and nature are unified as one, with no further division," and again: "To realize that there is neither cultivation nor nature, but only the single wondrous Dharma, the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), which is brilliantly luminous and without differentiation"—this is what is meant by merging and dissolution.
Thus, while explained separately according to the stages, although it is restricted to specific limits, [it ultimately reveals the non-duality of the absolute].

The essential purport of the *Yuanlun* (Treatise on the Perfect) is that reality actually pervades the six stages of realization; this refers to what is called the "single fusion of the principle-nature" (*li-xing*) and so forth.

Since this fusion and merging are pervasive, the discourse regarding the relative distinction between cultivation and nature (*xiu-xing*) should likewise apply from beginning to end. Therefore, the *Miaole* states:

"Precisely because the principle is one, the relative distinction between cultivation and nature involves separation and fusion. Is it not the case that one discusses separation and fusion precisely because of this oneness?"
To rely on a passage concerning "union" and claim that union and separation are restricted to what precedes [the present] is incorrect.
Is it that the union of that [past state] is not the union of the present? Or is what we now call "separation" a separation consisting of actual fragmentation?
Thus one knows that those ancients were people who relied on false authorities.

Having thrice stated the names and characteristics, the principles of cultivation (*xiū*) and nature (*xìng*) have been made manifest; the intent regarding their separation and union is contained therein. Thus, separation and union are not different from cultivation and nature.

However, as the meaning has not yet been fully revealed, it must be further demonstrated. Although the intent of separation and union is fundamentally derived from the Buddhas and Patriarchs, [it remains implicit].
However, because the name [of this text] originated with Jingxi, the *Fahua Wenju* (Commentary on the Lotus Sutra) and the *Wu'er Men* (Gate of Non-duality) discuss it at length.
Now, as for the terms "separation" (*li*) and "union" (*he*), many have previously offered explanations, yet none have captured the correct meaning; thus, there is no need for further evaluation.

I now maintain that by simply stating that the three dharmas are "unified," their significance is already complete—why labor over further inquiries? Nevertheless, if one must provide a formal exegesis, one must first understand what "separation" entails.

"Union" (*he*) is a term that implies opposition; since names do not necessarily share the same meaning, what is called "separation" (*li*) here carries the sense of opening, and thus union is contained within it—as in the phrase "constantly opening according to nature," where union is implied.
Furthermore, "union" carries the sense of identity, and thus separation is contained within it—as in the phrase "identically named as the true cause," where separation is implied.
This is not only the precise meaning of union and separation, but it also captures their mutual relationship.
The purport of this section may be explained from this point onward. What is their characteristic? It is that they do not emerge apart from that from which the three and one arise;
thus, the "three and one" is itself the essence of their separation and union. Therefore, it is appropriate to know this first: the so-called "three" refers to name, characteristic, and function;
the "one" refers to substance. Thus, from name, there is what is called substance; from characteristic, [there is function].

Regarding essence and characteristic, they are subsumed under function; as for that which is opposed to essence and function, it is simply one (the meaning of this is found in various texts, so there is no need for further citation here).

Furthermore, whenever "three" and "one" are mentioned, there is a distinction between their general and specific characteristics, and a difference between their mutual inclusion and individual possession.

For example, "one" refers to nirvāṇa and "three" refers to the three virtues; these three are discussed solely within the context of the single nirvāṇa—this is the aspect of their general characteristic.

Regarding the "possession of the three and one": first, if one takes up a single dharma and treats it as either one or three, these are the individual characteristics (biphasa) of each being one or three.

The *Myōraku-ki* states: "Combining those three natures into one refers to the Dharmakāya; it is combined only when contrasted with cultivation (second phrase).

Regarding nature, it is eternally opened (third phrase). Generally, whenever texts clarify that nature and cultivation are each a single dharma—such as 'one earth' or 'one rain' (fourth phrase)—since the analogy is not of a single intent, how could they be identical?
Furthermore, it does not exceed four meanings: first, the functional capacity..."
1. It removes [defilements] like a golden probe; its nature-virtue (*prakṛti-guṇa*) and its conditions—the *pratyaya* and *upāya*—are collectively termed the "correct cause" (*samyak-hetu*).

This is illustrated by two examples where the names and meanings of the two [aspects] are each predominant, as the *Myōraku* states: "Names are received according to what is predominant," and "The three are bound together into one" (these two points correspond to the second phrase above).

2. Its essence and virtues are perfectly complete, as the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says: "Directly [it is] the Dharma-body," etc. (this corresponds to the first three and second phrases above). 3. Its Dharma... [text fragment]
The meaning of practicing by taking mutually corresponding categories as one's primary objects of focus (which is also the fourth phrase) should be elucidated through four principles;
furthermore, these four examples should be applied universally across all teachings. Thus, although the textual expressions are numerous, they do not exceed these [four].

Only by adapting to what is appropriate does the manifestation of the teaching become boundless; each must accord with its own specific meaning and cannot be discussed in a narrow or fixed manner. — Xi.
Master Guan exclusively relies on the passage concerning the "correspondence between cultivation and nature" (*xiuxing hehe*) to establish a fixed formula for the classification of teachings.

If, according to him, cultivation must necessarily correspond to nature, then this would merely follow the principle of "following the stronger," thereby losing the intent of perfect completeness (*yuanju*) and contradicting the meaning of the preceding text;
thus, his interpretation is incorrect. Alternatively, one may universally establish the fourfold grid of cultivation and nature, opening and closing, etc., to refute his argument.

There is nothing that is not permissible; it is simply that taking a single grain of gold as the covenant for the union of nature and its cultivation, and opening the phrases for their correspondence, is slightly inconvenient.
If one grasps the present meaning, why must it be so?

Regarding the four examples of the method of abandonment (*prahāṇa*), if one examines various texts, there are numerous instances where the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*) are analyzed through the methods of separation and combination; these precedents are not limited to one.

If one fails to grasp the comprehensive explanation that governs them all, how can one organize them to achieve a unified system? That being so, how many such general categories of examples are there? According to what was previously shown:
Whether one elucidates it by means of the three meanings of extensive, concise, and intermediate; or whether one subsumes it under five or seven meanings;

or whether one employs a fourfold analysis (*catuṣkoṭi*) to distinguish them—all these are different ways of establishing doctrinal principles according to the specific textual passages. Thus far, we have not yet discussed the intent regarding their "accordance" (*yù*) and "application" (*yòng*).

If considered in terms of accordance, there are gains and losses, and thus a lack of parity in their relative excellence. If considered in terms of their withdrawal (*duó*), they are too diffuse to have a unifying principle, and thus their true nature remains unseen.

second, the characteristics of the teaching according to its suitability, which involve both the universal and the particular. As for what is meant by the general principle of separation and combination, it refers precisely to the characteristics of the three and nine dharmas.
