when they are not simultaneous, although they face the same object, one is excluded by the other. As the *Saṃdhinirmocana Sūtra* states: "When five mentalities arise simultaneously, there must necessarily be one predominant part."

The statement that "another consciousness arises simultaneously" means that the five sensory consciousnesses operate together with the five mental consciousnesses (*manovijñāna*). Furthermore, the *Zhulin* (Pearl Forest) states:

"For example, when the visual consciousness first falls upon an object, it is called the 'sudden falling mind' (*saṃtīraṇa-citta*); at that same time, the mental consciousness has not yet previously apprehended this [object].

This statement implies that [the sudden falling mind] does not operate together with the mental consciousness. As it is with the visual consciousness, so it is for the other sensory consciousnesses by analogy. Thus it is said.

Thus, that which arises in response to an object is the five sensory consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna*), while that which simultaneously takes an object as its condition is the five mental consciousnesses (*pañca-manovijñāna*).

Therefore, when taking direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) as an object, there are two consciousnesses functioning together; however, when taking inference (*anumāna*) or conceptualization (*vikalpa*) as an object, only the mental consciousness is engaged, as the five sensory consciousnesses have no function at that time.
Thus, the mental consciousness takes two kinds of objects, whereas the five sensory consciousnesses take only direct perception.

Therefore, the *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary) says: "The simultaneous consciousness that takes as its objects both the present five sense-objects and the past [sense-objects]—this is precisely what is meant.
Thus, if one understands this consciousness, the so-called "simultaneous consciousness" can be known from it.

However, when the substance of this simultaneity is the six consciousnesses pervading all the sense organs, they are called the "five consciousnesses"; furthermore, when they share the same objects as the five mental consciousnesses (*manovijñāna*), they are called... [the simultaneous consciousness].
Although the simultaneous mental consciousness (*sahabhū-manovijñāna*) differs in name from the [other] consciousnesses, the consciousness itself is one and the same.

Since ancient times, however, people have been deluded by mere terminology and have sought to establish a so-called "simultaneous mental consciousness" as something distinct; such arguments regarding simultaneity are all untenable because they lose sight of the fundamental principle.

Now, it is said that since it shares the same object of perception (*ālambana*) as the five sensory consciousnesses, the meaning of "simultaneous" is established. This is merely what the text indicates.
Because there are distinctions between the universal and the particular, such as arising and non-arising, or functioning and non-functioning, various texts speak of these matters differently.

For instance, when it is said that the five sense-consciousnesses arise simultaneously with the mental consciousness (manovijñāna), this indicates that the six consciousnesses function at the same time;

furthermore, it is stated from the perspective of the five sense-consciousnesses being "that which is produced. This does not mean that "simultaneity" refers exclusively to [the relationship between the sixth and the others].

Regarding the six consciousnesses, the subtle explanation that the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) is simultaneous [with the five] is precisely because the mental consciousness encompasses both the arisen and the unarisen;
since this refers to a consciousness that has already arisen, it excludes the first moment.

Once the mental consciousness itself has transformed into the conceptualizing [consciousness], it does not necessarily arise simultaneously with the five consciousnesses, as the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states: "The mental consciousness..."

At other times, there are no visual and other consciousnesses because they have previously ceased; if they were to arise simultaneously, as stated in the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra*, would this not be the same as [the case of] simultaneous contact?

By extending this principle to its logical conclusion, one can grasp it through reflection. It is sufficient for scholars to understand how to apply the meaning according to the text and to master its transitions.
Regarding what are called the characteristics of the seventh and eighth consciousnesses, one should first know their names in this context.
The meaning of "identical and different" (yì tóngyì) sequentially demonstrates the characteristics of the eight consciousnesses.
As for why it is called "identical and different," the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states: "The subtle *ālayavijñāna* (dhātuvijñāna), through the accumulation of habitual tendencies, forms a violent torrent.

Yet, while its name refers to the seventh consciousness, its meaning refers to the eighth; as the commentators say (and so forth), which consciousness is this actually? [The answer is: It is not identified by its name here.
Definitions must establish names based on their meaning; however, according to the subtle terminology, it is precisely the eight consciousnesses that are designated as *ādāna*.

I shall now elaborate upon this by means of two meanings: first, by discussing them horizontally in terms of essence (*tattva*), and second, by distinguishing them vertically in terms of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*).
When discussing them horizontally in terms of essence, *ādāna* is none other than *ālaya*, for there is no separate essence; it is merely a designation according to its specific function.

The reason this scripture gives it a distinct name different from others, designating it specifically as *ālayavijñāna* (storehouse consciousness) while fundamentally referring to the eight consciousnesses, is because it follows the sense of "clinging to a self" (*ātma-grāha*) and serves as the cause for the subsequent phrase regarding the "torrential stream of habitual tendencies. Thus, it is named accordingly;

in reality, its subtle essence is the eighth consciousness. It is only when distinguishing them vertically according to their characteristics that the seven consciousnesses receive their respective names.
The eight consciousnesses are named *ālaya-vijñāna*; since their characteristics are distinct, their names must not be conflated.
This is why Tiantai, following the names to distinguish them, presented them vertically according to a single path, each for its own reason. How could they be mutually obstructive?
Yet, those who provide commentaries by explaining the eight consciousnesses through their alternative names know only the first meaning, but do not realize that there is [more].

The reason why the subsequent interpretation does not fully accord with Xiachuan’s teaching is that while the Sanskrit term is indeed general, its attempt to synthesize it with the three dharmas not only fails to correspond to either the Chinese or the Sanskrit original—thereby clearly contradicting our Patriarch—but also leaves the two previous meanings with no point of convergence;
thus, it is certainly not worth adopting. Nevertheless, as for Siming’s direct citation of the "seven consciousnesses," since that is not [the intended meaning],...

In the primary exegesis of the scriptural text, if one provisionally relies on names to verify meanings, there is no harm. Only by attaining these two meanings can one know that the names and meanings of the seventh and eighth consciousnesses have their proper destination.
However, as for clarifying the characteristics of the eight consciousnesses, it is truly not easy to elucidate them as they appear scattered throughout the sūtras and śāstras;

I shall now briefly indicate them. Regarding the general and specific characteristics: the general characteristic refers to what is termed the "source of the mind" (*cittadhātu*) of all sentient beings.

It is called the *tathāgatagarbha* (Tathāgata-store) and also the *ālayavijñāna* (store-consciousness), among other names (as found in the *Bai fa shu* and *Zong jing lu*; these various synonyms are omitted here as they are not essential for the exposition of its characteristics).
This consciousness is a synthesis of the true and the false; it contains and stores all phenomena, possessing the seeds of both the wholesome and the unwholesome.

Through the perfuming and transformation by ignorance (*avidyā*) and other factors, the various defiled and pure phenomena are thereby produced. Therefore, it is collectively termed the *ālayavijñāna*. This is its general [definition].
Regarding the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*): if one distinguishes the characteristic of discernment (*pariccheda-lakṣaṇa*) in contrast to other consciousnesses, as stated in the *Xuánwén*:

"If it were different from these two consciousnesses, it would be the ālayavijñāna" (as cited previously). The reason for this difference is that, when contrasted with the nine consciousnesses, there is the distinction between the mobile and the immobile;
when contrasted with the seven consciousnesses, there is the distinction between discrimination and non-discrimination. Thus, the *Qǐxìn lùn* states: "Because it relies on non-awakening, the mind..."
"Movement is what is called karma (*karma*); this refers to the movement of the mind within the *ālayavijñāna*. Furthermore, it says:
"Transcending all limits, it manifests solely based upon the mind, never departing from *tathatā* (suchness). This means that what is perceived by the *ālayavijñāna* is devoid of discrimination.
Precisely because it is without discrimination, it is not entirely false; and because it is not entirely false, it is close to the Real. Since there still remains...
Because it is active, it is not entirely real; because it is not entirely real, it still belongs to the delusive.
This is therefore the ultimate limit where reality and delusion meet, wherein defilement and purity, good and evil, are stored.

Furthermore, as the *Zangshu* (Treasury Commentary) distinguishes the union of reality and delusion through four propositions, this is both subject to arising and ceasing and yet neither arises nor ceases—just as the ocean contains both motion and stillness; it is also like that.
As for the claim that there are differences among various texts regarding the characteristics [of consciousness], this [work] shall provisionally correct them based on these [principles].
To discern [the nature of] consciousness:

the mind is the source from which consciousness is established, and consciousness is the foundation from which phenomena arise; however, because consciousness possesses both defilement and purity, [phenomena] are produced.
The Dharma is not uniform because various schools of thought follow divergent paths; thus, proponents and opponents dispute one another over what is right and wrong.

Those who assert "this is correct" use strength to support the weak, while those who recognize "that is incorrect" turn from the inferior to align with the superior. Consequently, in establishing consciousness and the arising of dharmas, there are instances of overturning one's own tenets to assist another’s doctrine.
I shall now clarify this in sequence. For example, in the past, the masters who propagated the *Dilun* school were divided into the Northern and Southern branches.

Regarding those who translated the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, there were differences between the Liang and Tang dynasties due to their respective interpretations, resulting in differing systems for establishing the consciousnesses (*vijñāna*).

Some established nine consciousnesses, such as the *amala-vijñāna* (Liang Paramārtha), while others established only eight consciousnesses, such as the *ālaya-vijñāna* (Tang Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang), asserting that "nine consciousnesses" is merely a different name for the same thing.

As for the interpretation of the *Dilun* school, they likewise relied upon the eight consciousnesses, yet distinguished between them based on the difference between the true and the false. Both [traditions] are thus consistent in this regard.
As stated in the text (and so forth), it is simply because their established systems of consciousness differ that their reckonings of the phenomena of arising vary.

Among those who discuss the phenomena of arising based on their established systems of consciousness, there are those who reckon true and false based solely upon the eight consciousnesses; there are those who correlate the phenomena of arising by means of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* and the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*;
these are all matters of how the texts are applied, and do not mean that the characteristics of the texts themselves are fundamentally contradictory.
What is meant by this? As the text states: "The translations by Paramārtha rely on the *amala-vijñāna*, while later translations rely on the *ālaya-vijñāna*.

This is because these [schools] establish their discourse on the arising of phenomena based on the theory of consciousness. Generally speaking, the Liang dynasty school relies on the real (*tattva*), while the Tang dynasty school relies on the delusory (*mṛṣā*).
However, if we consider the eight consciousnesses, it is not that Paramārtha does not rely on the delusory; for he also reckons the *ālaya-vijñāna* as being indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).

Because ignorance gives rise to all phenomena, the [Treatise on] Emptiness (*Śūnyatā-śāstra*) merely collects them [under the heading of emptiness] rather than denying their dependence on the Truth (*tattva*).

Alternatively, it may be because one calculates that all phenomena arise from the *dharmatā* (dharma-nature) within the eight consciousnesses. From this, we know that the two treatises differ in their establishment of the consciousnesses—due to the discrepancy in the number of consciousnesses being eight or nine—but they are consistent in their arising of phenomena, as each calculates that phenomena arise from either the True or the False.
Furthermore, the text says: "The *Dilun Lun* (Treatise on the Expansive Stages)..."

The Master [Huiyuan] held two different views: the Northern School of the Land of Characteristics (Xiangzhou) reckoned the *ālayavijñāna* as the basis of support, while the Southern School of the Land of Characteristics reckoned *tathatā* as the basis of support.
Both of these were calculations based on the eight consciousnesses regarding the true and the false.
This is because that which is reckoned as "true" by the Southerners still relies upon the *ālayavijñāna*. As the text states: "If the people of the Land [of Characteristics] clarify the *ālaya*..."
Since this is the truly eternal, pure consciousness, those who falsely conceptualize it can be known; thus, it differs from the old translation of the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*.

However, as for those who apply the same textual pattern [to other schools], they are taking the various individual conceptualizations as being similar, rather than applying the pattern to the establishment of the consciousnesses themselves.

As for why the *Xuánwén* (Explanatory Text) focuses exclusively on the comparison with the *Dìchí* (Yogācārabhūmi), it is because the Great Master saw only the Liáng dynasty version of the *Saṃgraha*, and thus the text does not mention the Táng dynasty version.
The commentator only begins to mention this in the *Wen zhong* (Within the Text) regarding Jingxi;
however, the specific selection of the Southern School is intended primarily to contrast it with the Liang dynasty translations to demonstrate the characteristics of their respective positions.

Thus, he does not briefly mention the Northern School, not because the *Dilun* school is exclusively "True" (*zhen*) and the *She lun* school is exclusively "False" (*wang*), but because the difficulty of overturning their fundamental tenets and assisting their calculations lies elsewhere—it is simply that they are difficult to refute.

The text says: "The *Wen* (Text) states: 'Furthermore, the *She dacheng* (Mahāyānasaṃgraha) arose; this refers to the Liang dynasty version of the *She*. The Liang version of the *She* originally relied upon the Āmra-vihāra [manuscript], yet it is said that it also calculates *ālayavijñāna* to assist the Northern School—why is this?
Furthermore, it says: 'The *She dacheng* elucidates the meaning of the ten superior characteristics (*daśa-viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*), which all consider to be profoundly ultimate;
this is certainly the Liang version of the *She*. Yet, it is said that if the *Dilun* school were to cause their tradition to flourish, would it not indeed be the *Dilun*?"
Whether one argues from the perspective of the North or the South, one cannot avoid the hindrance of doubt (and so forth). Now, I shall explain it:
if one grasps the intent of the aforementioned application and its meaning, as well as the doctrine of the universal and the particular, there is nothing difficult about it.

Let me briefly conclude with a single statement to assist both schools in their deliberations, so that both may clearly understand: all of these [positions] arise because they conflate the establishment of consciousness (*vijñāna*) with the phenomena of birth (*jāti-dharma*).

Regarding this confusion: if one understands that the establishment of consciousness (*vijñāna*) as a distinct arising phenomenon is universal, what prevents the Liang dynasty’s synthesis from also reckoning the *ālayavijñāna* as assisting [the system], just like the Northern School?
Thus, the phrase "also reckons" is likely said in contrast to the Northern Land;

since it is the same as the Northern Land, its reckoning is superior to the Southern School, thereby causing the Southern Land’s various sects to turn southward toward this synthesis. This can also be understood.
People do not see this, and how many times have they been mired in confusion regarding the characteristics of phenomena?

Now that the explanation is as it is, what difficulty could there be? Nevertheless, these are all explanations concerning the general systems of thought; their evaluation has already been conducted in works such as the *Xuan* (Profound) and the *Zhi guan* (Cessation and Contemplation).
But when it comes to discussing the specific tenet of our own school regarding the establishment of consciousness and the arising of dharmas, what is the case? It is said:
It would be appropriate not to treat this as a definitive conclusion, but rather to discuss it further by way of a general overview of its essential principles;
furthermore, since students should gain understanding for themselves upon examining the text, I have not taken the time to elaborate on this here.

Regarding the differing interpretations of whether the *tri-piṭaka* bodhisattvas sever or suppress afflictions, it is difficult to establish a definitive certainty; yet, among those that are both certain and correct, is there not only the "excellent exposition"?
Although the old treatises concerning the meaning of whether the *tri-piṭaka* bodhisattvas sever or do not sever delusions have been discussed down to the present day, they remain [unresolved].
Returning to the One, there are none who do not claim that what is "severed" is wrong while what is "not severed" is right;
yet because their views are already settled, few exert themselves to seek the ultimate correctness, and such instances are rare.

Now, taking the general purport of the scriptural divisions as a basis to fully establish the doctrine of non-severance, it is hoped that this meaning will become clear, so that those who delight in sophistry may have no [grounds for contention].
In attacking this [position], there are generally three arguments: first, the alignment of the intent of the teaching; second, the refutation and establishment regarding the purport of the sections;

and third, the analysis of the structural connections and hidden implications within the text. Now, regarding the alignment of the intent of the teaching: considering the origin of this teaching’s emergence, it was truly because the small-capacity roots could derive no benefit from the sudden [teaching];
thus, by suspending the Great [Vehicle] and bestowing the Small [Vehicle], the primary aim was for the two vehicles, while the secondary aim was for Bodhi.

If the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas—who harbor loathing and distress toward birth and death—were to hear it said that Bodhisattvas have already severed [the bonds of existence] yet are born again, those of inferior faculties would surely doubt, thinking, "This will be combined with our own teaching," and thus refuse to accept it.
This is why the Buddha conceals the true aspect and does not speak of it directly, as he intends to carry out his provisional teachings for those of lesser capacity;
this is as stated in the text of the *Sijiaoyi* (The Meaning of the Four Teachings). Nevertheless,...
It is not improper to explain for those present who possess such faculties by means of the provisional arising of the six perfections as worldly phenomena to provide a salvific application;
yet, if one were to fulfill the teaching [to its ultimate limit], the person would be discarded. This, moreover, is a case of attaining both through the "concealed aspect" (p’u-hsiang).
The text of the *Miaoxuan* is an example of this. Thus, because it is the concealed aspect, it is said that [the afflictions] are not severed; otherwise, they should be severed.
Ya said: "Since the teaching does not state that [the bodhisattva] abandons [defilements], on what basis is this established? Even if such a thing were to exist, it could simply be set aside.

That those of old occasionally made this claim—that the 'covering characteristics' (fùxiàng) are [abandoned]—is incorrect. Regarding the so-called 'doctrinal intent of the schools' concerning refutation and establishment (*pratiṣedha-prasthāpana*), if it is truly as previously stated, then there certainly exists such a bodhisattva.
That the teaching does not speak of abandoning delusions is precisely in accord with the intent of the doctrine; yet the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* (Dàlùn) rejects this."
If one asks, "What is meant by 'a great error'? the answer is: it is precisely because [the Abhidharma] accords with the intended meaning of the teaching that it is rejected;
one must understand the principle of refutation and establishment. Thus, the *Miaoxuan* (Profound Meaning) says:

"In the *Abhidharma-vibhāṣā-śāstra*, the meaning of the Bodhisattva is explained, yet Nāgārjuna frequently refutes it, claiming that it errs regarding the Buddha’s skillful means; therefore, it must be refuted and corrected."
Because the Buddha’s skillful means require that this be established, the Great Treatise (*Mahā-śāstra*) fundamentally explains the *Prajñāpāramitā* by abolishing one and preserving three.
Thus, wherever the Mahāyāna is used to refute the Hīnayāna, the entire teaching of the Tripiṭaka is what is to be abolished; how could it concern merely the single principle of the Bodhisattva?
Therefore, while the Sūtras establish [the truth] and the Śāstras refute [error], each has its own intended meaning; otherwise, their words would be contradictory.

However, those who pursue the convergence [of teachings] yet lose the essential intent, instead extract the meaning of the Bodhisattva from the commentaries on the Mahāyāna sūtras that they propagate;
this is both a fault of losing the Buddha’s skillful means (*upāya*) and a manifestation of the commentator’s own lack of understanding.
Therefore, it is especially worthy of refutation. If, however, one were to expound the Buddha’s skillful means, then it must be established. Thus, the *Myōryaku* (Wondrous Joy) says: "A..."

The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* also clarifies that there are bodhisattvas who have not severed their fetters (*asaṃkṣipta-saṃyojana*), yet it refutes the provisional [teachings] by stating they do not exist;

this does not mean they are entirely absent, but rather that although the sutras mention them, they are not entirely non-existent—it is simply that they are said to be "non-existent" in order to refute the provisional.

Those who are deluded, however, conversely rely on this to claim that there are indeed those who have severed their fetters; this is incorrect. Only when one’s refutations and establishments are conducted in this manner can one avoid clinging to a single [view].

It is difficult to understand what is meant by "the textual phases of subduing and severing" (*fudan*). Upon examining various texts, it appears that while most speak of "subduing," there are only three instances where "severing" (*duan*) is mentioned.
These refer to: (1) designating "subduing" as "severing"; (2) severing by means of tainted wisdom (*sāsrava-jñāna*); and (3) severing at the conclusion of the fruit (*phala*).
None of these are what is meant here by "severing. How could they be worth discussing?

It has long been discussed in the verses on the "House-to-House" (Kulaṃkula) that, within the stages and fruits of the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna), there exists what is called the "House-to-House" practitioner;
this explanation is also settled. Why wait for a reiteration? Nevertheless, what I shall now set forth is precisely to clarify that established doctrine.

Now, to speak briefly of the "house-to-house" (kulaṃkula) type: this refers to the fact that their places of rebirth among humans and devas are not fixed. Generally, one might expect there to be nine such types;

however, regarding those who are moistened by the desire for existence (*bhavarāga*), there are seven. This is because, in the first case, the afflictions are coarse and difficult to sever, and the power of their insight is weak, so they have few grades but undergo many births.

In the subsequent cases, the grades correspond accordingly, and in the final case, it is the reverse of the above; such is the natural principle of the sequence. Therefore, although there are nine grades of affliction, there are [only] seven births.
Seventh, furthermore, the regulation of the frequency of fruits differs from the principle of "moistening birth" (upapatti-saṃdhi), for this is a delusion arising from the fruit;
it establishes the boundaries by taking the Once-returner and Non-returner as its divisions.

Although this is generally the case, those who sever [the fetters] and realize [the fruits] vary according to their faculties and natures—there being those who proceed gradually, those who follow a sequence, and those who leap over stages. Regarding those who leap over, there is...

Fundamentally, there are small, medium, large, and very large [degrees] of abandonment; however, those that are gradual are considered "lower," those that are intermediate are "middle," and those that are transcendent are "upper.
Furthermore, what is gradual is fixed, whereas what is transcendent is not fixed. Precisely because it is not fixed, there are the categories of small, medium, large, and very large.
Regarding the afflictions abandoned, there are those abandoned simultaneously, those abandoned at different times, and those abandoned first through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).

Thereafter, regarding the abandonment of views (*dṛṣṭi*), there are those who abandon them through knowledge that is either with outflows (*sāsrava*) or without outflows (*anāsrava*). "Simultaneous" refers to transcending and abandoning [the afflictions] all at once;
"sequential" refers to abandoning them according to their order. "Abandoning first and seeing later" refers to the fundamental abandonment.

Thus, the fundamental abandonment is abandonment by means of knowledge with outflows. When one subsequently abandons the views, it is then that the realization of the fruit (*phala-sākṣātkriyā*) is discussed; however, this too is limited to three [stages].
It is simply because the outflow-tainted wisdom (*sāsrava-jñāna*) is weak that it suppresses [the defilements].

If the final afflictions of thought (*citta-kleśa*) could not be severed by outflow-tainted wisdom, then those who sever them fundamentally would not realize the four fruits. As for all other cases of "leaping" or "gradual" advancement, these are severed by untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*).
The reason this is clarified first is to provide a foundation for what follows; if one grasps this essential point, one should reflect further upon its implications.
It is half [of the path]. Thus, what makes the exposition difficult lies in defining the verses that are recited.

In the *Abhidharmakośa-kārikā* (etc.), and when the *Śraddhā-pratipatti-śāstra* (or *Vibhāṣā*) is cited in the *Śikṣāsamuccaya* and the *Mohe zhiguan*, it says: "Transcending and severing five grades is called 'Family-to-Family' (*kulaṃkula*).

Yet, in the *Miaoxuan*, it is stated: "Severing from one up to five grades constitutes this [path of] Family-to-Family. Furthermore, the *Fuxingzhuan* says: "Whether by transcending or by following the sequence..."

Regarding the progressive abandonment of the third and fourth [categories of afflictions], the nature of these faculties and their transcendence of the sequence are difficult to clarify, as the status of what is abandoned may differ depending on whether one is progressing or not;

thus, from ancient times, there has been no single consensus on this matter (and so forth). Now, I shall provide an explanation: if one follows the *Abhidharmakośa*, the order of the verses is appropriate;
however, if one follows the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, the tenets follow divergent paths. Why is this? According to the commentary of that treatise, it states: "That is to say, the stream-enterer..."

When one who has entered the stream (*srotāpanna*) further abandons the afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), being fully endowed with three conditions, they are designated as a "family-to-family" (*kulaṃkula*).
Since it is said that they have "further abandoned," they are no longer those who abandoned [the afflictions] fundamentally or by leaping over;

furthermore, since it is said they are "fully endowed with three conditions," this also distinguishes them from others who lack these requirements—how could this not be the sequential abandonment mentioned in the verse? This is already clear based on this explanation alone, let alone what is stated in the *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary).
If one draws out and explains this, it further states: "This sequence of the meaning of 'severance' is the same as that in the present text;

is this not precisely the conclusion of the *Abhidharmakośa* verse, which matches the current *Zhi guan*? However, according to the original *Zhi guan*, the term "family-to-family" (*kulaṃkula*) is not applied to "sequential severance";
yet, when Jingxi cites that [text] to explain this, he has fully utilized the *Xuan wen*’s analysis of the first through the fifth stages of severance to interpret this treatise.

The purport of the *Jiājia* (Family-to-Family) is thus: the sequence of stages for severing [afflictions] as stated in the *Xuánwénběn* (Profound Textual Basis) also culminates at the fifth stage (*wǔpǐn*).

However, those who argue this is not so are mistaken; it is simply that the discussion is summarized within this interval. In reality, it still corresponds to the meaning of the *Abhidharmakośa* regarding the third and fourth stages.
As for the statement in the *Fùxíng* (Subsidiary Practice) regarding "whether by leaping over or in sequence," since the preceding text already states:
Having first attained the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*) among human beings, it is no longer a case of simultaneous elimination; thus, it is certainly not a minor leap.

The *Vyākhyā* (Commentary) explains: "Because there is progress—whether the rebirths received are more or less, or whether they exceed this limit—is 'progress' not indeed the meaning of 'leaping' (*abhisamkrama*)?
Therefore, one should know that this is merely a designation for a 'leap' within the context of the sequential [attainment]."
This is identical in sequence to the predecessors, yet distinct in its underlying meaning. Now, as for those who find fault with it for lacking scriptural evidence—here is this explicit text;
why labor over other authorities? Thus, the sequence of the verses and their meanings converge upon a single principle. Nevertheless, why must they follow this specific order?

Previously, none had perceived this intent, and thus their explanations remained unsettled. I shall now set forth its significance: it is because [the subject matter] transcends [ordinary categories].

If one exceeds their capacity, they will fall short; thus, "exceeding" and "falling short" cannot be established as constant principles. Furthermore, it is because that which is fixed is necessarily not the remainder.

Such is the nature of the specific sequence of the verses. As for why the *Vaibhāṣika* school maintains such divergent paths, it is because this [system] treats the *kulaṃkula* (one who goes from family to family) through the theory of transcendence and abandonment, and thus differs from the *Abhidharmakośa*. Although their fundamental dispositions (*indriya*) differ, there is no contradiction.

It is not necessary that all who skip stages (*ūrdhvaṃsrotas*) must be "family-to-family" (*kulaṃkula*); for although one who has transcended by abandoning [defilements] may reach the fifth stage, the efficacy of fully destroying rebirth has not yet been achieved.
Therefore, it is said that these five stages are identical to the four stages; this means that both skipping and following the sequence can possess the sense of being "family-to-family.
Thus, the two treatises may speak differently, which is not due to a difference in the faculties of the practitioners, nor is it a matter of suppressing one to conform to the other.

Moreover, even this assembly has not entirely avoided error. Speaking from this perspective, although the calculations based on the treatises apply to both [types of abandonment], the verses, when analyzed according to the text, restrict them to sequential abandonment alone;

thus, their respective explanations are distinct and clear. As for other lingering doubts regarding the meaning of the text, there are those who have provided detailed expositions, so I shall treat them briefly here.

Regarding the meaning of the five sons of the Buddha turning their minds toward *nirvāṇa* as explained in the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra*, there is a passage concerning five types of persons who attain *bodhi* after dwelling in the land of skillful means for eighty-four thousand *kalpas*.

This is because it is difficult for those in the first three fruits [of the śrāvaka path] to do so; since their delusions regarding the outflows (*āsrava*) are not yet exhausted, they have not yet transcended the realm of existence.
Thus, although the predecessors have debated this at length (and so forth), there has been no leisure to examine whether their arguments are right or wrong;
for now, I shall simply conclude by stating: one must first not exhaustively penetrate the delusions to attain birth [in the Pure Land].

This is clearly evident from the meaning of the text in the "Chapter on Manifesting Illness" (*Nirvāṇa-sūtra*) and the statement in the *Fuxingji* that after seven births, one enters *parinirvāṇa* spontaneously. All of these must...

It is appropriate that one may reach up to the fourth fruit; however, regarding the mention of the first, second, and third fruits in the text, the *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary) explains this clearly as well.
Thus it says: "The names such as Srotāpanna and so forth are designated from their original standpoint," and further:

"Because of the sharpness or dullness of their faculties, they emerge from the world after passing through kalpas of varying lengths. While all people know these passages, few have truly grasped their essential meaning.

Because they follow from the root and the source, many are confused by this; what is now called "following from the root" simply means that, for the time being, according to the specific destination within the assembly of *nirvāṇa*, there are these five types of persons.

In reality, all must proceed according to the degree of their afflictions (*kleśa*) through successive births until those afflictions are exhausted before they can finally exit the realm of existence.
Furthermore, the mention of following from the "root" of sharp or dull faculties is still based on the present life.
The depth of one’s realization of the fruit while dwelling within the boundary is used to judge whether one’s faculties will be sharp or dull on a subsequent day outside the boundary. Why is this so?
Because these individuals gather at the same assembly, yet some dwell in the shallow stage of the first fruit (srotāpanna), while others reach the ultimate stage of the fourth fruit (arhat);

this proves that their faculties are indeed either sharp or dull. Consequently, even though they spend kalpas outside the boundary, the duration of those kalpas differs—some being long and others short—and this is not to say otherwise.

Since that land still retains the distinctions of the three or four fruits [of the śrāvaka path], the *Myōraku-ki* (Record of Wondrous Joy), in its commentary on the passage concerning the sharpness or dullness of faculties, states:
"First, among the five [categories of practitioners], the first three are dull because they abide in the fruits. This sufficiently clarifies the present meaning.

As for the fact that the sutra preserves the discourse on the path of teaching (*kyōdō*) with the intent to compel the immediate manifestation [of the fruit], this is also a matter of course according to the principles of doctrine; for now, I shall rely merely upon the text.
The resolution of the objection is thus.
This concludes the section on Contemplation, specifically the discourse on the truth and falsity of the objects of contemplation.
The teaching must not fail to be correctly understood, and contemplation must not fail to be clear. If the teaching is incorrect, the wondrous Way becomes muddled within partial vehicles;
if contemplation is unclear, the fundamental tenets become hidden within deviant interpretations.

Thus, the reason why the teaching and contemplation of this particular school must be distinguished has long been necessary. Now that the gate of teaching has been clarified above, the gate of contemplation should likewise be discussed.

Later, in the *Yiyao shi* (Commentary on the Essential Points), regarding the passage on "a single thought-moment," there are two explanations—one concerning the real and one concerning the false—which refute the divergent views and clarify the correct meaning;
this was not stated without thorough detail. Yet, even in later generations, there remain those who are still ignorant of it.

There is no other reason for this than that the commentators themselves did not initially discuss the fundamental principles and essential purport, but instead became mired in a mere entanglement with the literal phrasing.
Therefore, regarding these two paths, one cannot rectify their respective doctrines. If truth and falsehood are not rectified, then emotion and wisdom cannot be distinguished;
if emotion and wisdom are not distinguished, then the purport of the teaching remains obscure; if the purport of the teaching is obscure, then understanding and practice lose their proper direction;

and if understanding and practice lose their proper direction, then the discourse on the fundamental path becomes disordered therein. Consequently, there arise the notions of the correct and the biased, and of the non-true and the true.

Once right and wrong have been adjudicated, the object and the contemplation can be correctly established, and the subject and the object can be distinguished. Once the subject and object are distinguished, the meaning of the text finds its proper destination.

When the meaning of the text finds its destination, those who engage in reflection and cultivation will no longer be confused; they will subsequently attain the state where subject and object are forgotten.
Only when this is achieved is the ultimate principle of truth and falsehood realized. Therefore, I shall now briefly expound upon this through ten points.
(As stated above). First, regarding the general principle of truth and delusion:
although the sacred teachings transmitted to the East constitute a vast treasury of the Dharma, if summarized in a single word, they do not transcend the realm of truth and delusion.
The transformation of Buddhas through both the real and the false is entirely contained herein; the Tiantai school of teachings is precisely that which expounds this transformation of Buddhas.
Although the specific teachings of different times differ, one must necessarily take the two gates of the real and the false as the pivotal keys of this school.

Without these, it would be insufficient to fully exhaust our Way. Thus, we know that the real and the false are of great significance, and for this reason, we must first discuss them in their grand scope.
The substance is first designated by name, and subsequently explained in terms of cultivation and nature, and phenomena and principle.

What is meant by "name"? It refers to the "True," which signifies reality as well as accordance with reality; and the "False," which signifies delusion as well as confusion. "Phenomena" (dharma) refers to the reality underlying a name;
that reality does not exceed the ten realms and encompasses both the universal and particular meanings. The universal meaning is as follows... (and so forth).

Within this distinction, there are further differences regarding the universal and the particular. Universally, the ten realms are discussed in relation to one another, much like the conventional sense of good and evil (and so forth).
Particularistically, the Buddha-realm is the truth while the nine realms belong to delusion; this is the ultimate principle.

However, when explained in terms of cultivation and nature (*śikṣā* and *prakṛti*), the single true Dharma-realm is fundamentally beyond delusion and awakening; how could the mind of equal enlightenment be said to involve cultivation?

It may be said that realization is neither true nor false; yet, although it is neither true nor false, the inherent virtues (*xingde*) are perfectly complete, and every phenomenon (*dharmadharmāḥ*) is distinct and manifest.
Therefore, the nature does not abide fixedly, but arises entirely from the nature itself, transforming and creating the ten realms according to conditions of defilement or purity.

Thus, while the nature is neither true nor false, cultivation involves both truth and falsity—this is the meaning of the dialectical discussion. Since the inherent virtues are perfectly complete, how could...?

If one were to claim that truth and falsehood exist outside of nature (*xing*), then since nature itself is admitted to fully possess both truth and falsehood, what obstacle would there be to their mutual integration and dissolution?
Thus, it is also possible to discuss them as being "neither true nor false. This, moreover, is a matter of discussing their respective meanings.
Nevertheless, although truth and falsehood exist within nature, because they are fundamentally integrated and quiescent, they are collectively designated as "true. This is the "True" [of the title].
It is not established in opposition to the delusory; rather, it is the reality that is neither true nor delusory. Therefore, the *Śraddhotpāda Śāstra* states:

"That which is called True Suchness (*tathatā*) has nothing to be discarded, because all phenomena are entirely true; nor is there anything to be established, because all phenomena are entirely suchness.
Furthermore, the *Non-duality Gate* says: "Although turbidity is originally present, its entire substance is pure."
This is precisely that meaning. Although within the cultivated there is both the real and the false, because the real is established in opposition to the false, they are collectively termed "false.
Thus, the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* says: "By speaking of the false, all the real is revealed; yet false and real are equally two kinds of falsity. Furthermore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
"Both the Buddha and nirvāṇa—these two dharmas—arise from false dharmas. This is what is meant. Since it is so with the cultivated and the innate, it is likewise so with phenomena and principle.
This is because phenomena and principle do not transcend the cultivated and the innate. This is still an explanation based on the analytical distinction of doctrinal categories (*arthamukha*).

However, when one uses principle to harmonize phenomena and uses phenomena to encompass principle—speaking from the perspective where principle and phenomena are fused—the true and the false share the same source, and bondage and liberation are non-dual.
Because the true and the false share the same source, that which emerges is fundamentally one; because that which emerges is fundamentally one, [the two are inseparable].
Reality is itself delusion, and delusion is itself reality; this is why bondage and liberation are non-dual. To realize this one principle, reality and delusion become clearly distinct.
This is the general outline.
Second, the two treatises on emotion and wisdom, delusion and awakening.

Now, regarding the discourse on the real and the false, there are those who speak in terms of the essence of the Dharma (*dharmatā*), and there are those who speak in terms of emotion and wisdom (*jñāna*).

Although these two types of discourse are identical in their terminology, the manner in which they define the real and the false differs. That which was indicated previously pertains to the essence of the Dharma;

whether in its fundamental nature (*prakṛti*) or in its cultivation (*bhāvanā*), it is universally so. Because this refers to the essence, it remains eternally one from beginning to end, and thus there is no concealment or manifestation.

If there were no concealment or manifestation between difference and identity, then the essence would be neither true nor false. Because it is neither true nor false, its very substance is empty and harmonious;

because it is empty and harmonious, it is unimpeded. Being unimpeded, it possesses the capacity to receive perfuming (*vāsanā*); since perfuming has both defiled and pure aspects, emotional consciousness (*citta*) and wisdom (*jñāna*) thus arise accordingly.
Wisdom constitutes its true aspect, while emotion constitutes its false aspect. Although their substance is non-dual, their functions are mutually opposed; therefore, by means of the defiled...
To take emotion as a condition is that from which emotion arises; it is why emotion arises and wisdom perishes. Therefore it is said: "When emotion arises, wisdom is obstructed.
When conceptualization transforms and the essence becomes distinct, the delusive dharmas of the nine realms come into being. To take purity as a condition is that from which wisdom arises;
it is why wisdom arises and emotion subsides. Therefore it is said: "Turning one's back on the dust [of defilement]."
To unite with awakening and turn back from delusion toward the true is to possess the true Dharma of the Buddha-realm;

yet this is still merely a discourse on the mutual inversion of emotion and wisdom, not a treatise on the essence of the Dharma. If we discuss emotion and wisdom in terms of the essence of the Dharma, then emotion refers to the delusion of all ten realms, while wisdom refers to the liberation of all ten realms.
Liberation constitutes the true, while delusion constitutes the false, as previously explained.

The general principle is precisely this: that which is referred to as the "Essential Point" (Jiyao) states that when one is attached to emotional states (*qing*), both the pure and the defiled are stained;

yet when one abides in the rational nature (*lixing*), both the pure and the defiled are pure. Furthermore, the *Fahua Wenju* (Commentary on the Lotus Sutra), in the section on Non-duality, says: "When the three thousand realms exist within the principle, they are collectively termed ignorance; when the three thousand realms are realized as the fruit, they are all called eternal bliss.
This is exactly that meaning. Although truth and falsehood are universal, emotional states and wisdom remain restricted; because they are restricted, both are understood.
This wisdom still belongs to the Buddha, while this state of delusion belongs to the nine realms. Thus, wisdom belonging to the Buddha is the ultimate limit of enlightenment;

delusion belonging to the nine realms is the beginning and end of confusion. The beginning of delusion starts from the True [Nature]; when delusion is transformed, it immediately becomes enlightenment.
The culmination of enlightenment reaches the Nature; the culmination of the Nature is the return to the Source. However, as long as delusion has not yet been transformed, [the return does not occur].
Thus, when the whole is present within principle, one must investigate principle to transform delusion; yet as long as understanding is not ultimate, one remains bound by emotion.
One must illuminate emotion to reach the understanding of principle. When principle is understood, emotion becomes wisdom in its entirety; when deluded, wisdom becomes emotion in its entirety.

Although emotion and wisdom appear to be opposites, their substance is fundamentally one. Thus, although there is a beginning and an end, in terms of their essential nature, there is no beginning and no end.

Regarding that which has no beginning or end, yet speaks of beginning and end: it begins with that which is neither true nor delusive, giving rise to both the true and the delusive; it ends by returning to the single nature. This may also be called "arising from the true to produce the delusive. Why is it that while the beginning and end are both true, the one allows for the arising of delusion while the other does not undergo further change? It is said: their substance is one, but their wisdom differs. What is meant? The substance of the Buddha-nature is eternally quiescent and devoid of form, yet its function is to respond to conditions and manifest all phenomena. Because its substance is one, there is no distinction between before and after; because its function is diverse, there is the differentiation of the true and the delusive. Therefore, when the function is exhausted and returns to the source, it is called "returning to the true"; when the substance is obscured and the function arises, it is called "arising from the true to produce the delusive. Thus, although the substance is fundamentally unchanging, the function is subject to arising and ceasing. This is why the Tathāgata’s wisdom is eternally constant, while sentient beings’ minds arise and cease. This is the meaning of the statement: "The Tathāgata’s wisdom is eternally constant, while sentient beings’ minds arise and cease. Furthermore, the Tathāgata’s wisdom is eternally constant because its substance is one; sentient beings’ minds arise and cease because their functions differ. This is the meaning of the statement: "Because the substance is one, there is no distinction between before and after; because the function is diverse, there is the differentiation of the true and the delusive. Regarding "because their essence is one": because the fundamental [nature] is interfused, it receives perfuming; through receiving perfuming, delusion arises. Originally, there is no difference in principle between these two.
However, as for the distinction in wisdom, because of the realization of the ultimate, it is unchanging and non-reverting;
thus, being solely the True, there is no further production of delusion. This is precisely the meaning of the analogy of perfect enlightenment (yuanjue) melting away gold ore, and so forth. Now...
Thus, while the substance is fundamentally non-different, that which undergoes change and that which does not reside in the interval between emotion (*qing*) and wisdom (*zhi*).

Therefore, emotion and wisdom correspond to the two modes of cultivation—contrary and compliant. Because emotion is contrary, it turns its back on the nature and produces delusion; yet the substance, though not hidden, becomes hidden. Because wisdom is compliant, it realizes the nature and constitutes practice;
yet the substance, though not manifest, becomes manifest. This concealment and manifestation belong to the other [the modes of cultivation], while the substance and nature remain eternally constant.
That which remains unchanging from beginning to end—if one understands this principle, then one will recognize why it is that emotion is thus constituted and wisdom is thus constituted;
by analogy, the distinction between delusion and awakening, and the truth and the false, can be known. Their single substance is mutually inverted, and through this they may be understood.
If one attains the reality of this, its meaning must find its proper destination; one will not be blinded regarding the primordial source, for the principle itself will be free of obstruction.

The Three Treatises establish the teaching to elucidate that the essence of phenomena is of one suchness, where the holy and the ordinary are equal; this is not merely for the sake of establishing a teaching. Now, as for why the teaching is established:
it is because the Sage perceives that emotional affliction (*kleśa*) and wisdom (*jñāna*) can be mutually transformed. Thus, when affliction is transformed into wisdom, [the teaching is established].
It is sufficient to lose fundamental wisdom when one turns toward emotions; yet it is also sufficient to enter the Way when one acts accordingly.

Thus, he established teachings to bequeath to the world, so that those with the karmic capacity might receive them and realize transformation. Thereafter, they turn confusion into understanding and turn the ordinary into the sagely.

From the sagely to the most sagely, reaching the ultimate limit—the Sage’s task of establishing the teaching is thereby complete. However, because the purport of the teaching has both general and specific aspects...
The Dharma has degrees of depth because sentient beings have varying capacities, whether sharp or dull; thus, it is taught as either "identity" or "separation.

Although there are differences among the four teachings—Small and Great, Partial and Complete, Provisional and Real—all of them serve to clarify the True by confronting the False and to destroy the False by means of the True.
This is the intended meaning within each respective stage. (As stated... However, if one considers the trans-sectarian, universal meaning, then the first three teachings are all inclusive.

All [stages] prior to this belong to the delusory; only from the "Perfect" (yuan) onward is it truly real. This is because, according to the Separate Teaching (biejiao), everything up to that point belongs to the turning away from nature and constitutes delusion.

Although this is the case regarding the gate of teaching, the reality of the Dharma (fati) is not so. Nevertheless, when discussing the reality of the Dharma by way of the gates of teaching, there is a difference in terms of "immediacy" (ji) and "separation" (li).
Now, setting aside the Tripitaka and Shared Teachings to discuss the Separate and Perfect Teachings: in the Separate Teaching, one speaks of the Real while remaining separate from the delusory.

Therefore, while delusion belongs to that which is to be negated and is distinguished from the True, when one applies contemplation to the object of observation, one observes only the truth within delusion;

it is not that delusion itself is the truth. For this reason, others focus exclusively on the principle of nature (*dharmatā*), negating the nine [categories] to reveal the one, and employing restrictive exclusion to point specifically toward the pure *tathatā*.
Furthermore, it is said that the mind which acts as the creator is the dharma created; they are not identical.
In the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao), one speaks of the true within the deluded; thus, while delusion is that which is sublated, the true is not manifested as something separate.
As for employing contemplation to observe the object, one directly contemplates that the very substance of delusion is itself the true, with no true apart from it.

Even when speaking of severing or shattering [delusion], this is done solely in terms of "severance" based on their identity; to say "removal" implies that the act of shattering lacks any mark of shattering. Therefore, for a person of the Perfect Teaching...

To be able to realize that the three paths are themselves the three virtues (*triguṇa*), that the nine realms have nothing to be destroyed, that the Buddha-dharma realm is the penetration of delusion as truth, and that contemplating the aggregates (*skandha*) achieves the inconceivable—all of this depends on this very point.

These differences in whether one speaks of identity or separation exist because the faculties of those to be taught are either sharp or dull; thus, although the teachings speak of identity and separation, their essence is fundamentally not different, for...

Because their essence is not different, the statement that "wisdom is identical" is a discourse in accordance with principle, while the statement that they are "separate" is a description following worldly sentiment.
To accord with principle is the Real (the ultimate), and to follow sentiment is the Expedient (the provisional); this is the reason for the distinction between the Separate and the Perfect.

The Separate may involve separating from delusion, whereas the Perfect must involve identity; indeed, the Perfect lacks any separate [delusion], as it takes those partial dharmas in their entirety to manifest the Perfect Principle. Only then...

This is what is called "perfection" (yuan). Now, for one who receives the Perfect Teaching and cultivates the Perfect Contemplation, how could they possibly abandon the delusory to contemplate the real?

Or is it that there is no delusion to be contemplated? If one contemplates only the real while remaining detached from the delusory, this is to be entirely ignorant of the essential meaning expounded by the Perfect School.
The four treatises explain that the ultimate goal of practice differs;

this is why the teaching opens up understanding, and why understanding establishes practice. Practice must establish the objective realm and the contemplation, resulting in realization and cultivation.
Their ultimate aim is fundamentally one, as indicated previously by the principle of perfect expression. Since one speaks of the True within the delusory, is it not so?
To explain it in this way and to contemplate it in this way may seem as though there were no different paths;
however, when explaining through abstract discourse and practicing according to actual reality, one cannot help but distinguish between their explanations.

Because the explanation is made through abstract discourse, one relies on the purport of the perfect and complete teachings to realize that the essence of dharmas is fundamentally wondrous, that deluded emotions are empty and pervasive, and that all is solely inconceivable—how, then, could there be any further false aggregates?
Although it is not explicitly stated that one should contemplate the false, it is permissible to do so; this is likely why many people of old spoke of "contemplating the real.
However, to claim that the understanding of the subtle is likewise the case for practice is incorrect.

One fails to realize that if practice is distinguished based on the reality [of the mind], then all sentient beings from the very beginning have never been separated from thought, continuing even up to the stage of Equal Enlightenment.
If there is even a subtle thought not yet forgotten, it is said that the "three thousand" phenomena have not yet been fully manifested and the essence remains obscure;
is this not because the stage has not reached its ultimate limit, and thus thoughts are not yet forgotten? When thoughts are not yet forgotten, emotions are not yet exhausted.

As long as even a single thought or emotional conception remains, this is precisely the realm of the delusions of the five aggregates (*skandhas*). Although there are differences in degree—whether thick or thin, strong or weak—one must nevertheless illuminate these emotions to penetrate the underlying principle.
"Manifesting the True within the false" (*ji-wàng-ér-xiǎn-zhēn*) precisely demonstrates the efficacy of the Perfect Contemplation (*yuán-guān*) in shattering the false to reveal the True;
it is the essential point for entering the realm of the *skandhas* (*yīn-jìng*) and giving rise to contemplation from within principle. Therefore, the *Yào-yòng* (Essential Uses) states:

"Extensively demonstrating wondrous understanding is entirely inconceivable"—this refers to the meaning of "resolving through emptiness" (*jiě-yuē-xū-lùn*) mentioned here. It further says: "Establishing practice and cultivation requires distinguishing the locus"—this refers to what is presented here.

Practice is the meaning of discerning [the truth] based on reality; therefore, one knows that although both understanding and practice are sudden and perfect, since the empty and the real differ, the true and the false must be distinguished.
Thus, while speaking of the "true" is highly consistent with principle, it is not yet permissible regarding phenomena;

whereas observing the "false" does not contradict the nature and is most appropriate for cultivation. Now, we are establishing the objects and the contemplation specifically according to the gate of phenomena and the gate of cultivation.
How could one not take the discourse on contemplating the delusive as the standard for the object and contemplation within the Perfect Teaching?

If the five treatises establish the path of the school and attain the essential principle that distinguishes the current understanding and practice, then the truth regarding the object and contemplation, as well as the real and the delusive, will naturally become clear; what further explanation is needed?
Therefore, prior to our nine patriarchs, no dissenting views were heard, precisely because they profoundly understood this principle.

It was only when understanding (*jie*) and practice (*xing*) became conflated and undifferentiated—where some settled their practice based on understanding, while others used practice to disparage understanding, or claimed that both were equally valid—that difficulties regarding the meaning of the texts first arose. As for these difficulties concerning the meaning:

However, while objects encompass all phenomena, when taking the mind itself as the immediate reference, the mental factors are characterized by awakening and delusion, and objects consist of the real and the false.

Now, does one contemplate the real or the false? The real does not require contemplation; if contemplation were to exist for the false, then contemplating while retaining the false would not be the perfect contemplation (*yuan guan*).

This is the difficulty regarding "text" (*wen*): in general, whenever there is a contradiction between the real and the false within a text, this applies (and so forth). Thus, it is the path of the school (*zong tu*).

It was from this point that the distinction between the real and the false was first established, giving rise to the discourse on the "two or three graveyards. Consequently, the practice of honoring ancestors was adopted;
now, in the *Ten Non-dual Gates*, the single thought-moment (*ekacitta-kṣaṇa*) is directly treated as the numinous awareness and quiescent essence of true nature.

This interpretation takes the single thought-moment as the very object of contemplation, meaning one should contemplate the real. Furthermore, there are others who entirely refuse to establish the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and sense-bases (*āyatana*) [as objects of contemplation].
If one maintains that what is observed is "only the inconceivable," then one is observing only the True (the ultimate reality).

Although these two views arise from studying this very school, they have formed distinct perspectives; those who have criticized them since ancient times as the "Mountain-Outside" (Shan-wai) school are referring to this.

The explanation of the Four Ming (Siming) school, as previously shown through its interpretation of practice and conduct, may be said to clarify their distinct tenets. Although [this distinction] has not existed from the beginning...
While this may lean toward one extreme, it is nonetheless permissible to establish the thesis of "contemplating delusion" (*guanwang*) based on the instructions for the gate of practice (*xingmen*).
As the *Yishu* states: "In your *Fuzong ji*, you take the contemplation of deluded thoughts as the central thesis," and so forth.

However, delusion is not contemplated as delusion; rather, because contemplating delusion is itself the realization of the True, it is called "penetrating delusion to realize the True. This leads us to the subsequent section...

"To further support our school, one must provide further instruction... (as stated at length). Furthermore, Gushan said: "In the past, people contemplated the real; today, people contemplate the delusory.
I now penetrate the delusory mind of the six consciousnesses to reveal the wondrous principle of the Three Truths.

However, although these words are superficially the same, their intent is vastly different. This is merely taking the shifting conceptualizations of another school and turning them back into one's own doctrine.
Thus, while it is indeed skillful in its phrasing to simultaneously accept and refute the assertions of both schools, the underlying principle is not yet correct.

When examined according to their fundamental tenets, this is merely observing the "True" (zhen). Why? Because they have already attributed the mind of the three natures (*trisvabhāva*) to the noumenal principle (*li*), which is that which creates;
furthermore, when discussing the general and the particular, they take the principle to be the general principle. Is the principle not, therefore, the "True"? Moreover—

This means that if fabricated phenomena are not complete, they cannot encompass the three thousand [realms] to return to principle; only when they are complete do these phenomena belong to the three thousand.

Thus, the phenomena are entirely what is to be sublated and are by no means identical to the ultimate meaning. Although it is said that one penetrates delusion to contemplate the truth within delusion, if this were truly the same as the teaching of the Four Ming (Siming), why would you not adopt it?
Judging from this, although we know the phrase "penetrating delusion" is used, it is fundamentally not the same.

Regarding the principle of contemplating delusion, although Xiachuan did not explicitly clarify its doctrinal basis, his *Wenxin jie* (Explanation of the Heart of the Text) also interprets it as being subsumed within a single thought-moment (*ekacitta*).
The text states: "It is simply that phenomena are gathered into principle; taking principle as the totality is distinct from pointing specifically toward pure true suchness (*tathatā*).
If one were to take only a single moment within phenomena as the totality, how could there be the sense of gathering the particulars? This is...
Since Qian Tong was identical to Gushan, he subtly supported the latter’s interpretation while covertly disparaging Siming.

If one were merely to correct Gushan’s errors, there would be no need to discuss Zhechuan; yet if one were solely to refute the fallacies of the "Mountain-Outside" (Shanwai) school, there would be no need to evaluate Gushan’s doctrines.
Thus, the manner in which the Shanwai school was refuted and the true lineage made manifest is exactly as set forth in the *Yijiao*.
Simply by reading those texts, one will see for oneself their merits and defects; there is no need to wait for further refutation.
The six treatises support the school and capture its essential meaning;
the teachings of the Four Ming Masters do not have some separate "school tenet" (zongzhi), but rather consist precisely in being able to clarify that very tenet.
Regarding the statement that "the essential tenets of the Four Clarities (Sì-míng)" may be found elsewhere, this is incorrect.

However, if one examines the *Zhǐyào* (Essentials), it reveals two paths—understanding (*jiě*) and practice (*xíng*)—and shows that the objects of contemplation consist of both the true (*zhēn*) and the deluded (*wàng*), thus not being biased toward a single extreme. Nevertheless, when it speaks of the "object of contemplation," it is primarily based on the path of practice;

therefore, in establishing its tenets and defining the object, it takes the contemplation of the deluded as its core. Thus, the text [states]... (etc.). Yet, since there is no separate, distinct tenet system [apart from this], [the claim of a unique school is unfounded].
This is not merely my own speculative assertion; rather, its basis is found in Jingxi [Zhanran].

For instance, in the *Fuxing* (Commentary on the Profound Meaning), there is a passage stating, "First, to further clarify the objects of contemplation," which refers precisely to the three categories (*sanke*). Is this not, in fact, taking the category of the aggregates (*yinruan*) as the object of contemplation?

It is only in the subsequent section clarifying the practice of contemplation that the ten vehicles, such as the inconceivable object of contemplation, are discussed—these being the subject of contemplation.

At first, Shanwai mistakenly believed that this passage explicitly clarifies the cultivation of contemplation (*guan*), but it was only when Siming categorized and analyzed the text that he realized his error.

Having heard the correct meaning, he was able to rectify himself. This must have been because the distinctions between the object and the contemplation, as well as the truths of reality and falsehood, were so clearly established that there was no room for alteration;
thus, he was able to refute those heterodox views. Nevertheless, even Jingxi did not claim this for himself.
The meaning further arises from the textual characteristics of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*; these are the natural course of the path of contemplation (*vipaśyanā-mārga*).

That which is the natural course of the path of contemplation is the source from which the scriptural teachings emerge. Thus, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* contains the text concerning the "mind-creation," while Tiantai relies upon it to demonstrate the foundation of objective realm and contemplation—namely, what is called the single thought-moment of deluded mind within confusion.
