One must understand that this has a distinct underlying meaning. It is because *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* fundamentally clarify the mind’s inherent possession (*citta-svabhāva-pariniṣpanna*) that [the text] cites the mind’s activity (*citta-kṛta*) as an explanation;

it is to lead [the practitioner] toward this. Had there not been this intent, such an interpretation would not have been made. To cite activity as a demonstration of possession would be utterly inconsistent.
Furthermore, it would cause later students to mistake activity for possession—this is not what is meant here by "possession. Indeed, what is meant here by "possession" is precisely activity.
This refers to being endowed [with qualities] that are not produced through subsequent effort; therefore, it is specifically elaborated upon in this way.
To speak in terms of principle (*li*) is to accord with the purport of the *Fuwen* (Textual Commentary); to speak in terms of phenomena (*shi*) is to follow the meaning of the Sūtra.

Furthermore, according to the concluding demonstration at the end, the establishment of principle serves to subsume phenomena. Since phenomena are subsumed by principle, phenomena inherently possess their source; thus, one may directly realize them.

Observing principle through phenomena is why *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* are taught solely by way of "endowment" (*yōju*). Regarding the commentary’s use of the term "endowment" while also employing the word "comprehensive" (*kan*), the intent is as explained above;
this is also what is meant by the phrase "establishing meaning through the approach of phenomena and principle.

If one were to establish the meaning of "endowment" solely through the approach of phenomena and principle, there would be the distinction between "endowment of principle" (*ri-yōju*) and "endowment of practice" (*shu-yōju*). Now, it is precisely because of the endowment of principle...
The four meanings—cultivation, equipment, phenomena, and principle—and the two intentions are ultimately one. That they are ultimately one means they are neither identical nor different.
To say they are neither identical nor different is a realm beyond the reach of words and thought.
Regarding the meaning of the "three thousand" as both general and particular: the terms "general" and "particular" refer to their mutual integration and subsumption.

Now, the reason why these three thousand are integrated and subsumed is that they are manifested through the single nature (*ekaprakṛti*) to reveal their wondrousness. Therefore, when one perceives the integration and subsumption of all phenomena, [one perceives] the three thousand...
The essential point is indeed grasped; however, because that essential point is not easily clarified, it is for this reason that I speak of it.

Thus, the *Fenbie men* (Gate of Non-duality) states: "In sum, all is contained within a single thought" (*etc.*). Now, "in sum" means that all dharmas converge therein; "individually" means that each is accorded its own name.
To speak of the "sum" is to encompass everything without exception; to speak of the "individual" is to mention everything without omission. The "sum" possesses the quality of inclusion.
The individual functions have their distinct destinies, yet the general application is that the one is all and all is one;

this spontaneous mastery of rolling up and unrolling is the characteristic of harmonious integration (*yongshe*). That this is specifically revealed in the "Gate of Non-duality" (*Fenbie Ermen*) further articulates the fundamental intent of that gate.

Why is this? It is because while the ten profound subtleties (*shimiao*) of the *Xuanyan* represent the distinct aspects of the Dharma-characteristics (*faxiang*), [the Non-duality Gate] represents the cessation (*zhi*).
"Contemplating that the mind possesses the three thousand [realms]" is the general principle; it summarizes the ten profundities as the essential framework for the method of contemplation.

This is why these ten gates subsume the particulars into the general. This is precisely the reason why the *Yaojue* (Essential Instructions) focuses exclusively on the three thousand to explain the matter.
Furthermore, one finds that Jingxi said: "The three thousand, both in their general and particular aspects, are all empty, provisional, and middle," and he also said: "Dust..."
That the measure of the physical body is equal to that of the *dharmakāya* is precisely this principle. How could this be something unique to the gates of the teachings?
It is indeed found within the sūtras themselves. For instance, in the *Vimalakīrti*, there is the statement that "a single hair swallows the great ocean" and "a mustard seed contains Mount Sumeru";

this is because the Bodhisattva dwells in the inconceivable liberation (*acintyavimokṣa*). Furthermore, the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi-sūtra* speaks of "one being immeasurable and the immeasurable being one."

That the small manifests the great within itself and the great manifests the small within itself is because the Tathāgata unifies wondrous clarity—neither arising nor ceasing—with the Tathāgatagarbha.
Thus, all Buddhas and sages who achieve this inconceivable function of rolling up and unfolding the great utility invariably proceed by this path.
From this, one knows that the total integration of the single nature is the general principle.
The "separate" is the root, while the "three thousand dharmas" are the branches of the general and the particular.

When the root is raised to encompass the branches, each and every dharma functions as the entire substance of the nature of the fruit of the Dharma; thus, they mutually interpenetrate without exclusion.

When the branches are used to manifest the root, each and every nature is entirely empty, provisional, and the Middle; thus, their fusion and subtlety are inconceivable. This is what is meant by the root being fully manifested as the branches.
The branches are themselves the root; when the branches are fully realized as the root, the root is itself the branches. There has never been a root without branches, nor branches without a root.
This is likewise true for phenomena and principle, essence and function. Such is the nature of the Dharma according to the teachings of the Perfect and Sudden school.
Nevertheless, the masters of the Shanwai lineage take principle to be the general and phenomena to be the particular; they indeed establish their system in this manner.
I have already evaluated this in detail as you pointed out; to speak of it now, it is because you do not yet understand the doctrine of the fundamental and the derivative.
If it were truly as you say, there would be only the fundamental and no derivative; if there were no derivative, in what would the fundamental be subsumed?
If there were only the derivative and no fundamental, how could the derivative tend toward the fundamental? People of the present age merely...

One may know that the universal is identical with principle (li) and thereby subsumes the particular, yet one does not realize that the particular likewise depends upon principle to tend toward the universal.
If one were to divide principle into universals, then the particulars would have no principle; can the particulars indeed be without principle?

If the particulars were to possess their own principle, then the universal would also necessarily possess its corresponding fact (shi). If the universal lacks its fact, then it would be both coarse and solitary, which is untenable.
Furthermore, to take principle as the general is to invert the root for the branch; to take phenomena as the particular is to grasp the branch while losing the root.
If you have not yet understood, I shall further illustrate it through a metaphor: the meaning of the general and the particular is like the mutual reflection of the jewels on a celestial crown.
Now, why do these jewels reflect? It is because of their luminosity. Luminosity is analogous to principle, while the jewels are analogous to [phenomena].
This concerns the general and the particular. However, if one takes principle as the general, then taking clarity as the pearl is incorrect, for clarity is not actually the pearl.
By carefully analyzing the application of the analogy to the dharma, the error has no place to escape, for it contradicts the natural logic of the dharma.

If, however, one speaks of the four clarities (*caturvidha-vidyā*), it is not so; for the three thousand phenomena of both fact and principle each have their own general and particular aspects, which constitute the basis of the general and particular.
Originally, because the single nature (ekasvabhāva) subsumes all through its fusion with the one, the particular and the general mutually encompass one another;

although there is a distinction between phenomena (dharma) and principle (li), both are pointed to as being the single thought-moment (ekakṣaṇa) as the general. Furthermore, when this meaning is applied to the fundamental dharma, the underlying intent is likewise the same, as detailed in the *Shō* (Commentary).
Now, regarding this, we say: since the general and the particular are each discussed in terms of both phenomena and principle, it is revealed that phenomena and principle are non-dual.

This is the principle that within the Perfect Teaching (Enkyō), all is already complete. Since both the general and the particular apply to both phenomena and principle, the fundamental and the derivative are both present;
thus, there is no error of partiality or inversion as found in the "Mountain-Outside" (San-gai) school. The root of the general and the particular ultimately derives from the single nature (isshō);

therefore, it has never been the case that a single thought-moment alone was designated as the "general. Nevertheless, there are instances where it is specifically and singularly pointed out, which is done in accordance with the wording of the text for the sake of exegesis.

The commentary explains that while it would be sufficient to speak of them individually once the general principle is established, the fact that both are pointed to as "a single thought-moment" (一念) captures the intent of establishing the object of contemplation by taking what is proximate and essential.
Although two meanings are distinguished, there is in reality no duality of substance, for the totality is simply this one thought-moment.
This is precisely the principle of the *Zhi Guan Fu Xing* regarding the mind’s inherent possession (*xīn jù*) and the mind’s creative construction (*xīn zào*).

If one discusses the two "totalities" (zong) based on this very mindfulness, the totality of principle (li-zong) refers to the fact that the essence and nature inherently possess [all phenomena], while the totality of phenomena (shi-zong) is spoken of in terms of their transformation and creation.
Since these two totalities are thus established, the same applies to the two particulars (bie).

Therefore, one should know that the two meanings are merely different ways of speaking regarding the engagement with phenomena and the engagement with principle; as for why they are termed "totality" and "particularity," they are one and the same. Yet some...

To say that the Four Clarifications (*sisheng*) possess many meanings—both general and specific—is one who truly understands the terminology. Furthermore, when these are applied to harmonize with the fundamental teaching (*benfa*), they accord profoundly with the exegetical principles of our own school.

Now, while the fundamental teaching establishes the discourse on the general and the specific based on the cultivated (*xiu*) and the inherent (*xing*), this application of the general and the specific extends to both phenomena (*shi*) and principle (*li*).
How can one harmonize them? It is said: "One harmonizes their meaning; it is not merely a matter of the general and the specific."
This is how one accords with the fundamental Dharma. As for its meaning, the text states:
"One should know that all dharmas—whether phenomena or principles—are established from the root of non-abiding; this is precisely what is meant. Thus, regarding the fundamental Dharma, it is said:
"These four layers are all established through delusion regarding the true reality (dharmatā). Regarding the general and the specific, it is said: "If..."

If phenomena and principle are taken together, one refers to a single thought-moment within phenomena as the "totality" (*zong*). The reason this single thought-moment serves as the totality is that it is identical to the single nature (*yixing*);

thus, the meaning is perfectly consistent. However, this does not mean it directly coincides with the fundamental dharma (*benfa*). This is because the fundamental [nature] is itself the single nature, and the single nature is itself the principle (*li*).

Principle constitutes the basis for both the total and the particular; it is not the case that principle itself is the totality. One must understand that both the total and the particular are [the objects of]...
Although this was established as a formal doctrine, why was this question formulated? It is said: the question is posed for the sake of a general inquiry, yet the answer is not so;
this can be seen within the text itself. By clarifying it through this, one sees that there is nothing inconsistent in what Siming taught, as it is also what the principles of the Dharma require.
Therefore, by simply rectifying the assertions of these two schools, the various differing opinions of other masters need not be addressed further.
This shall be discussed later.

Regarding the meaning of the ten kinds of objects (*daśa-viṣaya*), although the *Samantabhadra-bhadracaryā-praṇidhāna-sūtra* (Puxian guan jing) briefly points them out, it does not explain them in detail; therefore, [this is provided] for the sake of future generations.

Human teachers have consequently produced many divergent theories; yet none fail to take the four kinds of evidential characteristics in the sutra text and the purification of the six sense organs as the ten objects (*daśaviṣaya*).
However, regarding the single object of Samantabhadra, there are variations in whether it is treated collectively or individually;

and regarding the single object of the Buddhas, there are differences in whether it is included or excluded, as well as in whether the sutra text explicitly designates it or not. Moreover, since these are all matters of interpretation, how can one definitively judge which is correct?

This is profound; thus, it is impossible to offer a definitive evaluation. Yet, within my own mind, I have privately sought its ultimate intent and found it to differ greatly from what I had previously heard.
Allow me to set forth this point: for Tiantai specifically designates this as the stage of the Ten Faiths; thus the *Xuanyan* (Profound Meaning) states:
"The *Puxian Guan* clarifies that prior to the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) there are ten objects."

The "realms" (dhātus) refer precisely to these stages. If one follows the traditional interpretation, then it would be appropriate to align these ten objects vertically with the ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*).

Otherwise, why point to this specifically as the stage of the ten faiths? Furthermore, if there were indeed a fixed sequence, which would be shallow and which deep, and what would come before and after?
Moreover, why do the signs of response and realization appear intermittently alongside the purification of the six sense faculties?

Why is it that after the stage of the Buddhas of the ten directions, one immediately attains the *svadhāraṇī* (旋總持) and the purification of the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍindriya-viśuddhi*), followed by the touching of the head (*mūrdha-abhiṣeka*) and the bestowal of the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*);
and why, after the stage of the emanated bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*), does one attain them again; and why, after the purification of the six sense faculties, does the touching of the head occur once more?
Furthermore, when the names of these stages are summarized, why is it said that the "eye-faculty" of Samantabhadra is always the first?
However, upon examining this, it is clear that one cannot yet equate these with the ten stages of the *śraddhā* (ten faiths) by using them to complete the ten objects.
If so, how should the current explanation be presented? It is said: from the present perspective, these are simply the very first stage among all the aforementioned objects;
therefore, it is for good reason that both are called "the first. This is because they are subsequently traversed throughout the ten stages of *śraddhā*.
As for realization, wisdom has degrees of depth and shallowness, while the object has clarity and obscurity; this is why there are ten stages.
However, the scriptural text details the first and omits the remaining nine, citing the beginning to make known the end. Ultimately, one enters the stage of right determination through non-arising;
by means of the latter, the former is revealed. Among the six sense faculties, there is both verticality and horizontality within the midst. One attains *dhāraṇī*...

From the first [stage] up to the second, the horizontal does not preclude the vertical; thus one knows that in the stage of fixed determination (*niyata-avasthā*) prior to non-arising, the objective realm must necessarily possess all ten [realms].
The meaning of the correspondence between the horizontal and the vertical should be understood in this way, for the Perfect [Teaching] (*pariniṣpanna*) must necessarily possess these two meanings.

The sutra text is as exquisitely subtle as embroidery in this regard; were it not shown in this manner, it would truly be difficult to unravel. Students of the commentaries should further investigate this.
Examine this in detail.
Regarding the practice and stages of the dhāraṇī, as for the ritual scripture, it says:
"To praise one's ancestors when they have done no good is a falsehood; to fail to recognize their goodness when it exists is [also a fault]."

To know and yet not transmit is a lack of benevolence; how much more so for my ancestor, whose wisdom, conduct, rank, and meritorious dharmas were profound and subtle—how could one fail to abridge them and transmit them?
Since ancient times, none have failed to regard the realization and rank of the Great Master as a point of doubt and difficulty;
this is because the Great Master’s conduct and rank possess both the fundamental and the manifest, and his fundamental nature is indeed equal [to that of the Buddhas].
Miaoxiang was a man who assessed others by their outward manifestations; setting aside his fundamental nature to discuss his traces, according to the *Biézhuàn* (Separate Biography), he said:
"If I were not to lead a retinue, I would surely purify the six sense organs for the sake of others at the cost of my own self, yet this would only be the level of the five ranks (*wǔpǐn*).

Nevertheless, as for the Dharma-gates realized, I have already attained *dhāraṇī*. Furthermore, the stage of *dhāraṇī* corresponds to the ten stages of faith (*shìxìn*)... If one considers that he had indeed attained *dhāraṇī*, [then...]
If the *dhāraṇī* is taken as the definitive reality, then the five grades should not be so; if the five grades are taken as the correct standard, then the *dhāraṇī* would be rendered confused.
To settle these two points: if we examine the traces of the teaching, the five grades should be taken as definitive.
As for what is realized, Jingxi and Siming were indeed concerned about this doubt and have already provided a thorough resolution to it, yet people [still harbor it].
The reason this was not yet perfected was that [the previous commentator] instead took other texts and established divergent interpretations as his explanation.
Now, by strictly adhering to the writings of the Two Patriarchs to expound their intent, the text says: "Since we now cite one out of the three [stages], it is called 'one.
Although [this stage] is generally explained in relation to the six sense organs and the seven levels of faith, when specifically clarified, it actually resides in..."

From the "Initial Mind" up to the passage "This, then, is the Great Master’s already realized [attainment]" (this being the subtle text explaining the stages), Siming immediately stated that although the three *dhāraṇīs* apply to both the beginning and the end, they are most clearly manifested at the stage of semblance (*sādṛśa-bhūmi*).

Although the text does not explicitly clarify the Great Master’s stage of practice, it would likewise be impossible to say that this is not a description of what he had already realized. However, as for the textual characteristics...

The meaning [of these categories] is obscured or difficult to perceive; I shall now explain it by means of two senses: namely, horizontal (transverse) and vertical, as well as universal and particular.

The text speaks directly only of the "vertical," yet the vertical must be contrasted with the horizontal. Furthermore, it speaks only of the "universal," yet the universal must be contrasted with the particular.

These terms appear alternately in the text, the underlying intent being that when discussed horizontally, there are three types within each stage (*bhūmi*), whereas when discussed vertically, they relate to the sequence of stages. Thus, the sense of "universal" applies throughout.
Regarding the distinct meanings of the beginning and end, their correspondence is as usual (etc.). Otherwise, how could there be a gateway of meaning that penetrates vertically?
Thus, when the Great Master states that one attains *dhāraṇī* at the stage of the five ranks (*pañca-varga*), this is precisely the penetration within the vertical progression.

By reconciling the text with its meaning, this can be understood. Nevertheless, one must further investigate the reasons for the distinction between the universal (*sāmānya*) and the particular (*viśeṣa*). Now, by means of...

Master Yì commented on this, saying: "In terms of the essence of contemplation (*guan*), they are identical and thus 'general' (*tong*); in terms of their positions and characteristics, they are distinct and thus 'specific' (*bie*).

As for the identity of the essence of contemplation, the *Shiqian* states: 'These three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* are the single mind of the three contemplations, which sustains all dharmas and functions as the universal retention (*dhāraṇī*), as it is said:
"One emptiness is all emptiness," and so forth. Furthermore, the *Yili* states: 'The five grades [of the ten faiths] are themselves contemplation.'"
The three contemplations practiced in the six sense organs are similar to the three contemplations from the first *bhūmi* (stage) onward, which constitute partial realization.
If one were to differentiate them, their names would indeed differ; however, in reality, they are one and the same.

It is precisely because they are manifested according to their respective stages that what the Fourth Patriarch [Zhiyi] called the "semblance stage" (*sī-wei*) attains its most manifest characteristics—namely, by means of the stage of the ten faiths (*shí-xìn*), one cuts off the afflictions of views and thought (*jiàn-sī*).

Because its meaning is thus revealed, this treatise, when advanced, does not contradict the general course of the scriptural teachings, and when receded from, it does not lose what the Great Master realized;
this is what constitutes the correct exposition. As for all other textual passages that have already been successfully explained by former commentators, I shall not further examine them here.
On the Method for Bestowing Peace of Mind:
In studying the Way of the Buddha, there is nothing else to seek but peace of mind. Now, why is the mind peaceful? Why is it not peaceful?
It is said that the source of the mind is fundamentally unmoving; what need is there for it to be "peaceful"? That which is called "peace" is merely a designation for the state when delusion ceases.
When the mind is in flux, it cannot return to its original nature; it must first be made tranquil before the nature can be restored.

If one asks how the mind comes to move: the mind has never actually moved. It is because a single thought suddenly becomes deluded and fails to realize that self and objects are equally one nature that movement occurs.
Thereupon, subject and object manifest, internal and external are established, and the boundaries of the phenomenal world take shape.
Once objects have arisen, the mind has something with which to respond; once the mind has come into being, it is susceptible to being enticed by objects.
Thus, the mind begins to follow along with circumstances, becoming attached to them. Objects are manifold, and the mind likewise becomes manifold.
The mind must have its affairs, and when these affairs are established, karma arises; when karma arises, retribution ensues. This is why the nine realms and the three paths are so chaotic.
Those who debate without ceasing all originate from the movement of a single mind;
this eventually leads to rigidity and immersion, flowing on until one forgets their original source, reaching a point where it is difficult to pull them back. Is there truly no way to save them?
The Buddhas and Patriarchs, in transmitting the world, must surely have had a method. This is why the Dharma for settling the mind was bestowed; however, as for that Dharma—

There is no bestowing in vain; according to the capacity of the vessel, what is appropriate varies, and thus there are distinctions of degree. For those of the highest caliber, there is no mind that can be settled and no dharma that can be bestowed;
this is called "settling the mind. Thus, when Subhūti asked the Buddha, "How should one dwell? How should one subdue the mind?
the Buddha directly told him, "One should dwell in non-abiding. When the Second Patriarch sought the settling of his mind from Bodhidharma, [the Master] said:
Mo said, "Bring forth your mind so that I may settle it for you. This is the settling of that which has no need to be settled;
it is called true settling. It is not a bestowal of something bestowed; it is the ultimate bestowal. There is no essential point for settling the mind more fundamental than this.

However, those who have attained the highest level do not always exist, and therefore this method is firmly established here. Next, there is the mind that can be settled, and there is also the method that can be bestowed.

According to our school’s teaching, one uses the threefold contemplation of the single mind to contemplate a single thought-moment, such that it cannot be apprehended as empty, nor as provisional, nor as the Middle.
When there is not a single external phenomenon that meets the mind, and internally the single mind is fused and dissolved, one rests in the principle of the Truths;
only then has one reached this state of settling the mind through contemplation of principle. Alternatively, some use the four...
By investigating the nature of a single thought as it arises, one realizes that it cannot arise from itself, nor from another, nor from both, nor without a cause.
Since it is ultimately impossible to apprehend its origin, one rests in the wisdom of emptiness;

this is the method of settling the mind through the contemplation of phenomena. Furthermore, in the *Mohe zhiguan*, the mind is skillfully settled through wondrous concentration and wondrous wisdom, following [the teachings].
Regarding their essential principles, there are sixty-four distinct methods of *anjin* (settling the mind), as seen in the *Genku*, the *Jijū*, and the *Kanhōkanmon*.
Furthermore, the *Anshin-hō* (Methods for Settling the Mind) contained therein may also be practiced; these are all methods for settling the mind revealed by Tiantai for practitioners.
Whether transmitted as oral instructions (*kubetsu*) or presented as the essentials of the mind (*shinkyō*), they are all methods for settling the mind. Thus, Tian... [text ends]
The gate of the terrace-pavilion represents reaching the state of no-mind through the mind;

although one may occupy its center, it does not exclude the upper or lower levels—this is why it is said to be fully complete. Furthermore, as for those who still possess a mind, the mind is not easily at peace;
one must forcibly establish regulations and strictly institute laws before the mind can be stilled. This takes the stilling of the mind as peace, yet it is not true peace.
As for "peace" (*an*), although there are those who cultivate it without ceasing, such practice is considered inferior.

Nevertheless, even among these various gradations, if one employs them skillfully, they are all sufficient to bring peace to the mind, still the delusions, and reach the fundamental source. This is what is meant in the *Xuanwen* (Mysterious Text) by the statement:

"Dhyāna is also like this; if one receives the method for settling the mind and practices according to the teaching, one will immediately attain the arousal of meditative concentration. How could this be otherwise?
Is that which is called Chan today merely a matter of lofty words devoid of substantial meaning? If this is so, then the Chan of today is not the Chan of antiquity.
Those who spoke of Chan in ancient times were still able to rely on words to embody the Way, practicing according to what was taught;
those who speak of Chan today are not like this—their practice of Chan is grandiose, eccentric, and bizarre.
The traps of words and phrases move in numbers of thousands and hundreds, such that one knows not where to turn; it is truly difficult to speak of.
This is because the Chan of antiquity was pure, whereas the Chan of today is often nothing but deception. If the Chan of antiquity were applied to people of today, it would surely have no effect;
if the Chan of today were applied to people of antiquity, it would likewise be of no benefit. Thus, what is appropriate for today must be suited to the present.
The Chan of antiquity was suitable for antiquity; as for the Chan of the present, it is without distinction of ancient or modern. It is man who finds it suitable. Alas!
How can one find an ancient person with whom to deliberate upon the Chan of antiquity?

The disciples Sanzang and Erzi were about to perform an act of *sāṃmā* (translated as "repentance" or "confession of faults"), for which they used what was called "the pervasive nature of incense and flowers" as their request. I said:
"This teaching regarding the pervasive nature of incense and flowers lies in the application of the mind, not in external objects; it lies in attaining the essential meaning."
It does not reside in language; do you wish to seek its essence through the language of phenomena?

Nevertheless, the teaching that the Way is difficult to comprehend is deeply related to the fundamental tenets of the Perfect School (*Yuanzong*), as well as its principles regarding mind, objects, and reality.
Therefore, it must be understood. Because of this, I shall speak of it. Furthermore, since ancient times, it has been taught that phenomena are partial while principle is all-pervasive. Moreover—
To discuss the vast by means of the narrow is merely to speak from the perspective of objective phenomena; how could it be the essential method for applying the mind and directing contemplation?
Nevertheless, please first present that former explanation, and I shall subsequently point directly to the meaning of our present view.
Furthermore, those who discussed this in the past all said: "A single fragrance or a single flower can pervade the entire Dharma-realm. Is this a matter of phenomena (*vastu*)?
If one speaks of principle (*li*), then since principle is fundamentally pervasive, why would it require phenomena (*shi*)? If one speaks of phenomena, how could objects possibly be pervasive?

Someone says: "Phenomena are pervasive. If so, by what means are phenomena pervasive? It is said: "Because principle reaches its ultimate limit, phenomena are integrated. This refers to the phrase from the *Fuxing* (Supplementary Commentary): "Principle reaching its ultimate limit, phenomena are pervasive.
Someone else says: "Principle is pervasive. If so, why does principle rely upon phenomena? It is said: [Because phenomena manifest that which principle contains.]
Principle has no fixed location, as it is omnipresent within phenomena; thus it is said that "only because principle is fully present can there be the functional utility of phenomena.
At its ultimate limit, it is said that "phenomena and principle are fully present in a single thought-moment. Although there are various other such explanations, they do not exceed this.

Though all of these possess both textual authority and logical meaning, the moment one speaks of the pervasiveness of phenomena or the pervasiveness of principle, one has already fallen into their conceptual trap.

How much more so when mind and objects have no mutual interaction at all? Even if one speaks in terms of phenomena (*dharma*) and principle (*li*), it is not appropriate to follow the explanations traditionally held.
Why is this? For both "pervasive" and "non-pervasive" are matters of phenomena; as for principle, there is neither pervasion nor non-pervasion.
One may only speak of that which is pervasive because it is identical to principle. If one were to directly contrast phenomena with principle and claim that principle is pervasive while phenomena—

As for that which is not all-pervasive, this again treats principle (*li*) and phenomena (*shi*) as two distinct things. If one says that principle is fundamentally all-pervasive, then how could phenomena not be so?
This is like saying that the world’s dependently arisen phenomena are also fundamentally unarisen.
Previously, it was also discussed that the broad and vast is itself the narrow and pervasive; some have said that the broad and vast is principle, while the narrow is phenomena. This—
This is certainly not so. Some say that if both "pervasiveness" (*biàn*) and "limitedness" (*guǎngxiá*) are both phenomena (*shì*), then this principle (*lǐ*) might be acceptable;
yet others say it is not acceptable to have both pervasiveness and limitedness as phenomena, but rather that pervasiveness itself constitutes the principle.

Now, when we say that pervasiveness has both broad and narrow aspects, we are speaking strictly in terms of phenomena; it is impossible to speak of breadth or narrowness regarding the principle, for the principle is not something subject to numerical quantity.
To indicate pervasiveness across all phenomena is called "broad"; to indicate pervasiveness within a single phenomenon is called "narrow.
Yet, when speaking in terms of pervasiveness itself, there is no distinction between broad and narrow. These are all explanations based on the commentaries of former scholars;

however, according to my own direct interpretation, this is not so. In essence, whether it be the pervasiveness of phenomena or the pervasiveness of principle—whether broad or narrow—all are the Dharma.

If it is already so, what is there to discuss? Even if you were to argue until the very end—until matters are perfectly resolved and principles are fully realized—it remains simply that the incense and flowers are fragrant by themselves, and my mind is itself.
If you wish to teach others to be all-pervasive, you have not yet seen this in a dream.
You must believe that pervasiveness and non-pervasiveness do not concern him at all; the principle does not even reside within the incense and flowers.
It is permissible to use these few scattered petals as a pretext for their manifestation; it is like a dragon sending down rain when it obtains water.
How could one seek the pervasiveness [of the rain] within a single drop? If you can see it here, you will recognize that the substance of the incense and flowers is pervasive wherever they are;
this has already been explained all at once. Nevertheless, for those who have not yet understood, it must be further expounded for them.
Pointing to this pervasive state is the beginning of what must be understood: the pervasive state resides solely within the substance of one's own mind.
If the substance of the mind is pervasive, then as for the six sense-objects and all phenomena imagined by the mind, not even a single hair’s breadth will be moved;
they will naturally accord with the nature (dharmatā) and be completely and universally pervasive without requiring any exertion. Just so, when has this mind ever not been pervasive? If you say...

If it were only now that this [mind] has become all-pervasive, then it would be something that was originally non-existent and now exists; how could such a thing be called "actionless practice in accordance with the nature"?
It is simply because, from the outset, one did not realize that this mind-nature is fundamentally omnipresent and perfect, and was instead turned by external objects.
Once fallen into the realm of dust, it immediately became limited and obstructed. Now, one must merely remove those previously existing limitations and obstructions, leaving nothing behind.
If this mind and its objects become like the great void, they will naturally return to their original state of universal pervasiveness;

one can then, in accordance with this vast and divine merit, perform wondrous Buddha-works. One sees that the entire mind is the Dharma and the entire Dharma is the mind, such that there is no longer a subject of thought nor an object of thought, and no longer a subject of pervasion nor an object of pervasion;
thus, the mind and its objects naturally become one as suchness. If indeed...
One cannot say that these phenomena are not pervasive; yet, even in principle, when have they ever been pervasive? Have you not heard the established analogy which says:
"How could all dharmas ever claim to be identical or different? One should know that everything arises from mental discrimination.

Applying this analogy, how could all dharmas ever claim to be phenomena or principles? Who is broad and who is narrow? Who is pervasive and who is not? It is likewise only [a matter of conceptualization].
All things arise merely from the mind’s conceptualization; how much more so this [Dharmadhātu], which is not reached by conceptualization?
For conceptualization is itself emotional ideation (*saṃjñā*). As long as even a single thought of emotional ideation remains unexhausted, one cannot be all-pervasive.
One must simply be like that which is described in the *Śraddhotpāda-śāstra*—free from thought and ideation—equal to the realm of empty space, pervading everywhere throughout the Dharmadhātu.
The marks themselves are the Tathāgata’s equal Dharma-body and mind; it is only when one accords with this principle that one attains it.
Although it is difficult for a beginner practitioner to reach this mind directly, one must not allow such difficulty to cause despondency, thinking, "I am a beginner and an ordinary person;
how could I possibly reach such a profound and wondrous state? As it is said:
This is precisely to create obstacles for oneself. Furthermore, have you not heard the Patriarch’s words: "The disciple studies as an ordinary person; the master studies as a sage"?
If one studies as a sage, it is further said that a beginner takes the supreme *sambhogakāya* (寂光) as the essence of contemplation.
How could this not be called the study of the Perfect and Sudden Mind-Only? Yet, regarding this principle, you instead give rise to regression.
One must necessarily hear what is profound without fear, hear what is vast without doubt, and when hearing that which is neither profound nor vast, possess courage in one's mind.
Based on the Perfect and Sudden Teaching, one must give rise to the perfect mind; only when one’s realization directly accords with this principle does one attain it.
Furthermore, this cannot be taken lightly. If you do not penetrate this principle, how can you speak of the single-mindedness of phenomena and principle? It is simply this.

If "contemplating reality with a single mind" does not refer to this very essence of mind, then since it cannot be "contemplating phenomena and principle with a single mind," how can you say that all things are like flames and illusions, being inconceivable? I bow my head to this non-attached mind.

If it is indeed the case that flames and illusions are inconceivable, does this not refer to this very essence of mind? Since it cannot be "inconceivable like flames and illusions," it is likewise so.
Why do you say that the nature of the one who prostrates and the object of prostration is empty and quiescent, and that their mutual resonance is inconceivable?
If this mutual resonance is indeed such, is it not precisely this mind that performs the prostration?

Since you do not understand this mutual resonance, how can you speak of the "three karmas" having a nature like space? If the nature of the three karmas is indeed empty, is it not precisely this body of the mind?

Since you do not understand that the nature of the three karmas is empty, how can you speak of reciting the transgressions of the six sense organs while maintaining the three types of repentance in mind?
If it is truly the repentance of the principle of non-arising (*wusheng lichan*), how could there be anything to maintain? Is this not precisely the substance of the mind?
Since you do not understand the repentance of the principle of non-arising, how can you say that when walking, every step leaves no trace, and when chanting, every sound is [pure]?
"Cutting off hearing is just like cutting off traces. Is that which cuts off hearing not this very essence of mind?
Since it does not even know how to cut off traces or hearing, how can one speak of the two kinds of emptiness—of phenomena and of persons—or of the wisdom of the contemplation of non-arising?

Is not the wisdom of the contemplation of non-arising itself this very essence of mind? Even if one were to further apply such analogies and explanations, they could never exhaust the matter; let us stop here.
Nevertheless, although the substance of incense and flowers pervades all things, a single principle runs through them;

thus, from the initial practice of "universal respect" (*sarva-gaurava*) to the final stage of "seated meditation and contemplative wisdom," none of these ten categories of ritual conduct fail to embody this very principle. If one realizes it, it is omnipresent;
if one does not realize it, one is entirely deluded. Furthermore, if one can extend this realization by analogy to other categories, it will not be limited merely to incense and flowers.

This is the teaching on the pervasiveness of the substance. Nevertheless, if someone were suddenly to ask, "Does this incense and flower pervade by way of its substance, its principle, or its phenomena?
one should simply say to them: "May this incense and flower pervade the ten directions... and so forth.
A Brief Explanation of the Preface by Pumenzi to the *Fuxing*:

In general, when reading texts, one must observe the author’s primary intent. Since this work is a preface to the *Fuxing*, the entire preface is dedicated to explaining the composition of the text itself.
Therefore, the opening line states: "Those who take emptiness and non-being as their principle are following the way of name-and-teaching (*mingjiao*)."

Those who have discarded and neglected written texts have deviated from the true meaning of composition; for while the preceding words were intended to express a partial preference, they served as a foundation for subsequent compositions.
Thus, it was said that those who take "emptiness and non-being" (xūwú) as their principle do not fundamentally constitute correct practice.

Laozi and Zhuangzi merely spoke of how scholars of later generations who venerate Laozi and Zhuangzi, upon seeing that [the latter] "smashed benevolence and righteousness" and "extinguished ritual and music," [came to hold such views].

This view maintains that the Way of the name-teachings of the Duke of Zhou and Confucius can be discarded; yet it fails to realize that Laozi and Zhuangzi certainly did not merely intend to "brandish clubs to destroy" them.
For now, I shall broadly cite parallel couplets to serve as an inspiration for instruction.

Some might claim that this passage disparages other schools, but that is incorrect; how could one ever disparage the fundamental principles of a work’s composition by never having spoken of them at all?
To reject [the use of] words out of fear that it might not be the author’s intent, or because it is simply not the proper literary style, is incorrect.

Now, to offer a rectification regarding those who leave behind written words: this is not a direct refutation of the Chan school. Rather, it is a general statement concerning those of later generations who have lost the essential meaning;
seeing that the Chan school maintains the doctrine of a "separate transmission outside the teachings," they claim that written words are [superfluous].

To leave behind [the teachings] while contradicting the principles of composition, and yet remain ignorant of the purport of the *biéchuán* (separate transmission), is this truly what it means to "leave behind words"?
If one adheres to the old interpretations, it would be like speaking to a fool who is incapable of understanding even a dream.

For one who wishes to rectify the foundation of the teaching, it must begin with our Buddha, the Sage, appearing in the world to establish the doctrine; thus it is said that the "Ancient Primal Brahma Kings" and others were all Buddhas. It is known, therefore, that the Buddha...

Throughout the ages, whenever the Buddha appeared to respond to the capacities of beings and after his parinirvāṇa, the subsequent councils have invariably taken the verbal teachings and written texts as their foundation.

How much more so in this final age, when faculties are dull and those who can intuitively comprehend the essence are rare; thus, the composition and preservation of written texts must especially not be abandoned.

If they were abandoned, one would merely remain mired in ignorance, content with one's own delusion; though one might wish to discuss the mind, one would be lost regarding the traces of the teachings, ultimately having nowhere to turn for guidance.

This is all there is; therefore it is said that the ultimate has its limit. Is it thus? To sit in silence throughout one’s entire life—this is precisely what was meant by the aforementioned "missing the essential point.
One must simply understand what is gained and what is lost; there is no necessity to name specific individuals.
For those who insist on forcibly naming them do nothing but provide a pretext for dispute, which is of no use now. Why not instead allow people to hear this and reflect upon it for themselves?

Is this not a transformation? Generally speaking, to desire to clarify the Way through one's own views while the eye of wisdom has not yet opened is like someone who, having not yet ascended to the steps, feels an elephant and each describes its color—whether it be white or black.
Is this not too premature a calculation? The two metaphors of feeling the elephant and the color of its milk appear together in the Great Sūtra (etc.).
Therefore, there is what is called "the mind itself is Buddha" as a gateway for awakening and entry; form is not... [text ends].

Regarding the distinction between the beginning and end of emptiness (wherein the beginning is emptiness and the end is form), whose traces are these doctrines? They are intended to lead one to merge with that which transcends all relativity;

what further use, then, are there for words and phrases? Such is the speech of those who are biased. Yet, it is also a scriptural statement that "the mind is Buddha" and "form is not different from emptiness.
Why, then, do you now reject these as being incorrect? I say: there is indeed no error in the scriptural statements; the error lies elsewhere.

If you hold to this [view] merely to discard written words, yet you already know that the mind itself is the Buddha, then since written words are surely not separate from the mind, why must they be discarded?
If one truly realizes that form is no different from emptiness, then written words—being form—are themselves no different from emptiness.

To discard the words is to discard emptiness; how could emptiness be something to be discarded? Examining it in this light, such a position joins with the scriptural teachings to form a perverse error.
Is it not the case that such divergent views arise because the Great Teaching has declined? Furthermore, they stem from being deluded regarding the identity and separation of words and letters.
Thus it is said: "Because one has not yet discerned that the nature of words and letters is itself the nature of liberation, and the nature of liberation is itself the nature of words and letters;
when both are seen as beyond separation, then words and letters are themselves the Way, and since even words and letters cannot be apprehended, how much less [could there be anything else]?"
Is there any reason to discard written words? For those whose mastery of *dhāraṇī* is profound, written words manifest the power of that *dhāraṇī*;
since one can attain the ultimate principle through the teachings, how could they be discarded? Thus, it is clear that the composition of written words must certainly not be abandoned;
this is why the doctrinal tradition of this school begins with Zhiyi and has been transmitted from master to disciple through successive generations.
There are extensive records and successive commentaries; as for the writings of Jingxi (Zhanran) on this record, the production of such texts may truly be called flourishing.
Thus it is said: "In the past, the works of the Worthy One (Zhizhe) comprised only ten fascicles.

That he extensively propagated his profound virtue (*xuan-de*) and greatly rescued those swept away by the overflowing torrent refers to how the Great Master manifested in the world and widely disseminated this profound virtue, as briefly described in the *Xuanyan* (Profound Words).
By virtue of these ten merits, he was able to refute the various masters of the "Three Souths" and "Seven Norths," bringing them all back to the orthodox path.
This is like the excellence of Yu’s regulation of the waters, which enabled the surging and overflowing currents to find their proper course and flow toward the sea; his achievement was truly great.
It is what Han Yu meant when he said: "He dammed the hundred rivers and directed them eastward, turning back the wild waves after they had already collapsed."
Therefore it is said: "I consult [you] regarding the overturning of the single basket of earth.

This "overturning of the single basket of earth" is a metaphor for beginning by seeking the Way at Mount Nanyue and ultimately succeeding in reviving the fundamental principle of the One Nature that had already fallen into ruin and severed its moorings; thus it is used as a metaphor for what has already collapsed.
Indeed, the Way of the Western Sage was revitalized by Nāgārjuna and then severed by Siṃha, but the Great Master revived and raised it once again; hence these words.
The source of our school’s fundamental tenets does not exceed these four propositions; thus it is said that [this work] "commands the lineage" and "establishes the ancient.
To take the *Madhyamaka-śāstra* as the master of the school is the method of contemplation one inherits; to take the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* as the ultimate goal is the dharma one realizes.
The way in which this single school is transmitted and maintained is entirely contained therein; it may truly be called grasping the essential point of the teaching.
Regarding Master Wei Gong’s prior cultivation of roots of virtue, tradition holds that he was the reincarnation of Xu Ling, who once made five vows at Mount Tiantai;
that he is now the grandson of a different generation is indeed not a departure from his original resolve.

As for the saying "to focus on the explanation of the teachings, how could one have leisure to worry about my own literary style," during the interval between the two Weis, the teachings were merely kept sealed and transmitted; their Way did not flourish until it was first widely propagated by Zuoxi.
Although I wished to compose a record to expound this text, I have not yet had the leisure; how could I claim such leisure? Therefore, I shall once again propagate it at Bítán.
"Propagate" (bǎngyáng) means to spread abroad; "Bítán" is named after its location, signifying that the author of the record may dwell there to propagate and compose his writings.
Lèozhōu (Zuoxī) also knew of my intent, as he once remarked that the two gates of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* are equal.
The Master of the Commentary himself once spoke thus, sighing that this record must not fail to be transmitted.

As for its unification of myriad practices, the Way of Stopping and Contemplation (*śamatha-vipaśyanā*) is vast; as for its penetration of the single principle, the merit of the Perfect and Sudden (*yuan-dun*) is profound.
Although the Dharma-gate is such as this, the text may contain errors of corruption, discrepancies, or heterodox doubts interspersed therein. Now...
The ancient explanations are not uniform; thus, they must be distinguished, corrected, and further elucidated.

This is why the Master of the Record meticulously analyzed and reflected upon them, intending to guide the profound current so that the Way of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* would not be obstructed for future generations—this is the intent of this *Shuji*.
Its substance is plain yet not vulgar; such descriptions of its literary style show it has attained its proper place in elegance. Broad.

The purport of this "Abridged" [text] is not merely that of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*; rather, when it is said that the sūtras and śāstras have both extensive and abridged versions, it refers to their being intended for those of sharp and dull faculties.
This present text is likewise so, because "superior" and "inferior" correspond to "sharp" and "dull. As for the phrase "how could it be only...
and so forth, this further states that the composition of this record serves as an aid for understanding and practice, as well as the underlying purpose for its title.
"Intertwining" (*cuòzōng*) means to synthesize and unify what has been taught; "encompassing" (*yìnguò*) means to organize and systematize its phenomenal characteristics (*xingxiāng*).

Because it encompasses and organizes its phenomenal characteristics, the wondrous operation of the "Three Multiplicities" (*sānduō*) suddenly ascends—that is, it swiftly reaches the Precious Abode (*bǎosuǒ*).

Because it synthesizes and unifies what has been taught, the profound insight of the "One Vehicle" (*yīshèng*) is "tun"—meaning it accords perfectly. (The character for "tun" should be written with the "moon" radical.)

Regarding the meaning of "threefold many" (*trimukha-bahula*), interpretations vary. Some explain it based on scriptural passages from the *Prajñāpāramitā*, stating that one should extensively make offerings to the Buddhas, extensively serve virtuous friends, and extensively inquire about the essentials of the Dharma at the sites of many Buddhas.
Others take the integration of the three modes of practice (*trividha-yoga*) as the Great Vehicle to constitute the "threefold many.
Still others take the three contemplations (*trividha-vipaśyanā*) and so forth as the "threefold many," asserting that these all encompass a multitude of dharmas.

In this regard, one may obtain either the text or the meaning; the choice lies with the individual. Alternatively, there are distinct names and characteristics from which [the meaning] emerges, awaiting those of broad learning (and so forth).
Thus, the intent behind the title does not go beyond "understanding" (*jie*) and "practice" (*xing*);

it is shown through the metaphors of "crossroads" and "directions," which may be called an excellent analogy. In essence, understanding is like a single eye: when looking out from it, there is no fixed direction.

The divergent practices at the various corners are like traveling a thousand *li*: there is no lack of distinctions between different paths, and from beginning to end, they are separated by heaven and earth; their words and deeds are consistently at odds. Their depth and shallowness vary according to their kind, and their speech and understanding likewise differ. This is based on the preliminary discussion of those who, in a general sense, speak of establishing the *jian* (commentary) and the *fuxing* (auxiliary practice) to encompass the whole. This means that "auxiliary" (*fu*) must necessarily possess both the "able" (*neng*) and the "object" (*suo*). That is to say: [...]* *Note: The original text contains a lacuna indicated by ellipses.* Furthermore, the *jian* and *fuxing* are not separate entities. The *jian* is precisely the *fuxing*, and the *fuxing* is precisely the *jian*. Why? Because the *jian* is the principle of the Dharma-realm, while the *fuxing* is the practice of the Dharma-realm. Since the principle and the practice are non-dual, how could the *jian* and the *fuxing* be distinct? Therefore, it is said: "The *jian* is the *fuxing*; the *fuxing* is the *jian*. It is also said: "The *jian* is the *fuxing*; the *fuxing* is the *jian*. This is because the *jian* is the principle of the Dharma-realm, and the *fuxing* is the practice of the Dharma-realm. Since the teaching serves as that which assists and practice is that which is assisted, designating them with these two terms allows for the simultaneous presentation of the entirety of both understanding (*prajñā*) and practice (*caryā*).
As for the understanding and practice of the Perfect and Sudden [Vehicle], they have never been divided; when practice is integrated with understanding, then practice is likewise without distinction.
When practice is verified by understanding, then understanding is also characterized by degrees of depth. Although understanding may vary in its depth, from beginning to end it remains non-dual.
This is why both the practice and the understanding of this Perfect and Sudden [teaching] are so sublime. Thus, from afar he came down here;

these words record that the Master transmitted and propagated the Way of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* throughout the world. Consequently, those who studied under him gained great benefit in great numbers.

This was truly because the Way found its propagation through a worthy person, and thus its movement was not in vain. I, a student of the final age, have humbly ventured to compose this preface for the record.
The time may now be known.

The śramaṇa Zhipan relates:
The Sage of the Tathāgata, who opened up the provisional to reveal the real and manifested the traces to reveal the fundamental, transforming the world and future generations, is called the Buddha.
His disciples, who transmitted the Way in succession to serve as patriarchs for the world, are called the Ancestors. Their...
Because it is truly a single path, when the Tathāgata was about to cease his transformative activity, he entrusted the Unsurpassed Great Dharma to Kāśyapa.
Kāśyapa sustained it for twenty years before entrusting it to Ānanda. Ānanda maintained the Dharma and propagated its teachings for another twenty years before entrusting it to Śāṇakavāsin.
Continuing down through thirteen generations, it reached Nāgārjuna, who was the first to commit it to writing.
The *Prajñā* [literature] sets forth the path of the three contemplations for realizing the ultimate; this is known as the *Madhyamaka-śāstra*.

Upon its translation and transmission to the land of China (Dongxia), the Northern Qi dynasty established it as a method of contemplation based on their own prior awakening and realization, transmitting it to Nanyue.

Nanyue received its essential meaning and, through his awakening to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, purified his six sense faculties, transmitting it to Tiantai. Tiantai was the first to establish the doctrine of the five periods and the eight teachings for its application.

When he brilliantly elucidated the wondrousness of the *Lotus Sūtra*’s revelation and fully expounded the principles of its objective realm (*viṣaya*) and contemplation (*vipaśyanā*), at that time, Zhāng'ān took up his brush to record these as commentaries (*shù*) and treatises (*lùn*).
Thus, the Way became greatly illuminated. In the lineage of the *Lotus Sūtra*’s celestial palace, Jìshì lectured and propagated the teachings;
among those who inherited his Dharma, only Zuǒxī was peerless. Among the disciples of Zuǒxī, only Jīngxī was able to uphold the orthodox tradition, composing various records (*jì*).
In assisting the ancestral wisdom, the dissenting views of the Qingliang school were thereby silenced;
in propagating the primary truth (*paramārtha-satya*) through writing, none could match the flourishing of this era.

For this reason, scholars of the world have taken the lineage from Nāgārjuna down to [Zhiyi] as the Nine Patriarchs to maintain the ancestral sacrifices—this indeed has its justification. From Jingxi [Zhanran] onwards, this Way has been used for transmission.

As for those who transmitted [the teachings], there were Master Sui (Xuansu), who promoted the Way, and Master Xiu, who expounded the Way without ceasing; yet during the many calamities of the Huichang era, the volumes of the teachings were scattered and lost.

Regarding the sublime expositions and lofty discourses of Master Zhengding (Wumen Daoxuan) and Masters Wai, Xu, Song, and Er, the only treatises transmitted through the three generations were those on *śamatha-vipaśyanā* (calm abiding and clear observation).
When the Dharma-fortune was about to flourish at Luoxi (Master Zhili), Heaven granted the Ruyi Kingdom (King Qian Chu of Wuyue) the opportunity to seek out these lost texts from海东 (Haedong, Korea).
Thereupon, the scriptural teachings were restored, and Baoyun succeeded in propagating them for twenty years.
Then, Fazhi of Siming—born as a son of the Buddha and appearing at the edge of the sea—recorded all the teachings and lineages that the masters of Pilin had not previously recorded;
he practiced all four kinds of samādhis, which are difficult for others to perform. These are the words of Ciyun regarding his ultimate realization.
At that time, there were those who propounded divergent views, such as the masters Zhao, Yuan, and others, whom the world of the day designated as "Schools Outside the Mountain" (Shanwai).
Yet Fazhi alone enjoyed the reputation for reviving the teachings and contemplation (*jiaoguan*).

From the rise of Xingdao until Siming, spanning eight generations, it was precisely through these individuals that the orthodox lineage was sustained and the Great Teaching was glorified; this is surely why one should look back to their example and emulate them.
To employ [this tradition] so that they may attend the assembly alongside the nine patriarchs, thereby honoring and exalting their Way— this may indeed be permissible. Thus,
among the monasteries of the present Chan school, wherever the Way of Tiantai and Siming is expounded,

if one could initiate the practice of universally enshrining [the lineage] from Nāgārjuna down to Fanzhi as the seventeen patriarchs and establish them side by side in their respective positions, it would truly demonstrate a profound insight into the reverence of later students.
The Ancestor’s heart reveres the Way; this is respectfully deliberated.
The Discussion on Honoring the Ancestor within the Lineage (concluded).
